# KitePlayer and KiteFFmpeg: a full audit

**Auditor:** Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), working as sixteen reading agents and thirty-nine verifying agents under one coordinator, all the same model.
**Date:** 2026-11-08.
**KitePlayer commit examined:** `d5bb627e0ed35e0b2e3176689fa737a12bad9f94` ("Merge the issue sweep: 95 tracker issues fixed", 2026-11-02, `main`).
**KiteFFmpeg commit examined:** `f79ba0864c8697f91ef5e3509b46b115afc7dcd7` ("docs: describe the current feature graphic in the readme alt text", 2026-10-25, `main`).
**Status of every claim:** unpublished until the owner has checked it. Nothing here has been posted anywhere.

## 1. How this audit was made, and how to read it

### 1.1 Method

The two checkouts were split into sixteen lanes, each small enough for one agent to read its files in full rather than skim them. The lanes were: the engine's actor and open path, its seek, sync and track machinery, its subtitle and output tail, the audio clock and the rings and sinks, the video path and colour, the public API and the documentation, the Kotlin parsers, networking and adaptive streaming, the FFmpeg backend module, the views and Compose layers and the samples, the audio visualiser, the web worker and libass, build and distribution and CI, KiteFFmpeg's C layer and build, KiteFFmpeg's Kotlin binding, and a last lane for design at the scale of the whole system, cross-module knob collisions and the capability matrix.

Each finder was told to attack, not to describe: to trace a suspected defect to the lines that cause it, to look for the guard elsewhere before claiming the guard is missing, to quote the code with file and line, to state a scenario a person could reproduce, and to say how to check the claim. Each finder was given the complete list of open issues in both trackers so that known work would not be raised again, and was told to treat the decisions recorded in both `CLAUDE.md` files as settled unless it had new evidence.

Every finding was then handed, in batches of seven, to a separate verifying agent that had not seen the finder's reasoning beyond the finding itself. The verifier re-read the cited code and was asked to refute. It could confirm, mark plausible (the mechanism is real but it could not reproduce the exact consequence by reading alone), refute, or mark the finding as a duplicate of an open issue. It could also correct the severity, the locations, the claim or the reproduction steps, and where it did the entry below carries both the finder's and the verifier's version.

The numbers: 212 findings were raised, 202 survived (197 confirmed, 5 plausible), 9 were refuted and 1 was a duplicate of an open issue (#393). The refuted ones are listed in Appendix B with the verifier's reason, so they are not raised again without new evidence. The agents spent about 14.6 million tokens and made about 2,080 tool calls, nearly all of them reads and searches.

### 1.2 What was not done

No code was built, no test was run and no device was touched. The only network traffic was three verifiers checking a claim against an upstream source: FFmpeg's `hls.c` at the tag KiteFFmpeg pins, Compose Multiplatform's WebGL render target at the version the project uses, and the state of three issues in the tracker. Every other claim rests on reading. That is why every entry carries a "How to check it yourself" paragraph: the owner is the first person who will run anything. Where a finder could not read a file it said so, and Appendix A lists for every lane exactly what was and was not read. The audio visualiser (60,000 lines) and `PlaybackCore.kt` (17,351 lines) were read in parts, and the coverage statements name the parts.

Claims about mpv, VLC, Media3 and AVPlayer in the capability matrix come from general knowledge of those players, not from measurement, and are kept coarse for that reason.

### 1.3 How an entry is laid out

Each finding has an identifier (`F-001` upward, ordered by severity, then repository, then area), and carries: severity, kind, repository, area, the lane that found it, the verifier's verdict and the finder's own confidence; the file and line ranges; the evidence, quoted from the code; the claim; a concrete scenario; the impact; a suggested fix; how to check it; and the verifier's note. The verifier's note is the most useful paragraph when the claim looks surprising, because it was written by an agent trying to knock the finding down.

Severity means: **high**, a viewer or an integrator will meet it in ordinary use and it is wrong in a way they will notice; **medium**, real and reachable, but on a narrower path or with a smaller consequence; **low**, correct to fix, unlikely to be seen first; **info**, a fact worth recording, a proposal, or a confirmation that a suspected problem is not one.

Kind means: a **defect** is behaviour the code has today that is wrong; **design** is a shape that costs correctness, speed or maintainability without any one line being wrong; **performance** costs time or memory; **public API** is what a consumer meets; **documentation** is prose the tree contradicts; **test gap** is a promise the suite cannot see; **proposal** is a capability or a cheap win, not a defect.

### 1.4 Findings two lanes reached independently

Several pairs were raised by two lanes that could not see each other. They were kept as separate entries on purpose, because two independent readings of one problem are stronger evidence than one, and because each pair's two entries name different lines and different consequences. The pairs are: F-004 and F-060 (the web worker's whole-request timeout); F-021 and F-094 (a release can ship the libass Android natives jar empty); F-019, F-020 and F-162 (Android keep rules for the ServiceLoader providers); F-073 and F-074 (the JNI log forwarder attaching a thread per line, in KiteFFmpeg); F-092 and F-192 (a local libass chain wins over the pinned release); F-126 and F-175 (the renderer contract's "refused frame counts as dropped" against the schedule's "refused is not dropped").

### 1.5 KiteFFmpeg

KiteFFmpeg is an independent project with its own tracker, and nothing in it should need to know about KitePlayer. Its findings are gathered in section 14 and are to be fixed there. Four findings are marked "both": the media library has to change first and the player follows. The rest of this file is about KitePlayer.

## 2. Executive summary

### 2.1 The verdict

The engine is sound where a player is usually unsound. Sixteen agents went looking for the classic failures of a media engine and did not find them: no packet or frame is closed twice or leaked on the common paths; the actor really does own every session mutation from its lanes; every command reply completes exactly once on every path traced; the seek machine's order of operations is right and bounded; every position is a `Long` of microseconds and the only `Double`s are rates applied once; the two audio rings (Kotlin and C11) run the same single-producer single-consumer protocol with the right memory order; the device callback's call set in the C ring is three symbols; the BS.1770 K-weighting coefficients match the Recommendation to 1e-15 and the gating is right; the BT.601, BT.709, BT.2020, FCC, PQ, HLG, BT.2390 and Catmull-Rom constants in every shader match the standards by hand arithmetic; the Teletext Hamming decoder is exact over 20,000 random words; the fMP4 rewrite's edit-list and B-frame rules hold against a two-frame reorder; the worker protocol copies every public field and its test would catch a new one; the libass driver's change detection and premultiplied output are right; and in KiteFFmpeg no memory-safety defect was found in the helper units, the handle table or the JNI adapter on a full read, the patches stay inside FFmpeg's own parser bounds, and the blocking-bridge argument written in `CLAUDE.md` holds exactly as written (F-196 records that as a positive result).

What the audit found instead is that the risk lives at the seams, and the seams have a shape. Where one rule has two halves in two places, one half has been fixed and the other has not. Where an interface member has a default, a capability degrades without a word. Where a lifetime is shared, one failure travels further than it should. Where a platform was retrofitted (Swift, Java, the browser), the headline promise stops at the border. These four shapes account for most of the 202 entries, and they are cheaper to fix as shapes than one entry at a time.

### 2.2 Fix these first

The twelve findings below are the ones that will reach a viewer or an integrator soonest. Each is small to fix.

1. **F-002 (high).** One exception from the app's byte reader cancels the plain `Job` that every HLS segment read shares, so a single 404 or connection reset ends the whole stream instead of skipping the segment. Every https stream on a phone goes through this reader. The tests only ever make the reader return null, never throw, which is why it has not shown. A `SupervisorJob`, or rethrowing without reaching the parent, fixes it.
2. **F-001 (high) with F-034 and F-030.** Once the audio stream has ended before the picture, the ring's last anchor is frozen at the last real sample while the clock free-runs. Pause, rebuffer or reach Ended and the #646 rule pulls the position back to the end of the audio; on resume the picture plays at half speed until the clock catches up. A speed change in the same tail never reaches the picture. A pause inside the last fraction of a second runs both end-of-stream deadlines against a ring that cannot drain and cuts the remaining audio. The fix is one freshness rule in the paused-anchor branch, and F-028 is the missing test.
3. **F-003 and F-004 (high), with F-060.** On the web the worker is one thread, and every byte it reads from http arrives through a synchronous XMLHttpRequest for a window that grows from 1 to 16 MB. During the request nothing else runs, and the page's audio queue is 85 ms deep, so every window fetch is silence and a frozen picture for the transfer time. The 30 s stall budget is applied to the whole request, so a healthy link under about 4.5 Mbit/s fails as `SourceStalled` while bytes are still arriving. The browser tests fetch from localhost and measure the page thread, so they cannot see either.
4. **F-026 (medium).** The actor throws away every worker death whose cause is a `CancellationException`, while `launchWorker` now forwards a stray one as a failure (#589). Only the video lane wraps decoder exceptions in its own type. In the demux, audio decode, audio feed and video schedule lanes a stray cancellation ends the lane silently and the player sits in Buffering with no error, which is the one outcome the actor design exists to prevent.
5. **F-029 (medium).** A handler that throws between `close()` and the Close command executing takes the exceptional branch, which settles the mailbox and rethrows without tearing the session down. Workers, decoders, source and audio device are left running with no owner behind a `RuntimeCompromised` report.
6. **F-027 (medium) with F-035.** Resuming a paused live stream whose transport cannot pause (UDP, RTP, raw TCP) parks all five workers and releases them with no flush. Issue #592 taught the audio decode lane to keep what it held; the video decode lane still closes the frame and packet it holds and the audio feed lane abandons the unwritten rest of its buffer. The one test of this path asserts only position and status.
7. **F-021 and F-094 (medium).** The switch that turns a missing NDK or chain into a failure for the libass Android natives jar is never set by `publish.yml`, and nothing opens the jar after the build. A release can ship it with no `.so` inside and every job stays green. F-019, F-020 and F-162 are the related Android shrinking gap: `kiteplayer-io` ships no keep rules, `kiteplayer-network`'s live inside the AAR's `classes.jar`, and no CI job ever builds a shrunk app that contains them.
8. **F-015 (medium) with F-014.** The memento's text form writes every request header value and the full URI with its query string, and the Android resume card stores that text in plain, backup-eligible `SharedPreferences`. A library that redacts every URI it prints hands bearer tokens and signed URLs to that store without a warning. The same memento promises every setting and drops `MediaItem.growth` and the flash guard.
9. **F-050 (medium) with F-172, F-173, F-181 and F-053.** The capability flags that are supposed to make silent degradation impossible are themselves wrong or absent: the Android surface renderer answers `appliesAdjustments = true` while its MediaCodec path has no colour matrix; `setRenderQuality` and `setHdrPolicy` are no-op defaults on the renderer SPI, so the default Android view and the desktop view ignore them; a backend that leaves `interrupt()` defaulted makes `stallTimeout` a dead knob; asking for debanding silently turns the Catmull-Rom kernel off on both GPU renderers; and no test checks a real renderer's flags against what it draws.
10. **F-061 (medium) with F-055, F-056 and F-057.** The text parsers had a deliberate "every character read a bounded number of times" pass; the byte readers and two text parsers did not. `Webm.retrack` recurses once per nested element with no depth limit, and a stack overflow on Kotlin/Native is not a `Throwable`, so a crafted DASH WebM segment is an iOS crash. `XspfReader` and `LrcParser` are quadratic on a hostile line, and a TTML paragraph with many timed spans is quadratic and uncapped. F-159 records that the fMP4 and WebM readers have no mutation fuzz while every text parser has one.
11. **F-016 and F-013 (medium).** Every config and item data class validates with `require()` and declares no `@Throws`, so a bad value terminates a Swift app rather than throwing, and `KitePlayerJava.create()` hides the one checked exception it can throw. Together with the `Duration` encoding problem already filed as #393, iOS from Swift is today a wrapper the project does not yet ship, not a polish item.
12. **F-036 (medium) with F-037.** The schedule hands a frame to the renderer only once wall time has reached the frame's target, so no renderer can aim at a refresh, and the display interval that every renderer reports is stored in `VideoPlayback.vsyncIntervalNanos` and read by nothing but a test getter. Issue #696 names the judder; this names the mechanism and the dead plumbing. The SPI text and the test both say the interval improves pacing, and it does not.

### 2.3 The shapes behind the findings

**Half-fixed rules.** The overlay withdrawal is written three times with two canvas choices, the cue prune twice, the seek abort cleanup three times verbatim, and the video and audio decode lanes answer a non-flushing park differently (F-033). The #646 anchor rule was added without a freshness check (F-001). The #592 fix reached one lane of two (F-027). The quadratic-entity fix reached `XmlMini` and not `XspfReader` (F-055). The #657 allocation fix reached the visualiser's scan path and not its display path (F-084). The design lane's own example of this shape, a gapless rule written three times, was refuted by its verifier (Appendix B), which is itself a useful data point: the file has fewer divergent copies than it looks like it has, and the ones it has are where the recent bugs were.

**Defaults that degrade silently.** `VideoRenderer` has 20 members and 13 default to a no-op or `false`; `PlayerMediaSource` has about 25 defaulted members. The documentation says the player refuses what it cannot do with a typed error, and for the whole renderer side that is not true today (F-050, F-172, F-173, F-181, F-053, F-058, the HDR and spherical cells of the matrix).

**Shared lifetimes and failure routing.** The HLS lifetime `Job` (F-002), the actor's outcome handler (F-026), the close path's exceptional branch (F-029), the fallback decoder's `isDrained` getter closing the active decoder from the actor (F-041), the player scope that is never cancelled (F-113 and F-109), and the sibling coroutines that write actor-owned fields outside the mailbox (section 5) are all one question: who decides what a failure means, and today the answer is often coroutine parent-child semantics by accident.

**The retrofitted platforms.** The web worker takes no `PlayerConfig`, no memento, no thumbnails and no renderer attach (F-188), carries 120 KB of Ktor it never calls (F-097), reads through a synchronous window (F-003) and never redraws a held picture (F-054). Swift gets raw `Int64` durations and uncaught `require()` (F-016, #393). Java cannot catch the factory's exception or implement `ExternalClock` (F-013, F-079). The Compose path on Android falls to software decoding inside any `Dialog` (F-023), ignores window insets (F-025), and ships unclickable controls on the desktop by default (F-106).

**Soft failures in the release pipeline.** Build plugins log a warning and carry on when a native half cannot be built (F-021, F-094), the size ratchet treats a shrink as a note (F-100), the attestation signs a second local build rather than the uploaded bytes (F-022), the emscripten that builds `kiteass.wasm` is unpinned (F-095), and a sibling checkout's chain wins over the pinned one with no check (F-092, F-192).

**Prose drifting from the tree.** Thirty-one documentation findings. The protocol list, the external-subtitle format list, the cancellation design doc, the audio sink contract, the renderer contract, the worker size, the licensing files, the iOS linker flags and both `CLAUDE.md` files each say something the code no longer does. Each is small; the project's own `CLAUDE.md` names this as its measured failure mode, and the measurement here agrees.

## 3. Design assessment, subsystem by subsystem

**The actor and its lanes.** One coroutine owns all session state, every lane parks at a boundary of its own choosing through a handshake of flags and conflated channels, epochs are stamped at every hop as a second line of defence, and the packet queue, quiesce, seek machine and release ledger each name their failure modes in comments. This is the right design and it is well executed. Its weakness is the exception taxonomy at the edges (F-026, F-029), sibling coroutines on the session dispatcher that bend the "all mutation on the actor" rule (F-113 and F-109), a release that parks the five workers one after another and can spend the whole close budget before cancelling (F-112), and the fact that the production dispatcher shape (`limitedParallelism(1)` over `Default` and `IO`) appears in no test at all (F-122). If one thing were rewritten it would be worker failure reporting: one wrapper type for every lane, applied in `launchWorker`, so the actor never guesses from the exception class whether a lane died on purpose.

**Seek, sync and tracks.** The seek machine is a real state machine with the right order, superseding handled from inside the long waits, and the end of stream is six separate conditions each with a bounded recovery. The time arithmetic is sound throughout. The structural gap is the audio clock as position authority once audio stops flowing (F-001, F-034, F-030), and seeking under a slow or stalled network: the demux lane parks only at its loop top, so a seek issued during a slow segment fetch is refused after two seconds, and a seek pending when the stall timeout fires is dropped while the recovery reopens at the old position (F-032). Every player the project measures itself against aborts the read to honour a seek; fixing it needs a decision about interrupt semantics, because today an interrupted FFmpeg read poisons the source.

**The subtitle and output tail.** Ownership holds everywhere traced; the overlay withdrawal rule is honoured on every retire path; the #563 reopen is careful and covered by seven tests. The weak spots are the pause-refused live resume (F-027), a typeset render job whose "I own the lane" flag is cleared only on normal exit so one cancellation can stop ASS rendering for the rest of the track (F-128), and the null-means-unchanged contract being read against the typesetter's last render rather than against the glass (F-198).

**Audio.** The clock law, the playout timeline and the ring protocol are correct and argued in the code. The channel matrices follow libswresample. The weakest component is the rate converter: 32 taps under a Blackman window give a transition band about a third of Nyquist wide, so the top octave droops and near-Nyquist aliases are rejected by only 12 to 46 dB while the documentation claims a deep stopband (F-082); more taps or a Kaiser window fixes it for a few million multiply-adds a second. The platform sinks carry the remaining risk: the Android `AudioTrack` is opened at the platform minimum buffer and its own underruns are never read (F-049), the desktop sink packs to 16 bits without dither (F-169), the equaliser runs recursive float filters with no denormal protection (F-114), and the Kotlin ring's anchor reader spins without bound where the C ring gives up (F-123).

**Video and colour.** Every constant checked matches the standard; frame ownership is sound; the flash guard reaches every renderer that holds pixels; the premultiplied alpha contract holds end to end. The structural weakness is frame pacing (F-036, F-037), and HDR at the edges: a PQ or HLG stream that declares only its transfer is tone mapped as BT.709 because KiteFFmpeg fills undeclared primaries from the picture height without looking at the transfer (F-062, marked both), and the Apple picture-in-picture layer flips the whole picture between HDR pass-through and tone-mapped SDR at every cue edge (F-051). The AWT renderer allocates a full-frame image per presented frame (F-052), the web canvas never redraws a held picture (F-054), and debanding silently disables the kernel (F-053).

**Public API and documentation.** The split between conflating state flows and lossy events, the typed error hierarchy with redacting `toString`, validate-at-construction and the no-replay event flow with a lossless twin are coherent and match the code where traced. The API was written for Kotlin on the JVM and retrofitted for everyone else (F-013, F-016, F-079, #393). The memento stores secrets in plain text on Android (F-015). Thirty-one documentation entries are the measurement of drift.

**Parsers.** The byte readers bound every length against the buffer before they allocate, the fMP4 rewrite arithmetic is right, the Teletext and CEA-708 tables are right, and the text parsers had a bounded-reads pass with a cost test behind it. Robustness is uneven: `Webm.retrack` recursion (F-061), `XspfReader` and `LrcParser` quadratic scans (F-055, F-056), TTML span splitting (F-057), a handful of unguarded index reads on short boxes and records (F-157), and no mutation fuzz for the byte readers (F-159). TTML also drops a paragraph with a begin and no end where the spec gives it an indefinite end (F-178), and one unreadable time expression discards every cue of the document (F-179).

**Networking and adaptive streaming.** The adaptive module really has no HTTP in it, the Ktor reader is thin with explicit timeouts and a measured rate, the segment store is careful (digest names, temp file plus rename, lock file, holders never evicted) and its coherence cases are proven on a real server. The seam with FFmpeg's HLS demuxer is where the problems are: a byte-range segment costs two requests, the first from byte 0 (F-164); an empty or xlink Period refuses the whole manifest with a message that blames the container (F-047); the ABR rate is measured mostly on the first megabyte with the connection time folded in, so step-ups starve on high-latency links (F-046). One high-severity claim from this lane, that `hls.c`'s persistent-connection path leaks a reader per segment through the trust_io_open patch, was refuted by its verifier (Appendix B); the owner should still read that entry, because the verifier's reasoning depends on one branch of `hls.c`.

**The FFmpeg backend.** One class owns the container, every timestamp crosses one mapper once, and the hardware fallback never shows a frame twice. The thread model has two seams: the shared lifetime `Job` (F-002) and `isDrained` read from the actor with a side effect (F-041). A variant switch reads playlists over the network while holding the lock the demux thread needs (F-042), and AES-128 fMP4 streams with two or more variants are read whole and decrypted in Kotlin on the demux thread (F-147).

**Views, Compose and samples.** One attach state machine drives three native views and one controls model drives three control sets; the Compose canvas path keeps every per-frame read inside the draw phase. The seam between a Compose consumer and a native-view consumer is where it degrades: picture-in-picture rotation reaches only the native view (F-058), the Android canvas path binds its GPU tier to the Activity window so a `Dialog` gets software decoding (F-023), the controls ignore insets (F-025), the controls overload defaults to the one desktop path where controls cannot be clicked (F-106), and one television-remote path crashes the composition (F-024).

**The audio visualiser.** The analysis core matches its documents down to recomputed constants, ownership between the audio and drawing threads is clean, and the two safety tests really iterate the whole catalogue. The render harness runs on Skiko and the Android path is a different machine: three shader presets draw nothing for the whole of a Drop transition on Android (F-018), and the Android post-process rebuilds native objects every frame (F-086, F-087). The flash guard treats "held 0.3 s then released" like "faded over 0.3 s", so a fourth flash in a second gets through (F-017).

**The web worker and libass.** Carefully built in its small parts; the structural problem is the synchronous window read (F-003, F-004, F-060). libass's weak spots are operational: a load race on the web (F-044), a new typesetter re-reading up to 24 MB of system fonts on every ASS track selection (F-043), five pixel copies per changed frame on the web (F-045), and the publish switch nobody sets (F-021).

**Build, distribution and CI.** Unusually self-aware: every ratchet exists because something slipped once, CI runs tests on twelve platforms and counts them so a zero cannot hide. The soft failures around the native halves (F-021, F-094, F-100), Android shrinking (F-019, F-020, F-162), the attestation (F-022) and documented first-install steps copied from part of the tree (F-039, F-136) are the gaps, and the biggest risk is that the hardest evidence (R8, Windows playback, visualiser picture suites, physical devices) lives in scripts a human must run while the green tick reads as if it covered them.

**On the size of `PlaybackCore.kt`.** The line count is not the finding. The finding is F-033: the same rule in several hand-maintained spellings that already disagree, and the recent bugs sitting at exactly those divergences. Against that, the design lane's example of a gapless rule written three ways was refuted, and the actor, seek and tail lanes each said the file is in better shape than its size suggests. The honest verdict is that the file can keep its invariants for now, at the price of a growing list of places where a rule must be changed twice, and that a single named predicate per rule (withdrawal, prune, seek abort cleanup, park answer) is cheap now and expensive later. Splitting the file along its command and pass handlers would be a mechanical change that does not touch any invariant and would make the next audit cheaper.

**Across both repositories.** The backends of KiteFFmpeg drift from each other where the player will trip: the JVM backend holds its lock across the native seek and the native backend releases it (F-076), `interrupt()` after `close()` is a use-after-free on native, a typed error on the JVM and a no-op on the web (F-075), the web decoder maps every failure to `Internal` with code 0 (F-012), and the errors a player most wants to match (a timeout, a refused connection, the ENOSYS of a missing hardware decoder) are untyped and platform-dependent (F-067). The nested-open contract is the one thing to redesign there: hand the opener the byte range FFmpeg asked for (F-006), give byte-source opens a closed protocol whitelist that the opener widens (F-007), and route `data:` through the opener on the web (F-011). None of that is KitePlayer's to fix.

## 4. Capability matrix against mpv, VLC, Media3 and AVPlayer

Built from code, not docs. The KitePlayer column names the file that proves it. The other four columns are from general knowledge of those players and are coarse on purpose; #692 is the issue that asks for measurement. "End to end" means a viewer can use it on every platform the module builds for; "half" means it exists on some renderers or platforms and silently does not on others.

| Feature | KitePlayer | Proof or issue | mpv | VLC | Media3 | AVPlayer |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Adaptive bitrate, up and down | end to end | `PlaybackCore.kt` lowerVariant and the step-up on `MediaIo.networkBitsPerSecond` | yes (via FFmpeg) | yes | yes | yes |
| DRM playback | typed refusal only | `PlaybackError.DrmUnsupported`, decided out of scope | no | partial | yes | yes |
| Casting | missing | no Chromecast, AirPlay, MediaRouter or RemotePlayback symbol in the tree | no | yes | yes (Cast SDK) | yes (AirPlay) |
| Offline download of one rendition | missing | #680 | no | no | yes | yes |
| Low-latency HLS | missing | #458 | partial | partial | yes | yes |
| Live seek-back inside the window | missing | #677 | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| Picture in picture | end to end, with a caveat | `kiteplayer-view` has src@android, src@apple, src@jvm, src@wasmJs; the JVM one is an always-on-top app window, not system PiP | partial | partial | yes | yes |
| Media session and media keys | four of five platforms | Android, iOS, macOS, web sessions exist; `JvmMediaSession.isAvailable = false` by recorded decision | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| Background audio | Android and iOS | `AndroidBackground.kt`, `AppleBackground.kt` | n/a | yes | yes | yes |
| Hardware video decode | Android, Apple; Windows unproven; Linux none | KiteFFmpeg `docs/platforms.md`; #101, #695 | yes, all | yes, all | Android | Apple |
| HDR shown as HDR | half: two of fourteen renderers | `MetalVideoRenderer.kt` and `AndroidSurfaceVideoRenderer.kt` override `showsHdr`; Compose canvas tone maps everywhere | yes | partial | yes | yes |
| Dolby Vision | partial | `DolbyVision.kt`; #459, #485 | partial | partial | yes | yes |
| Subtitle formats and rendering | end to end: Kotlin tier plus libass on every platform but js | `kiteplayer-subtitles`, `kiteplayer-libass` | yes (libass) | yes | partial | partial |
| Audio passthrough to a receiver | missing | #180 | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| Spatial audio | missing | #699 | no | no | partial | yes |
| 360 degree video | half: three renderers | `projects()` overridden by KiteVideoRenderer, WebKiteVideoRenderer, AwtCanvasVideoRenderer; #586 | partial | yes | no | no |
| 3D or spatial video | missing | #697 | partial | yes | no | yes |
| Frame stepping | end to end | `KitePlayer.stepFrame` | yes | yes | no | yes |
| A-B loop | end to end | `KitePlayer.setAbLoop` | yes | yes | no | no |
| Speed with pitch control | end to end | tempo stage, semitone shift | yes | yes | yes (no semitones) | yes (no semitones) |
| Chapters and markers | end to end | `nextChapter`, `setMarkers` | yes | yes | partial | yes |
| Playlists and gapless | end to end | `openPlaylist`, gapless joins | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| Trick-play thumbnails | end to end for HLS and DASH plus generated | `HlsThumbnails.kt`, `DashHls.kt` | no | no | partial | no |
| Recording | all but web | `startRecording` | yes | yes | no | no |
| Flash guard for photosensitive viewers | every renderer but the direct MediaCodec surface | #562 | no | no | no | no |
| Analytics hooks | end to end | stats, events, lossless events, `KiteTrace` | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| Native Swift API | missing | #393, F-016 | n/a | yes | n/a | yes |
| Configuration on the web | missing in the worker | F-188 | n/a | n/a | n/a | n/a |

Reading the matrix: KitePlayer is ahead of Media3 and AVPlayer on format reach, subtitle fidelity, A-B loop, frame stepping, pitch control, trick play and the flash guard, and behind on the four platform-service features that need a vendor SDK (DRM, casting, offline, low-latency HLS). Against mpv and VLC the gaps are passthrough, Linux hardware decode and desktop media keys. What separates it from mpv today is less the feature list than the number of cells marked "half": a feature that exists on one renderer and silently does not on another is, to a viewer, a feature that sometimes does not work. F-202 proposes publishing this matrix as `docs/capabilities.md` and regenerating the renderer rows from a test that reflects each renderer's capability overrides so it cannot drift.

## 5. Where the sections are

Section 6 gives counts. Section 7 is the ranked index. Sections 8 to 13 hold every KitePlayer finding by kind, each grouped by area. Section 14 holds every KiteFFmpeg finding. ## 8. KitePlayer: defects

Behaviour the code has today that a viewer or an integrator would call wrong. Each entry names the lines, says what goes wrong and how to see it.

<!-- area: api/memento -->

### F-014 The memento promises every setting but drops MediaItem.growth and the flash guard

**Severity:** medium · **Kind:** Defect · **Repo:** KitePlayer · **Area:** api/memento · **Lane:** public-api-and-docs · **Verdict:** CONFIRMED · **Finder confidence:** high

**Where:**

- `kiteplayer-core/src/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/PlayerMemento.kt:12-19`
- `kiteplayer-core/src/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/PlayerMemento.kt:93-118`
- `kiteplayer-core/src/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/PlayerMemento.kt:231-262`
- `kiteplayer-core/src/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/KitePlayer.kt:1380-1426`
- `kiteplayer-core/src/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/KitePlayer.kt:638-640`
- `kiteplayer-core/src/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/KitePlayer.kt:766-768`
- `kiteplayer-core/src/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/MediaItem.kt:162-167`
- `kiteplayer-core/src/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/MediaItem.kt:333-337`

**Evidence:** PlayerMemento.kt 12-14: "What the text form cannot carry: [MediaItem.io] factories ... [MediaItem.externalSubtitles], [MediaItem.thumbnails], [MediaItem.videoFilter] and [MediaItem.audioFilter]. [asProperties] drops all five". `grep -c growth PlayerMemento.kt` returns 0: asProperties (93-118) writes uri, formatHint, startPosition, clip, title, artist, album, audioContent, runsIntoNext, headers, options, demux, externalAudio, linkedFiles, and never `growth`. KitePlayer.kt 1380-1381: "the queue, the item, the position and every setting the player holds, including balance, the equaliser, and every picture and subtitle setting". PlayerMemento has no flashGuard, abLoop or subtitleSafeArea field; PlayerState.kt 206 `val flashGuard: FlashGuard = FlashGuard.FollowSystem` is a published setting with its own setter. PlayerMemento.kt 44, 47, 66: "An accessibility setting, so it travels." MediaItem.kt 320-324: without growth the item "plays as a complete file".

**Claim:** asProperties drops a sixth field, growth, which is a plain Duration and could travel; fromProperties therefore rebuilds a growing item as a complete one. memento() also omits FlashGuard, an accessibility setting of the kind the memento's own comments say must travel, and the A-B loop, which setAbLoop's KDoc says belongs to the player and survives the next open. The KDoc claims of completeness are untrue.

**Scenario:** A DVR-style app records a broadcast to a file, plays it with MediaItem(path, growth = FileGrowth()), saves a memento at pause (or through KitePlayerResumption), and restores it after a process death. The restored item has growth = null, so playback ends at the file size seen at open and the still-growing tail is never played. A photosensitive viewer who turned FlashGuard.On loses it on restore.

**Impact:** Silent behaviour change on restore for growing files; loss of an accessibility setting; documentation that overstates what is kept.

**Suggested fix:** Write `queue.N.growthEndsAfter` (microseconds) in asProperties and read it back; add flashGuard (and arguably abLoopA/abLoopB) to PlayerMemento with a format version bump; correct both KDoc sentences to list exactly what is dropped.

**How to check it yourself:** `PlayerMemento.fromProperties(PlayerMemento(queue = listOf(MediaItem("/x.ts", growth = FileGrowth())), ...).asProperties()).queue[0].growth` is null. Set FlashGuard.On, take memento(), restore on a fresh player, read state.value.flashGuard: FollowSystem.

**Verifier's note:** `grep -n -i growth PlayerMemento.kt` returns nothing: asProperties (93-118) writes uri, formatHint, startPosition, clip, title, artist, album, audioContent, runsIntoNext, headers, options, demux, externalAudio and linkedFiles, and fromProperties (231-262) rebuilds `MediaItem(uri=..., headers=..., startPosition=..., formatHint=..., openOptions=..., demux=..., title=..., artist=..., album=..., audioContent=..., clip=..., runsIntoNext=..., externalAudio=..., linkedFiles=...)` with no growth argument, so a restored item has `growth = null` (MediaItem.kt 167 default). The class KDoc at 12-19 lists exactly five fields the text form cannot carry and does not name growth, which is a plain `FileGrowth(endsAfter: Duration)` (MediaItem.kt 333-335) and could be written like clip. MementoTest.kt has one 'properties round trip for items that carry only strings' test (282) and never mentions growth, so nothing catches it. memento() (KitePlayer.kt 1386-1426) copies no flashGuard and no abLoopA/abLoopB, and PlayerMemento has no such fields, while the KDoc at 1380-1381 promises 'every setting the player holds'. setAbLoop's KDoc (638-640) says the points 'belong to the player, not the media: like [setSpeed] they survive seeks and the next [open]', and setFlashGuard's (766-768) says 'the value belongs to the player'. The memento's own comments mark balance and subtitle settings 'An accessibility setting, so it travels'. Note the MediaItem.kt 320-324 quote is about a missing local-file provider, not about a null growth, but a null growth has the same outcome by the field's definition ('null, the default, for a file that is complete'). The growth drop is a defect against the KDoc's own list; the flash guard and A-B loop omissions are judgement calls supported by the player's own KDoc.

### F-017 The flash guard releases a held rise as a 'fade' after 0.3 s although the release is an instant jump, so a fourth flash in a second gets through uncounted

**Severity:** medium · **Kind:** Defect · **Repo:** KitePlayer · **Area:** audioviz/flash-guard · **Lane:** audioviz · **Verdict:** CONFIRMED · **Finder confidence:** high · **Related open issue:** 500

**Where:**

- `kiteplayer-audioviz/src/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/audioviz/viz/FlashGuard.kt:124-138`
- `kiteplayer-audioviz/src/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/audioviz/viz/FlashGuard.kt:178`
- `kiteplayer-audioviz/test/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/audioviz/FlashGuardTest.kt:26-34`

**Evidence:** FlashGuard.kt 124-130: `if (now - extremeAt > QUICK) { halfway = false; rising = !rising; extreme = wanted; extremeAt = now; return wanted }` runs before the hold at 135-138: `if (!rising && flashes.size >= most) { return extreme + step * HOLD }`. The hold branch returns without touching extremeAt, so while a rise is held extremeAt stays at the time the preceding fall ended; once 0.3 s have passed the next frame takes the fade branch and returns the full wanted value, counting nothing. FlashGuardTest.kt 26-34: `private fun busiest(shown: List<Float>, ...): Int { val counter = FlashGuard(mostPerSecond = 1_000); ... counter.limit(value, 0f, frameStep); if (counter.recent > most) most = counter.recent }`, so the test's counter is the guard itself and shares the rule. A Python port of Channel.allow (scratchpad guard.py) fed 3 quick flashes (3 frames low, 3 high) then 0.85 held 30 frames then 0.05 produced the output 0.05,0.85 x3, then 0.13 for 18 frames, then 0.85 for 16 frames, then 0.05; an independent leg counter (pairs of opposing changes >= 0.10 with the darker state below 0.80) finds 4 flashes in one second while guard.recent reports 3 (and 0 for the mostPerSecond = 0 variant).

**Claim (as corrected by the verifier):** When the guard is holding a rise at low + 0.08 and the music stays loud, the QUICK rule releases the full rise in one frame 0.3 s after the preceding fall, without counting it, because extremeAt is not advanced while holding. For the pattern 'three quick flashes then sustained loud' this lets a fourth flash into a rolling second while guard.recent reports 3, and under reducedMotion (mostPerSecond = 0) it passes one full-screen jump every 0.3 s of sustained loudness while recent reports 0. The fixture in the original check does not trigger it; the one below does.

**Finder's original claim:** The QUICK rule is meant to let a genuine slow fade pass, but it measures the time since the last extreme, not the slope of the change. A rise that the guard has been holding at low + 0.08 for 0.3 s is then released in one frame as a jump of about 0.7, which is a flash leg by WCAG's definition and by the project's own capture counter, yet the guard neither holds it nor adds it to `flashes`. The policy of at most three flashes in any rolling second is therefore not enforced by the runtime guard for the pattern 'three quick hits, then sustained loud', and the guard's own `recent` under-reports.

**Scenario:** Any drawing whose light follows lightFor(energy): a drum fill of three quick hits at 10 Hz followed by a chorus that holds the energy high for more than 0.3 s. The guard holds the fourth rise dim for 18 frames and then snaps the picture to full brightness. Under reducedMotion (mostPerSecond = 0) the same pattern passes a full-screen jump every time the music stays loud for 0.3 s, while ReducedMotionTest asserts guard.recent == 0.

**Impact:** The runtime half of the photosensitivity policy can pass four flashes a second on realistic music, and the unit tests that guard it cannot detect it because they count with the same code.

**Suggested fix:** Distinguish a held release from a fade: when the hold branch is active, either ramp the returned value from the hold level to the wanted value over the fade time (so the release really is a fade), or on release record the jump as a leg (count it in `flashes`) and keep holding while that would exceed `most`. Decide 'fade' from the wanted signal's own rate of change over recent frames rather than from time since the last extreme. In FlashGuardTest, count with an independent leg counter (the AreaFlashes class from FlashCaptureTest fed a one-pixel frame would do) instead of another FlashGuard.

**How to check it yourself:** Add to FlashGuardTest: frames = List(4) { listOf(0.85f, 0.85f, 0.85f, 0.05f, 0.05f, 0.05f) }.flatten() + List(30) { 0.85f } + List(30) { 0.05f }, run through FlashGuard() with 1/60 s steps via limit(value, 0f, step). Expect the output to sit at 0.13 from about frame 25 and jump to 0.85 at about frame 42 while guard.recent is 3. Count flashes on the output with a plain turning-point counter (opposing changes of at least 0.10 with the darker state below 0.80, no QUICK rule) or with FlashCaptureTest's area counter: expect 4 in the busiest second. Do not use the `busiest` helper, which is a FlashGuard and shares the fade rule. Repeat with FlashGuard(mostPerSecond = 0): same jump, recent 0.

**Verifier's note:** FlashGuard.kt is as quoted: 124-130 `if (now - extremeAt > QUICK) { halfway = false; rising = !rising; extreme = wanted; extremeAt = now; return wanted }` runs before the hold at 135-138 `if (!rising && flashes.size >= most) { return extreme + step * HOLD }`, and the hold branch returns without updating extremeAt, so extremeAt stays at the moment of the last fall while the rise is held. I ported Channel.allow line for line to Python and drove it at 1/60 s steps. The finding's own fixture (three cycles of 3 frames at 0.05 then 3 at 0.85, then 0.85 held) never engages the hold, because the first rise from the initial extreme is 'away' and not a leg, so the third flash completes on a rise and the following sustained high is not held; the finding's quoted output for that fixture is therefore wrong. The pattern that starts high does show the mechanism: ([0.85]*3+[0.05]*3)*4 then 30 frames of 0.85 produced 0.85/0.05 alternation for three flashes, a fall at frame 22, then 0.13 for frames 25 to 41, then 0.85 from frame 42: a one-frame jump of 0.72 released by the QUICK branch, with guard.recent reporting 3 and an independent turning-point counter finding 4 flashes in the busiest second (legs at frames 6, 12, 18, 41). With mostPerSecond = 0 the same shape gives one 0.13 to 0.85 jump per 0.3 s of sustained loudness and recent stays 0. The test helper FlashGuardTest.kt 29-34 `busiest` is `FlashGuard(mostPerSecond = 1_000)` fed the output, and it shares the QUICK rule: after the fall its extreme stays at 0.05 (0.13 is `back < step` and returns without moving extreme), so the release 0.33 s later reads as a fade and is not counted, which is why no existing test sees it. docs/audioviz-rendering-api.md 523-525 documents the rule as 'A change that takes longer than 0.3 seconds to cross the step is a fade', but the released change crosses the step in one frame; only the guard's own hold made the clock run out. FlashCaptureTest's area counter compares each frame with the one 0.3 s earlier, so it would count the release as a leg; it runs only in the survey.

### F-018 On Android, a Drop transition renders Alchemy, Pipe and Odyssey as nothing because the transition draws them into a bitmap where the shader cannot run

**Severity:** medium · **Kind:** Defect · **Repo:** KitePlayer · **Area:** audioviz/surface · **Lane:** audioviz · **Verdict:** CONFIRMED · **Finder confidence:** high · **Related open issue:** 683

**Where:**

- `kiteplayer-audioviz/src/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/audioviz/viz/VisualizerSurface.kt:745-761`
- `kiteplayer-audioviz/src/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/audioviz/viz/VisualizerSurface.kt:475-500`
- `kiteplayer-audioviz/src/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/audioviz/viz/VisualizerSurface.kt:536-540`
- `kiteplayer-audioviz/src/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/audioviz/viz/shader/ShaderPreset.kt:98-109`
- `kiteplayer-audioviz/src@android/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/audioviz/viz/shader/ShaderProgram.android.kt:20-21`
- `kiteplayer-audioviz/src/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/audioviz/viz/shader/TransitionBlend.kt:25-27`
- `kiteplayer-audioviz/src/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/audioviz/viz/VizDirector.kt:167-170`
- `kiteplayer-audioviz/src/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/audioviz/viz/VizDirector.kt:261-266`

**Evidence:** VisualizerSurface.kt 745-753: `if (blend.canDrawLayers(director.transition)) { ... } else { val from = stage.steady.frameFor(fresh, this, showing, state, scale, stats); val to = stage.arriving.frameFor(fresh, this, next, state, scale, stats)`. TransitionBlend.kt 25-27: `canDrawLayers(...) = transition == Crossfade || transition == StrobeCut || (transition != ZoomThrough && transition != WarpHandoff && maskProgram.available)`. VizDirector.kt 333-335: `AudioEventKind.Drop -> { val next = pick(upFrom(moodBucket(frame))); begin(next, allowed(VizTransition.ZoomThrough, next), frame, pulses = 4) }`. VizRenderer.render (485-496) draws into `buffers.canvas`, a GraphicsCanvas over an ImageBitmap, via `drawEchoLayer`, which calls the drawing's `draw`. ShaderPreset.kt 107-109: `if (!useRuntimeShader || !runs || !canDrawRuntimeShaders()) { withCamera(camera, fallbackParallax) { drawFallback(state) }; return }` with line 98 `open fun DrawScope.drawFallback(state: VizRenderState) {}`. ShaderProgram.android.kt 20-21: `canDrawRuntimeShaders(): Boolean = runtimeShadersSupported && drawContext.canvas.nativeCanvas.isHardwareAccelerated`. Only NeonLoFi.kt:37 and Contour.kt:106 override `hasFallback`/`drawFallback`; Alchemy, Pipe and Odyssey do not (grep of shader/*.kt and presets/*.kt).

**Claim (as corrected by the verifier):** On Android 13 and newer, a ZoomThrough change (the one every Drop uses, and WarpHandoff likewise) renders both drawings through VizRenderer into bitmap-backed canvases, where canDrawRuntimeShaders() is false, so Alchemy, Pipe and Odyssey draw their empty default fallback and the shader side of the change shows only the palette background for the whole change. The mask-unavailable case only adds to this on a 13+ device whose mask shader fails to compile, since older Android never lists these three drawings.

**Finder's original claim:** On Android a bitmap-backed android.graphics.Canvas reports isHardwareAccelerated false, so canDrawRuntimeShaders() is false inside VizRenderer.render. For a ZoomThrough transition (and for any transition when the mask program is unavailable) the directed surface renders both drawings into bitmaps through that path. A ShaderPreset then takes the fallback branch, and the default fallback draws nothing, so the bitmap stays transparent and the stretched result is the bare background. The Skiko build does not have this problem because canDrawRuntimeShaders() is always true there, which is also why the JVM render harness never sees it.

**Scenario:** Android 13 or newer, AudioVizState.directed = true, music with a supported Drop event (or any caller setting director.preferred = VizTransition.ZoomThrough). The director picks a drawing from the Mid or High shelf, which holds Pipe, Odyssey (Mid) and Alchemy (High). For the 4-pulse transition (about 1.7 s at 140 bpm) the shader side of the transition shows only the palette background: an outgoing Alchemy vanishes at the start of the change, an incoming Pipe pops in at the end instead of rushing in from far away.

**Impact:** A visible black-out on every Drop transition that involves three of the fifteen drawings, on the platform most users will run the visualiser on. It contradicts the rendering document's promise that full-screen shaders stay on the GPU during transitions.

**Suggested fix:** Either exclude ZoomThrough (and the mask-unavailable path) for a drawing that paintsWholeScreen and has no fallback, falling back to Crossfade through drawTransitionLayers, or give ZoomThrough a layer-based form (both drawings drawn straight on the canvas with scale transforms and alpha) so no shader preset is ever rendered into a bitmap on Android. A cheaper stop-gap: in canDrawLayers treat ZoomThrough as a layer transition on Android when either drawing is a ShaderPreset without a fallback.

**How to check it yourself:** Without a device: read the eight locations above in order and confirm that Alchemy.kt, Pipe.kt and Odyssey.kt contain neither `hasFallback` nor `drawFallback` (grep both names under kiteplayer-audioviz/src/.../viz/shader). On an Android 13+ device: set state.directed = true, state.director.preferred = VizTransition.ZoomThrough, show Alchemy and play a track with a drop; the Alchemy side goes to the plain background for the whole change, while the same change with preferred = VizTransition.Crossfade keeps it drawn.

**Verifier's note:** Every link in the chain is in the tree as quoted. VisualizerSurface.kt 745-753 takes the else branch for ZoomThrough: TransitionBlend.kt 25-27 `canDrawLayers(...) = transition == Crossfade || transition == StrobeCut || (transition != ZoomThrough && transition != WarpHandoff && maskProgram.available)`, and the else branch calls `stage.steady.frameFor(...)` and `stage.arriving.frameFor(...)` for both drawings whatever their trail. frameFor (504-510) calls render (475-500), which draws through `scope.draw(into, into.layoutDirection, buffers.canvas, size) { drawEchoLayer(...) }`, and FeedbackBuffers (521-540) makes `front = ImageBitmap(wanted, tall).also { frontCanvas = GraphicsCanvas(it) }`: a bitmap-backed canvas, whose android.graphics.Canvas reports isHardwareAccelerated false. ShaderProgram.android.kt 20-21 `canDrawRuntimeShaders(): Boolean = runtimeShadersSupported && drawContext.canvas.nativeCanvas.isHardwareAccelerated`, so ShaderPreset.kt 105-109 takes `withCamera(camera, fallbackParallax) { drawFallback(state) }` and line 98 `open fun DrawScope.drawFallback(state: VizRenderState) {}` draws nothing. Only Contour.kt:106/1072 and NeonLoFi.kt:37/181 override hasFallback/drawFallback; Alchemy.kt, Pipe.kt and Odyssey.kt do not, and they sit on the shelves a Drop picks from (Alchemy.kt:58 `bucket = VizEnergy.High`, Pipe.kt:57 and Odyssey.kt:66 `bucket = VizEnergy.Mid`; VizDirector.kt 240-243 `upFrom` maps Calm to Mid and everything else to High). VizDirector.kt 167-170: `AudioEventKind.Drop -> { val next = pick(upFrom(moodBucket(frame))); begin(next, allowed(VizTransition.ZoomThrough, next), frame, pulses = 4) }`, and `allowed` (261-266) returns `how` unchanged when no preferred way is set, so a Drop always uses ZoomThrough. The author knew the path exists: ShaderPreset.kt:106 says `// A snapshot into a bitmap during a change of drawing lands here on Android.` and VisualizerSurface.kt:771 says `/** Only history needs a bitmap. A full-screen shader keeps executing on the window's GPU. */`, but that protection (drawTransitionEcho) is only reached through the canDrawLayers branch, which excludes ZoomThrough and WarpHandoff. No Android-side override of VizRenderer or FeedbackBuffers exists (src@android/.../viz holds only PixelImage, PostProcess, ScenePostEffect, mesh, presets, shader). The Skiko actual is `canDrawRuntimeShaders(): Boolean = true` (ShaderProgram.skiko.kt:21), so the JVM harness cannot see it, and docs/audioviz-rendering-api.md:614 says no phone has run the visualiser yet. One narrowing: the 'any transition when the mask program is unavailable' half only matters on Android 13 and newer with a mask shader that fails to compile, because below 13 VizCatalog.kt:69-70 `canRunHere() = this !is ShaderPreset || runtimeShadersSupported || hasFallback` keeps Alchemy, Pipe and Odyssey out of the catalogue entirely. Not a duplicate: #683 asks for latency and cost measurement on a phone, not this rendering fault.

### F-019 kiteplayer-io's Android providers are found by ServiceLoader but ship no keep rules, and no CI build ever shrinks an app that contains them

**Severity:** medium · **Kind:** Defect · **Repo:** KitePlayer · **Area:** build/android · **Lane:** build-distribution-tests-ci · **Verdict:** CONFIRMED · **Finder confidence:** medium

**Where:**

- `kiteplayer-core/src@android/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/internal/MediaIoProviders.android.kt:8-10`
- `kiteplayer-io/resources@android/META-INF/services/io.github.yuroyami.kiteplayer.spi.MediaIoResolverProvider:1-2`
- `kiteplayer-network/resources@android/META-INF/proguard/kiteplayer-network.pro:1-3`
- `kiteplayer-sample-android/proguard-rules.pro:1-3`
- `verification/network-consumer/android-app/build.gradle.kts:40-46`

**Evidence:** MediaIoProviders.android.kt:9-10: `ServiceLoader.load(MediaIoResolverProvider::class.java, MediaIoResolverProvider::class.java.classLoader).iterator().asSequence().toList()`. The io services file names `io.github.yuroyami.kiteplayer.io.ResourceUriResolverProvider` and `io.github.yuroyami.kiteplayer.io.LocalFileResolverProvider`. `find . -path '*META-INF/proguard*'` returns only kiteplayer-libass-android-natives/resources/META-INF/proguard/kiteplayer-libass.pro, kiteplayer-network/resources@android/META-INF/proguard/kiteplayer-network.pro and the sample's empty file; nothing under kiteplayer-io. The network rule file says why rules exist: `# Discovery metadata names these classes. Preserve names and the provider constructor under R8.` The sample's proguard-rules.pro says `the release build must survive R8 on the default optimized rules plus the libraries' own consumer rules`, but kiteplayer-sample-android/module.yaml sets no minify setting, and the only R8 build, verification/network-consumer, depends on `kiteplayer-core` and optionally `kiteplayer-network` (lines 42-45) and runs only by hand with a device serial.

**Claim:** R8 does not keep classes merely because META-INF/services names them; it keeps them only when it can rewrite the exact `ServiceLoader.load(X.class, X.class.getClassLoader()).iterator()` pattern into direct instantiation, which needs every listed class present with a default constructor and the optimizer enabled. The two sibling modules ship keep rules for exactly this reason; kiteplayer-io does not. When the rewrite does not apply (an app using proguard-android.txt with -dontoptimize, or a future R8 that changes the pattern), both io classes are removed and the META-INF/services file survives, so the iterator throws ServiceConfigurationError at the first player open, or, if swallowed, Compose resource addresses on Android stop resolving. Nothing in CI exercises either outcome: the sample is built unminified and the R8 probe never includes kiteplayer-io.

**Scenario:** An Android app with `isMinifyEnabled = true` and `proguard-android.txt` (the non-optimizing default of many templates) adds `kiteplayer-compose:0.3.0`, follows the README and opens a Compose `Res.getUri` asset. In the release build R8 strips ResourceUriResolverProvider and LocalFileResolverProvider; the debug build works, the release build either crashes at `KitePlayer()` with `ServiceConfigurationError: Provider io.github.yuroyami.kiteplayer.io.ResourceUriResolverProvider not found` or quietly loses the resolvers.

**Impact:** Release-only breakage on Android, the platform with the most users, found by the consumer rather than by the project.

**Suggested fix:** Add kiteplayer-io/resources@android/META-INF/proguard/kiteplayer-io.pro with `-keep class io.github.yuroyami.kiteplayer.io.ResourceUriResolverProvider { *; }` and the same for LocalFileResolverProvider, placed where AGP reads it (see the next finding). Add a minified release build of kiteplayer-sample-android to the Linux job (the verification Gradle build already exists under verification/device-tests/sample-android; set isMinifyEnabled for a release variant and assert in mapping.txt that both io provider classes survive). Consider catching ServiceConfigurationError in platformMediaIoProviders and warning once, so a stripped provider degrades instead of crashing.

**How to check it yourself:** In verification/device-tests/sample-android/build.gradle.kts add a release buildType with isMinifyEnabled = true and proguardFiles(getDefaultProguardFile("proguard-android.txt")) (non-optimizing), build assembleRelease, then check build/outputs/mapping/release/mapping.txt and `unzip -p <apk> META-INF/services/io.github.yuroyami.kiteplayer.spi.MediaIoResolverProvider` for ResourceUriResolverProvider and LocalFileResolverProvider; absent from both means stripped. Repeat with proguard-android-optimize.txt to see whether only the ServiceLoader rewrite saves them. Compare with KtorMediaIoResolverProvider in the same mapping, which has a keep rule.

**Verifier's note:** All cited evidence is present. kiteplayer-core/src@android/.../MediaIoProviders.android.kt:8-10: `ServiceLoader.load(MediaIoResolverProvider::class.java, MediaIoResolverProvider::class.java.classLoader).iterator().asSequence().toList()`. kiteplayer-io/resources@android/META-INF/services/io.github.yuroyami.kiteplayer.spi.MediaIoResolverProvider names `io.github.yuroyami.kiteplayer.io.ResourceUriResolverProvider` and `io.github.yuroyami.kiteplayer.io.LocalFileResolverProvider`, both declared `internal class` (src@android/.../ResourceUriResolverProvider.kt:22, src@jvmAndAndroid/.../LocalFileResolverProvider.kt:16) with KDoc `Found by ServiceLoader, so a public class in bytecode with a constructor that takes nothing`. The only .pro files in the tree outside build/ are kiteplayer-libass-android-natives/resources/META-INF/proguard/kiteplayer-libass.pro, kiteplayer-network/resources@android/META-INF/proguard/kiteplayer-network.pro (`-keep class io.github.yuroyami.kiteplayer.network.KtorMediaIoResolverProvider { *; }`) and the deliberately empty kiteplayer-sample-android/proguard-rules.pro; nothing under kiteplayer-io or kiteplayer-core keeps the io providers. No direct code reference keeps them either: on Android there is no `MediaIoProviders.register(...)` call for them (that line exists only in src@posix/.../LocalFileResolverProvider.kt:29). kiteplayer-sample-android/module.yaml has no minify setting, verification/device-tests/sample-android/build.gradle.kts has no isMinifyEnabled or proguardFiles, and the one R8 build, verification/network-consumer/android-app/build.gradle.kts:41-45, depends on kiteplayer-core and optionally kiteplayer-network only, with proguard-android-optimize.txt (line 27). The lazy `discovered` at kiteplayer-core/src/.../MediaIoResolverProvider.kt:58-60 does not catch ServiceConfigurationError. One nuance for the owner: R8 rewrites META-INF/services contents and may drop entries for pruned classes, so the quiet-loss outcome is at least as likely as the crash; the finding already names both.

### F-021 A release can ship kiteplayer-libass-android-natives with no .so: the switch that would fail the build is never set and the publication check does not look inside the jar

**Severity:** medium · **Kind:** Defect · **Repo:** KitePlayer · **Area:** build/publish · **Lane:** web-worker-wasm-libass · **Verdict:** CONFIRMED · **Finder confidence:** high

**Where:**

- `build-plugins/libass-android-natives/src/androidNatives.kt:19-24`
- `build-plugins/libass-android-natives/src/androidNatives.kt:33-47`
- `.github/workflows/publish.yml:153-156`
- `.github/workflows/publish.yml:180-183`

**Evidence:** androidNatives.kt:22-23 comment: "Without an NDK or a chain the jar ships no library and the build says so, unless `KITEPLAYER_LIBASS_REQUIRE_ANDROID_JNI=true`, which a release build sets."; 33 `val require = System.getenv("KITEPLAYER_LIBASS_REQUIRE_ANDROID_JNI") == "true"`; 38-39 and 45-46 log a WARNING and continue when `require` is false. publish.yml sets only `KITEPLAYER_LIBASS_REQUIRE_ALL_HOST_JNI: "true"` at 155 and 182. `grep -rn REQUIRE_ANDROID_JNI .github scripts CONTRIBUTING.md CLAUDE.md` returns nothing. PublicationReadiness.kt has no mention of `libass`, `lib/` or `.so` (grep).

**Claim (as corrected by the verifier):** The Android half of libass is the one half whose absence is not turned into a failure on the publish path. KITEPLAYER_LIBASS_REQUIRE_ANDROID_JNI is never set by publish.yml, `check publication` reads POMs only, and the artifact-size check only notes a jar that shrank. CI's Linux job does verify the sample APK carries lib/<abi>/libkiteplayer_libass_jni.so for all three ABIs, but the uploaded jar is built separately on the macOS publish runner, so an NDK probe or chain download failure there ships a signed, attested jar with missing libraries and a WARNING in the log.

**Finder's original claim:** The Android half of libass is the one half whose absence is not turned into a failure on the publish path. If the NDK probe fails on the runner (the NDK comes from `ANDROID_NDK_LATEST_HOME`, which the player's own CLAUDE.md notes can move) or a chain download fails, the jar is built, signed, attested and published with one or no `lib/<abi>/libkiteplayer_libass_jni.so`, and `KiteLibass.isAvailable()` is false on Android with a TypesetterUnavailable warning in every app.

**Scenario:** A publish run on a runner image whose latest NDK is missing or incompatible: the log says WARNING and the build goes on; the uploaded jar has no native library; every Android consumer of that version loses libass until the next release.

**Impact:** Exactly the "quietly ships without that half" failure CLAUDE.md guards against for the JVM jar and the web module, left open for Android.

**Suggested fix:** Set `KITEPLAYER_LIBASS_REQUIRE_ANDROID_JNI: "true"` beside the host switch in publish.yml, and make `./kotlin check publication` (PublicationReadiness) open the natives jar and require `lib/arm64-v8a`, `lib/armeabi-v7a` and `lib/x86_64` entries. While there, fix CLAUDE.md, which says the publish path passes `-Pkiteplayer.libass.requireAllHostJni=true`; the plugin reads the environment variable, not a property.

**How to check it yourself:** `grep -rn REQUIRE_ANDROID_JNI .github/ scripts/` (only the plugin source mentions it). Then with ANDROID_NDK_HOME, ANDROID_NDK_ROOT and ANDROID_NDK_LATEST_HOME unset and no SDK at the default paths, run `./kotlin publish mavenLocal -m kiteplayer-libass-android-natives` and `unzip -l ~/.m2/repository/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer-libass-android-natives/<version>/*.jar | grep '\.so'`: the build succeeds with a WARNING and the listing is empty. Fix is to set KITEPLAYER_LIBASS_REQUIRE_ANDROID_JNI=true on both publish steps, or to add an `unzip -l` check of the jar to the Publication readiness step.

**Verifier's note:** androidNatives.kt:22-23 "unless `KITEPLAYER_LIBASS_REQUIRE_ANDROID_JNI=true`, which a release build sets", 33 `val require = System.getenv("KITEPLAYER_LIBASS_REQUIRE_ANDROID_JNI") == "true"`, 38-39 and 45-47 log WARNING and continue when it is false. A repo-wide grep for REQUIRE_ANDROID_JNI hits only those two lines, so the "release build sets" promise is unkept: publish.yml sets `KITEPLAYER_LIBASS_REQUIRE_ALL_HOST_JNI: "true"` at 155 and 182 and exports `ANDROID_NDK_HOME="$ANDROID_NDK_LATEST_HOME"` (142, 188, 196) but never the Android switch. `./kotlin check publication` runs PublicationReadiness.checkLocalPublication (350-383), which parses POMs only; no mention of lib/ or .so. check-artifact-size.sh (run in ci.yml:233) treats a jar far below baseline as `"note: lower the baseline"`, not a failure (compare(), line ~152), so a 3.3 MB baseline (artifact-size-baseline.txt:49) shrinking to a few KB passes. One partial guard the finding missed: ci.yml:590-601 in the linux-jvm-android job (ubuntu-24.04) builds the sample APK and fails unless `lib/<abi>/libkiteplayer_libass_jni.so` is present for all three ABIs, and publish.yml runs the whole of ci.yml on the published commit. That proves the Linux runner's NDK and chain produce the libraries, but the jar that is actually uploaded is built in the `publish` job on `macos-latest` (publish.yml:115), by a separate build with that runner's NDK, and nothing inspects it. So the claim stands, narrowed: the scenario is an NDK or chain failure on the macOS publish runner specifically.

### F-094 The publish job can ship kiteplayer-libass-android-natives with no .so files and nothing in it would notice

**Severity:** low (finder said medium, verifier corrected) · **Kind:** Defect · **Repo:** KitePlayer · **Area:** build/publish · **Lane:** build-distribution-tests-ci · **Verdict:** CONFIRMED · **Finder confidence:** high

**Where:**

- `.github/workflows/publish.yml:150-158`
- `.github/workflows/publish.yml:178-189`
- `build-plugins/libass-android-natives/src/androidNatives.kt:33-50`
- `scripts/check-artifact-size.sh:149-150`

**Evidence:** androidNatives.kt:23 says the switch is one `which a release build sets`, and line 33 reads it: `val require = System.getenv("KITEPLAYER_LIBASS_REQUIRE_ANDROID_JNI") == "true"`. Without it, line 39 logs `WARNING: no Android NDK found, so the Android artifact carries no libass adapter.` and line 46 logs `WARNING: no ass chain for ... carries no libass adapter.` and `continue`s. publish.yml sets only `KITEPLAYER_LIBASS_REQUIRE_ALL_HOST_JNI: "true"` (lines 155 and 182); a grep of .github and scripts for REQUIRE_ANDROID_JNI finds no other hit. check-artifact-size.sh:149-150: `else if (bytes * 100 < base[key] * (100 - limit)) { verdict_line(..., "note: lower the baseline")`.

**Claim (as corrected by the verifier):** The Android libass adapter build downgrades a missing NDK to a warning unless KITEPLAYER_LIBASS_REQUIRE_ANDROID_JNI=true, the plugin's own KDoc says a release build sets it, and publish.yml never does; no publish-time check reads the jar's lib/<abi>/ folders and the size ratchet passes a shrunken jar with a note. A failed or tampered download of a pinned ass-chain zip is not such a path: it throws and fails the publish. The quiet failure needs a macOS runner image with no Android NDK anywhere resolveNdk() looks.

**Finder's original claim:** The Android libass adapter is built by a plugin that downgrades a missing NDK or a failed download of a pinned ass-chain-android-*.zip to a warning unless an environment variable is set, and the publish workflow never sets that variable. The publish job's only checks of the result are `./kotlin check publication`, which reads POMs, and the attestation byte comparison, which compares two builds that would both lack the file. The size ratchet in ci.yml treats a jar that shrinks by more than ten percent as a pass with a note. So a transient GitHub release download failure, or an NDK path change on the macOS runner image, publishes a kiteplayer-libass-android-natives jar whose lib/<abi>/ folders are missing for one or all ABIs.

**Scenario:** On a publish run, the download of ass-chain-android-arm64.zip from the KiteFFmpeg release fails once (GitHub returns a 5xx, or the asset is being re-uploaded). The plugin logs a warning, the jar is published with lib/armeabi-v7a and lib/x86_64 only, Central accepts it, and with the release input on it is immutable. Every Android app that depends on kiteplayer at that version then loads kiteplayer-libass, `System.loadLibrary("kiteplayer_libass_jni")` throws UnsatisfiedLinkError on arm64 phones, and the player warns TypesetterUnavailable and draws ASS with the Kotlin tier. The ci.yml APK check on the Linux runner cannot catch it because it is a different build on a different machine.

**Impact:** A silently degraded release for every Android user on the affected ABI, which cannot be withdrawn from Central. The project's own stated failure mode, a green tick that quietly skipped something, in the one job that matters most.

**Suggested fix:** Set KITEPLAYER_LIBASS_REQUIRE_ANDROID_JNI=true in every publish.yml step that builds (Publication readiness, Publish to Maven Central, the byte comparison), as is already done for the host JNI flag. Add one step after the Maven Local publish that unzips kiteplayer-libass-android-natives-<version>.jar and the kiteplayer-libass-jvm jar and fails unless each expected native file is present, the way the Linux job checks the APK. Consider making a shrink of more than ten percent a failure in check-artifact-size.sh for the native-carrying lines.

**How to check it yourself:** grep -rn REQUIRE_ANDROID_JNI .github scripts (no hit). On a machine with no ~/Library/Android/sdk/ndk or ~/Android/Sdk/ndk, run `ANDROID_NDK_HOME=/nonexistent ANDROID_NDK_ROOT=/nonexistent ANDROID_NDK_LATEST_HOME=/nonexistent ANDROID_HOME=/nonexistent ANDROID_SDK_ROOT=/nonexistent ./kotlin publish mavenLocal -m kiteplayer-libass-android-natives` and read the warning, then `unzip -l` the jar and see no lib/<abi>/*.so. To see that the download path is loud, edit one digest in kiteplayer-libass/ass-chain.sha256 locally (do not commit) and run the same publish without KITEPLAYER_LIBASS_ROOT and without ../KiteFFmpeg/native-libs/deps: it fails with BuildFailure, it does not warn. The fix is one line: add KITEPLAYER_LIBASS_REQUIRE_ANDROID_JNI: "true" to the three publish steps' env.

**Verifier's note:** Half right, half wrong. The code at build-plugins/libass-android-natives/src/androidNatives.kt:33-47 is as quoted: `val require = System.getenv("KITEPLAYER_LIBASS_REQUIRE_ANDROID_JNI") == "true"`, a null NDK logs `WARNING: no Android NDK found, so the Android artifact carries no libass adapter.` and a null chain logs a warning and `continue`s. Nothing in .github or scripts sets that variable (grep hits only the Kotlin source and its own KDoc at line 23, which says `which a release build sets`; the tree contradicts that KDoc). build-plugins/publication-check/src has no mention of `.so`, `lib/`, `jni` or zip inspection, and scripts/check-artifact-size.sh:149-150 does give `note: lower the baseline` on a shrink (baseline line 49: `kiteplayer-libass-android-natives android 3338113`). BUT the download-failure scenario is wrong. AssChain.find (build-plugins/build-support/src/AssChain.kt:58-69) returns null only through `val pin = pins[dirName] ?: return null`; kiteplayer-libass/ass-chain.sha256 lists all three Android assets, so `continue` at androidNatives.kt:47 is unreachable in the published tree. A failed download throws instead: Downloads.kt:56-58 `if (code >= 500) { ... throw IOException("GET $current answered HTTP $code") }` (retried by withDownloadRetries, then propagated), Downloads.kt:60 `if (code != 200) throw BuildFailure(...)`, and AssChain.kt:80-85 throws BuildFailure on a digest mismatch. So a 5xx or a re-uploaded asset fails the publish loudly. The only quiet path is resolveNdk() returning null (NdkVersionOrder.kt:48-62: three env vars, then ANDROID_HOME/ANDROID_SDK_ROOT/~/Library/Android/sdk/~/Android/Sdk), i.e. a macOS runner image with no NDK at all. publish.yml:187 and 193 export ANDROID_NDK_HOME from ANDROID_NDK_LATEST_HOME, so that path needs the image to drop the NDK, a narrow trigger. The CI APK check at ci.yml:596-600 does catch a missing .so, but on the Linux job's own build, as the finding says.

### F-096 The libass web module stamp keys on the chain's path, not its bytes, so a rebuilt local chain leaves a stale kiteass.wasm in the test resources and in the release zip built from them

**Severity:** low · **Kind:** Defect · **Repo:** KitePlayer · **Area:** build/web-assets · **Lane:** web-worker-wasm-libass · **Verdict:** CONFIRMED · **Finder confidence:** high

**Where:**

- `build-plugins/web-assets/src/webAssets.kt:116-136`
- `scripts/web-zips.sh:85-92`

**Evidence:** webAssets.kt:126-128 `val inputs = listOf(chain.root.absolutePath, source.readText().hashCode().toString(), driverDir.listFiles()... joinToString(",") { "${it.name}:${it.length()}:${it.lastModified()}" })` and 129 `if (!stamp.isFile || stamp.readText() != inputs || ...) buildWasmModule(...)`. web-zips.sh:88-92 builds the libass zip from `kiteplayer-libass/testResources@wasmJs/kiteass.*`, which this task wrote.

**Claim:** For a local sibling chain the stamp holds only the folder path; rebuilding libass, HarfBuzz, FreeType or FriBidi in `../KiteFFmpeg/native-libs/deps/wasm32/ass-chain` leaves the stamp equal and the old kiteass.wasm in place, so the browser tests and a locally built release zip carry the previous chain. The fetched-chain path is safe because its folder is replaced when the pin changes.

**Scenario:** The maintainer rebuilds the wasm32 chain with a libass fix, runs the web tests (green against the old module) and `scripts/web-zips.sh libass`; the zip on the release page still holds the unfixed libass.

**Impact:** Stale artifact on a developer machine; CI's fresh fetch is unaffected.

**Suggested fix:** Hash the four archives under `chain.libDir` (size plus mtime at least, or SHA-256) into the stamp.

**How to check it yourself:** Run `./kotlin task :kiteplayer-libass:tests@web-assets` once, then print the `.inputs` stamp in the task's `kiteass` cache folder (find it with `find . -path '*kiteass/.inputs'`): its first line is only `.../wasm32/ass-chain`, with no digest of lib/*.a. Then append a byte to `../KiteFFmpeg/native-libs/deps/wasm32/ass-chain/lib/libass.a` (or rebuild the chain) and rerun the task: no `[web-assets] web: kiteass.mjs + kiteass.wasm` line appears and testResources@wasmJs/kiteass.wasm keeps its date.

**Verifier's note:** The cited lines exist as quoted. /home/user/KitePlayer/build-plugins/web-assets/src/webAssets.kt:126-128 builds the stamp from `chain.root.absolutePath`, the driver source's text hash and the driver folder's name:length:mtime list, and line 129 skips `buildWasmModule` whenever `stamp.readText() == inputs` and kiteass.wasm exists. Nothing in that list reads the chain's archives. For a local chain `AssChain.find` (build-plugins/build-support/src/AssChain.kt:59-61) returns `Chain(dirName, it)` with `it` = `<deps>/wasm32/ass-chain`, a path that does not change when the sibling rebuilds libass.a, libharfbuzz.a, libfreetype.a or libfribidi.a in place, so the stamp stays equal and the old kiteass.wasm is copied forward by `writeIfDifferent`. The fetched road is safe as the finding says: `find` re-fetches into a fresh folder only when the `.sha256` marker differs from the pin (AssChain.kt:63-67), and a new chain means a new pin. The contrast with the other two libass roads shows this is the odd one out: `mergeAssChain` in build-plugins/libass-native/src/libassNative.kt is `@TaskAction(ExecutionAvoidance.Disabled)`, re-merges every run and writes `# libkiteass.a sha256 ${sha256(archive)}` into the def file (line 61), and `buildHostJni` (lines 86-140) deletes its staging folder and re-merges and re-links on every run, so both follow the chain's bytes. scripts/web-zips.sh:88-91 runs `./kotlin task :kiteplayer-libass:tests@web-assets` and zips `kiteplayer-libass/testResources@wasmJs/kiteass.*`, so a local release zip inherits the stale module. Only a machine with both a sibling wasm32 chain and emcc is affected; CI takes the fetched road. The owner's check is sound: the stamp ignores the chain's mtime and bytes alike, so replacing libass.a with different bytes and running the task prints no `web: kiteass.mjs + kiteass.wasm` line. A faster confirmation is to read the task's `kiteass/.inputs` stamp under the plugin's cache output: its first line is only the chain folder path.
