### F-055 XspfReader.decodeReferences scans forward to the next semicolon for every ampersand, so a playlist of ampersands takes time proportional to the square of its length

**Severity:** medium · **Kind:** Defect · **Repo:** KitePlayer · **Area:** playlists/xspf · **Lane:** kotlin-parsers-and-subtitles · **Verdict:** CONFIRMED · **Finder confidence:** high

**Where:**

- `kiteplayer-core/src/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/internal/XspfReader.kt:231-260`
- `kiteplayer-core/src/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/internal/PlaybackCore.kt:2271-2276`

**Evidence:** XspfReader.kt:237-239 `if (char == '&') { val semicolon = raw.indexOf(';', at); val entity = if (semicolon > at) raw.substring(at + 1, semicolon) else ""` and 256-257 `out.append(char); at++` when the entity is unknown. The same text, in XmlMini.kt:250-255, says why this is wrong: "the search for the `;` stops at the first character that cannot be part of a reference ... each character is read at most twice", with XmlMiniLimitsTest `ampersandsInTextAreReadAFewTimesEachNotOncePerLaterAmpersand`. The playlist bytes are read with the subtitle ceiling, PlaybackCore.kt:16262 `MAX_SUBTITLE_BYTES = 16 * 1024 * 1024`, then `Playlists.parse` at 2275.

**Claim:** A text node or attribute value holding N ampersands followed by one semicolon (or none at all) costs about N squared / 2 character reads and, when the semicolon exists, N substring allocations whose total size is also quadratic. At 16 MB that is on the order of 10^14 operations: an effective hang of whatever thread runs readPlaylistItems.

**Scenario:** A user opens an .xspf URL from a hostile or compromised server (or any XSPF whose text has a long run of unescaped `&` such as a title made of ampersands). `<playlist><trackList><track><title>` followed by several megabytes of `&` and a closing `;` never returns from Playlists.parse.

**Impact:** Denial of service through a playlist file, on every platform; XmlMini was already fixed for the same shape, so this is a missed sibling.

**Suggested fix:** Copy XmlMini's rule: after `&`, advance only over reference characters (ASCII letters, digits, `#`) and decode only if the next character is `;`; otherwise emit the `&` and continue from the next character. Add the equivalent of XmlMiniLimitsTest's counting test to PlaylistsTest.

**How to check it yourself:** In PlaylistsTest, time `Playlists.parse("<playlist><trackList><track><location>a</location><title>" + "&".repeat(200_000) + ";</title></track></trackList></playlist>", "/m/a.xspf")`; it takes seconds, and doubling the count quadruples the time. Compare with XmlMini.parse on the same text.

**Verifier's note:** XspfReader.kt:231-260 reads as quoted: for every `&`, `val semicolon = raw.indexOf(';', at)` scans to the first `;` anywhere later in the text node, `raw.substring(at + 1, semicolon)` copies that whole stretch, and when the entity is unknown the code falls to `out.append(char); at++` and the next `&` repeats both. Both the scan and the copy are proportional to the distance to the one semicolon, so N ampersands before one semicolon cost about N^2/2 reads and N^2/2 copied characters; with no semicolon at all indexOf still scans to the end each time. The text node handed in is `text.substring(at, next)` where next is the next `<` (line 183), so one `<title>` can hold the whole file. The file reaches it through readPlaylistItems (PlaybackCore.kt:2259-2275), read under MAX_SUBTITLE_BYTES = 16 MiB (line 16262), then `Playlists.parse(text, uri)`. XmlMini.kt:250-265 stops the `;` search at the first non-reference character (`while (stop < end && isReferenceChar(s[stop])) stop++`) with the KDoc saying each character is read at most twice, and XmlMiniLimitsTest:51 pins that; XspfReader has no such bound and no equivalent test (PlaylistsTest is its only test file). The quadratic mechanism is real and unguarded.

### F-176 ASS dialogue text after an opening brace with no closing brace is dropped, where libass draws it

**Severity:** low · **Kind:** Defect · **Repo:** KitePlayer · **Area:** subtitles/ass · **Lane:** kotlin-parsers-and-subtitles · **Verdict:** CONFIRMED · **Finder confidence:** high

**Where:**

- `kiteplayer-subtitles/src/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/subtitle/AssParser.kt:263-266`

**Evidence:** AssParser.kt:263-265 `ch == '{' -> { val close = text.indexOf('}', i + 1); if (close < 0) { i = text.length; break }`. Compare SubRipParser.kt:203 "An unterminated run stays text, as it does in FFmpeg" and InlineMarkup at 227-231, which only treats `{\` as a tag and keeps an unterminated run as text. libass's render loop (ass_render.c, the `(*p == '{') && (q = strchr(p, '}'))` test) treats a `{` with no `}` as an ordinary character.

**Claim:** A dialogue line such as `He said {smile` or a line whose override block lost its closing brace loses everything from the `{` on in the Kotlin tier, while libass and VSFilter show the brace and the words.

**Scenario:** An external .ass file (or an embedded ASS track rendered by the Kotlin tier when libass is absent) with one malformed override block: the rest of that line is blank on screen.

**Impact:** Silent loss of dialogue in the fallback tier, inconsistent with the typeset tier the same file gets when libass is present.

**Suggested fix:** When no `}` follows, append the `{` as text and continue (`current.append(ch); i++`), matching libass and the SubRip inline parser.

**How to check it yourself:** `AssParser.parse(document("Dialogue: 0,0:00:00.00,0:00:01.00,Default,,0,0,0,,He said {smile and left"))` yields a cue whose text is `He said ` (trailing text gone); libass renders `He said {smile and left`.

**Verifier's note:** AssParser.kt:263-265 `ch == '{' -> { val close = text.indexOf('}', i + 1); if (close < 0) { i = text.length; break }` leaves the loop; line 346 `flushSpan()` then emits what was collected before the brace, so `He said {smile and left` becomes a cue of text `He said ` with everything from the `{` on gone. No AssParserTest covers an unterminated brace (grep for unterminated/unclosed/no closing found nothing). libass master ass_render.c:2066-2080 confirms the comparison: `if ((*p == '{') && (q = strchr(p, '}'))) { p = ass_parse_tags(...) }` ... `else { code = ass_get_next_char(state, &p); break; }`, so a `{` with no `}` falls to the text branch and is drawn as a character. The project's own SubRip reader states the same rule at SubRipParser.kt:203 'An unterminated run stays text, as it does in FFmpeg'. Reach is the Kotlin tier only, since kiteplayer-libass typesets the primary ASS track when present, which matches the finding's scenario and low severity.

<!-- area: subtitles/charset -->

### F-177 A UTF-16 subtitle file without a byte-order mark is accepted as UTF-8 and parses to no cues

**Severity:** low · **Kind:** Defect · **Repo:** KitePlayer · **Area:** subtitles/charset · **Lane:** kotlin-parsers-and-subtitles · **Verdict:** CONFIRMED · **Finder confidence:** high

**Where:**

- `kiteplayer-core/src/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/internal/SubtitleTextDecoder.kt:214-217`
- `kiteplayer-core/src/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/internal/SubtitleTextDecoder.kt:350-361`

**Evidence:** SubtitleTextDecoder.kt:214-217 `bom(bytes)?.let { return it }; if (isValidUtf8(bytes)) { return DecodedSubtitleText(bytes.decodeToString(), "UTF-8", confident = true) }`. The validator at 380-405 accepts the byte 0x00 as ASCII (`b < 0x80 -> { i++; continue }`), and `bom` at 350-361 recognises only the three marks. Nothing looks for the alternating-NUL shape of UTF-16.

**Claim:** An ASCII-only SubRip or WebVTT file saved as UTF-16LE or UTF-16BE without a mark (iconv, some ripping tools, Windows tools told to omit the signature) is every other byte 0x00, which is valid UTF-8, so it is decoded as UTF-8 with confidence = true and every timing line reads as `0\u00000\u0000:...`; the parsers find no timing line and the load fails with "parsed to no cues" and no charset warning. A UTF-16 file with non-ASCII text fails UTF-8 validation and falls into the single-byte guess instead, which is also wrong. uchardet (what mpv uses) detects BOM-less UTF-16 from this NUL pattern.

**Scenario:** A viewer adds `film.srt` produced by `iconv -t UTF-16LE` or by a tool that writes UTF-16 without a signature. The track fails to load with a message about no cues, and the SubtitleCharsetGuessed warning that would let an app offer an override is not raised because the UTF-8 answer was confident.

**Impact:** A real but uncommon class of files is rejected with a misleading reason; the override path (decodeSubtitleBytesAs with UTF-16LE) exists but nothing points the app at it.

**Suggested fix:** Before the UTF-8 check, count NUL bytes at even and odd positions over the first few kilobytes; when more than, say, 30 percent of one parity is NUL and almost none of the other, decode as UTF-16 of that endianness with confident = false (or true when the text then parses). Add a SubtitleCharsetTest case with a BOM-less UTF-16LE SubRip fixture.

**How to check it yourself:** `decodeSubtitleBytes("1\n00:00:01,000 --> 00:00:02,000\nHi\n".encodeToByteArray().flatMap { listOf(it, 0.toByte()) }.toByteArray())` answers charset UTF-8, confident = true, and SubRipParser.parse on its text returns an empty list.

**Verifier's note:** SubtitleTextDecoder.kt:214-217 is as quoted: `bom(bytes)?.let { return it }; if (isValidUtf8(bytes)) { return DecodedSubtitleText(bytes.decodeToString(), "UTF-8", confident = true) }`. bom() at 350-361 matches only EF BB BF, FF FE and FE FF. isValidUtf8 at 380-405 takes `b < 0x80 -> { i++; continue }`, so a 0x00 byte is valid ASCII and a BOM-less UTF-16 file of ASCII text validates as UTF-8. Nothing in the file looks for the alternating-NUL shape (grep for utf-16 finds only the BOM branch, decodeUtf16 and the explicit-encoding path at 337-340). Because the UTF-8 branch runs before `fallback`, even an app's configured fallbackEncoding of UTF-16LE cannot rescue such a file. PlaybackCore.kt:719 raises SubtitleCharsetGuessed only `if (!decoded.confident)`, and line 763 is the `the external subtitle file parsed to no cues` refusal, so the user sees a no-cues failure with no charset warning, exactly as claimed. SubtitleCharsetTest covers UTF-16 only with a mark (lines 96-101, 716-719) and `valid UTF-8 without a mark is taken at its word` (106). The reproduction in the finding's check is correct. The explicit-encoding path at 337-340 (decodeUtf16 with from = 0) shows the decoder already can read BOM-less UTF-16 once asked, so a NUL-pattern detector before the UTF-8 branch is the missing piece.

### F-056 LrcParser.withoutWordStamps rescans to the next `>` for every `<` that is not a word stamp, so a line of `<` characters is quadratic in its length

**Severity:** medium · **Kind:** Defect · **Repo:** KitePlayer · **Area:** subtitles/lrc · **Lane:** kotlin-parsers-and-subtitles · **Verdict:** CONFIRMED · **Finder confidence:** high

**Where:**

- `kiteplayer-subtitles/src/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/subtitle/LrcParser.kt:152-174`
- `kiteplayer-subtitles/src/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/subtitle/LrcParser.kt:76`

**Evidence:** LrcParser.kt:374-379 `if (char == '<') { val close = text.indexOf('>', at); if (close > at && stampMicros(text.substring(at + 1, close)) != null) { at = close + 1; continue } }` then 385-386 `out.append(char); at++`. When the content between `<` and `>` is not a stamp, the next `<` searches again for the same `>` and takes another substring of it. Called from parse at line 292 for every stamped line.

**Claim:** For a line `[00:01.00]` followed by N `<` and one `>`, each of the N positions runs indexOf over the remainder and allocates a substring of the remainder, so time and garbage are both about N squared / 2. A 16 MB file (the external subtitle ceiling) is one line, so N can be 10^7.

**Scenario:** A hostile .lrc file (or lyrics in a song's tag that reach LrcParser) whose one stamped line is millions of `<` and a final `>`. Loading the file hangs the subtitle load; the fuzz test only mutates the small LRC seeds and never builds a long line.

**Impact:** Denial of service through a lyrics file; the other text parsers were given a bounded-read guarantee and a cost test, this one was not.

**Suggested fix:** Find the `>` once and remember it, as vttSpans does at WebVttStyles.kt:391-400 (`var close = body.indexOf('>')`, refreshed only when it is behind the cursor), and check the stamp with a bounded length (a stamp is at most about 16 characters) before taking a substring.

**How to check it yourself:** Time `LrcParser.parse("[00:01.00]" + "<".repeat(200_000) + ">")`; it takes seconds and quadruples when the count doubles. Add it to TextScanCostTest with the CountingText wrapper.

**Verifier's note:** The cited line numbers are wrong; the function is LrcParser.kt:152-174. The code is as quoted: `if (char == '<') { val close = text.indexOf('>', at); if (close > at && stampMicros(text.substring(at + 1, close)) != null) { at = close + 1; continue } }` then `out.append(char); at++`. For a line of N `<` and one trailing `>`, each `<` runs indexOf over the rest of the line and allocates a substring of it before stampMicros rejects it (stampMicros does check `text.length > maxLength` at line 142, but the substring has already been copied), so both time and garbage are about N^2/2; with no `>` at all the indexOf scan alone is still quadratic. It is called from parse at line 76, `withoutWordStamps(line.substring(at))`, for every line that begins with a time stamp, and the LRC parser splits only on line breaks, so one stamped line may be nearly the whole 16 MiB external file. TextScanCostTest covers the SubRip timing scanner, WebVTT tags and brace runs through CountingText but has no LRC case. The sibling parsers (WebVttStyles MAX_TAG_CHARS = 512, InlineMarkup) bound their tag scans; this one does not.

### F-178 A TTML paragraph with a begin and no end, dur or parent end is dropped, where TTML gives it an indefinite end

**Severity:** low · **Kind:** Defect · **Repo:** KitePlayer · **Area:** subtitles/ttml · **Lane:** kotlin-parsers-and-subtitles · **Verdict:** CONFIRMED · **Finder confidence:** high

**Where:**

- `kiteplayer-subtitles/src/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/subtitle/TtmlParser.kt:131-135`
- `kiteplayer-subtitles/src/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/subtitle/TtmlParser.kt:165`

**Evidence:** TtmlParser.kt:132-134 `var end = element.attr("end")?.let { parentBegin + clock.micros(it) } ?: element.attr("dur")?.let { begin + clock.micros(it) } ?: parentEnd` and 165 `if (end == null || end <= begin) return`. The body is walked with parentEnd = null at line 101 `walk(body, 0L, null, emptyList(), null, preserved)`. No TtmlParserTest fixture has a `<p>` with `begin` and neither `end` nor `dur` (grep of the test for `begin="` lines lacking `end=`/`dur=` found none).

**Claim:** TTML 1 section 10.4 ("Time Intervals") gives an element with a begin and no end or dur, inside a `par` container with no end, an end equal to its parent's end, which for a body with no end is indefinite: the paragraph is active from its begin onward until the document ends. The reader throws such paragraphs away, so a document written in the SubRip style of "each line shows until the next one" (begin on every `<p>`, no end) yields no cues at all. In the DASH `stpp` path the sample's span would have bounded the cue anyway (DashSubtitles.kt:39-41), so there the drop is pure loss.

**Scenario:** A DFXP or TTML file whose paragraphs carry only `begin`, or a packager that emits `<p begin="...">` in each stpp sample relying on the sample's duration. Every cue is dropped and the external file fails with "parsed to no cues".

**Impact:** Spec-legal documents produce no subtitles; the engine already has an OPEN_END mechanism (SubtitleCue.kt:37, OpenCues.kt) that would close such cues at the next cue's start, so the behaviour would be natural.

**Suggested fix:** When end is null after the three fallbacks, give the paragraph SubtitleCue.OPEN_END (the engine closes it at the next cue) or, for the file path, run the result through closingOpenEnds as SubRip does. Add a test with begin-only paragraphs.

**How to check it yourself:** Unit test: `TtmlParser.parse(tt("<p begin=\"1s\">one</p><p begin=\"3s\">two</p>"))` is empty today. Also check the stpp case: build one stpp sample holding `<tt><body><p begin="0s">x</p></body></tt>` with a 2 s sample duration and assert `DashSubtitles.mp4Cues` answers no cue, which shows the sample span does not bound it.

**Verifier's note:** Mechanism confirmed. TtmlParser.kt:101 `root.child("body")?.let { body -> walk(body, 0L, null, emptyList(), null, preserved) }` starts the walk with parentEnd = null. Lines 132-134 `var end = element.attr("end")?.let { parentBegin + clock.micros(it) } ?: element.attr("dur")?.let { begin + clock.micros(it) } ?: parentEnd` leave end null for a `<p begin=...>` with no end or dur under an untimed body/div, and line 165 `if (end == null || end <= begin) return` discards the paragraph before any cue is built. No test fixture in TtmlParserTest has a `<p>` with begin and neither end nor dur (grep confirmed). The DASH stpp path cannot rescue it: DashSubtitles.kt:83 `val cues = Ttml.cues(text)` runs TtmlParser.read first, and the clamp at lines 39-41 `val from = maxOf(cue.startMicros, start); val until = minOf(cue.endMicros, end)` only sees cues that survived, so a sample-bounded paragraph with only a begin is lost there too. HlsTtml.kt:134 `Ttml.cues(bytes.decodeToString())` has the same shape. The spec reading (par container with no end gives the child the parent's end, the body's being indefinite) matches what other readers do; ExoPlayer, for one, treats a node with begin and unset end as active from begin on. Severity low stands: files written that way are a minority, and the external-file case ends in the explicit 'parsed to no cues' refusal at PlaybackCore.kt:763 rather than a crash.

### F-180 A WebVTT or SubRip cue keeps `&#39;`, `&quot;` and other character references as literal text, because only four named entities are decoded

**Severity:** low · **Kind:** Defect · **Repo:** KitePlayer · **Area:** subtitles/webvtt · **Lane:** kotlin-parsers-and-subtitles · **Verdict:** CONFIRMED · **Finder confidence:** high

**Where:**

- `kiteplayer-subtitles/src/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/subtitle/SubRipParser.kt:121-128`
- `kiteplayer-subtitles/src/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/subtitle/WebVttStyles.kt:439`

**Evidence:** SubRipParser.kt:121-127 `internal fun List<StyledSpan>.decodeSpanEntities(): List<StyledSpan> = map { span -> val decoded = span.text.replace("<", "<").replace(">", ">").replace("&nbsp;", " ").replace("&", "&")`; WebVttStyles.kt:439 `return spans.decodeSpanEntities()` is the only decoding the WebVTT path does. The KDoc at 116-117 says "The four entities every subtitle file in the wild actually uses".

**Claim (as corrected by the verifier):** The WebVTT path decodes only `<`, `>`, `&nbsp;` and `&`, while the WebVTT cue text parsing rules consume any HTML character reference at `&`, so numeric references such as `&#39;`, `&quot;` and `&#8230;`, and named ones such as `&lrm;` and `&rlm;`, draw as literal text where a browser draws the character. The same four-entity table serves SubRip, where no specification requires decoding but the same converter output is common.

**Finder's original claim:** The WebVTT specification's cue text parsing (section 6.1, "WebVTT cue text parsing rules": on U+0026 AMPERSAND the tokenizer consumes an HTML character reference) decodes any HTML character reference, named or numeric, including `&#39;`, `&quot;`, `&lrm;`, `&rlm;`, `&#8230;`. Files written by common converters escape apostrophes as `&#39;` and quotes as `&quot;`, so this parser shows `don&#39;t` on screen where a browser shows `don't`.

**Scenario:** A WebVTT file from a converter that HTML-escapes its text (`&#39;`, `&quot;`, `&#8230;` for an ellipsis, `&lrm;` before Hebrew). Each such cue draws the raw reference.

**Impact:** Visible mojibake in ordinary WebVTT files, and the same in SubRip files produced by the same tools (FFmpeg's srt decoder also decodes only four, but mpv's and browsers' WebVTT paths decode all).

**Suggested fix:** Replace the four replace calls with one pass that decodes `&name;` for the WebVTT named set (amp, lt, gt, nbsp, lrm, rlm, quot, apos) and `&#NNN;`/`&#xHHH;` numeric references, leaving unknown references literal, as XmlMini.decodeReference does. Keep the pass linear (stop at the first character that cannot be part of a reference).

**How to check it yourself:** `WebVttParser.parseCueBody("don&#39;t say &quot;hi&quot;&#8230;").joinToString("") { it.text }` returns the text unchanged; the specification's reference parser in any browser renders `don't say "hi"…`.

**Verifier's note:** SubRipParser.kt:121-128 is as quoted: `decodeSpanEntities` replaces only `<`, `>`, `&nbsp;` and `&`, and WebVttStyles.kt:439 `return spans.decodeSpanEntities()` is the only decoding on the WebVTT path (grep for `&#`, `&quot;`, `&apos;` in kiteplayer-subtitles/src finds nothing but XmlMini, which TTML uses). WebVttParser.parseCueBody exists at lines 92 and 215 and calls vttSpans, so the owner's check recipe is valid. The WebVTT cue text tokenizer (W3C WebVTT, cue text parsing rules, data state) consumes an HTML character reference at every `&`, which covers numeric references and the named ones browsers know, so `&#39;`, `&quot;`, `&lrm;`, `&rlm;` and `&#8230;` render as characters in a browser and as literal text here. The KDoc at 116-119 states a deliberate choice of four entities but gives no reason for leaving out numeric references, so this is a gap, not a decided design. One narrowing: SubRip has no specification that calls for entity decoding at all, so the SubRip half is a convenience claim rather than a conformance one; the WebVTT half is spec-backed.

### F-182 FileUri.percentDecoded accepts a sign inside a percent escape, so `%+1` and `%-1` decode to bytes

**Severity:** low · **Kind:** Defect · **Repo:** KitePlayer · **Area:** uri · **Lane:** kotlin-parsers-and-subtitles · **Verdict:** CONFIRMED · **Finder confidence:** high

**Where:**

- `kiteplayer-core/src/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/uri/FileUri.kt:56-64`

**Evidence:** FileUri.kt:56-58 `val value = if (text[at] == '%' && at + 2 <= text.lastIndex) { text.substring(at + 1, at + 3).toIntOrNull(16) }` and 63 `bytes += value.toByte()`. Kotlin's String.toIntOrNull(radix) accepts a leading `+` or `-`, so "+1" is 1 and "-1" is -1.

**Claim:** RFC 3986 section 2.1 defines pct-encoded as "%" HEXDIG HEXDIG. A path such as `file:///tmp/100%-1.mp4` (a name containing a literal `%-1`) decodes `%-1` to the byte 0xFF, which then becomes U+FFFD in the string, so the file is not found; the correct reading leaves `%-1` as the three literal characters.

**Scenario:** A file whose name holds `%+` or `%-` followed by a hex digit, passed as a file: URI from a platform that did not escape the `%` (or an M3U/XSPF location written that way). The player opens a path with a replacement character instead of the real name.

**Impact:** Wrong file resolution for an unusual name; no security consequence.

**Suggested fix:** Check both characters are hex digits (`isHexDigit`) before converting, or use `Char.digitToIntOrNull(16)` on each and combine.

**How to check it yourself:** Assert `FileUri.localPath("file:///tmp/a%-1b") == "/tmp/a%-1b"` and `FileUri.localPath("file:///tmp/a%+1b") == "/tmp/a%+1b"`; today the first answers `/tmp/a�b` and the second a name holding byte 0x01. Fix shape: require both characters after `%` to be hex digits (e.g. `Char.isHexDigit` or a `[0-9A-Fa-f]{2}` check) before converting.

**Verifier's note:** FileUri.kt:56-57 `val value = if (text[at] == '%' && at + 2 <= text.lastIndex) { text.substring(at + 1, at + 3).toIntOrNull(16) }` and 63 `bytes += value.toByte()`. Kotlin's String.toIntOrNull(radix) accepts a leading sign (its implementation treats a first char below '0' as '-' or '+' and parses the rest), so `"-1".toIntOrNull(16)` is -1 and `"+1".toIntOrNull(16)` is 1; nothing in percentDecoded checks that both characters are hex digits. `(-1).toByte()` is 0xFF, which `decodeToString()` at line 71 turns into U+FFFD, so `file:///tmp/a%-1b` opens `/tmp/a�b`, and `%+1` yields a control byte 0x01. RFC 3986 pct-encoded is '%' HEXDIG HEXDIG, so both should stay literal text. No FileUri test covers a sign after a percent (grep found no FileUriTest with such a case). Low severity is right: a literal `%-` or `%+` in an unescaped file: address is rare, and the correct spelling of such a name escapes the percent itself.

### F-187 The worker sink takes the page's output latency once at start, before the AudioContext runs, and never updates it

**Severity:** low · **Kind:** Defect · **Repo:** KitePlayer · **Area:** web/audio · **Lane:** web-worker-wasm-libass · **Verdict:** CONFIRMED · **Finder confidence:** medium

**Where:**

- `kiteplayer/src@wasmJs/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/KitePlayerWorker.kt:653-705`
- `kiteplayer-output/src@wasmJs/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/output/WebWorkerAudio.kt:35`
- `kiteplayer-output/src@wasmJs/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/output/WebWorkerAudio.kt:104-115`
- `kiteplayer-output/src@wasmJs/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/output/WebWorkerAudio.kt:176-180`
- `kiteplayer-output/src@wasmJs/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/output/WebAudioSink.kt:179-188`

**Evidence:** KitePlayerWorker.kt:704 `latencySeconds = audio?.outputLatencySeconds` inside the Init message built once in `start()`; WebWorkerAudio.kt:336 `override fun outputLatencySeconds(): Double? = latencySeconds` (a constructor constant); 399-400 `(typeof s.ctx.outputLatency === 'number') ? s.ctx.outputLatency : ... baseLatency`. The page-side device (WebAudioWorkletDevice.kt:31) re-reads the context on every call.

**Claim (as corrected by the verifier):** The worker player reads `AudioContext.outputLatency` exactly once, in `KitePlayerWorker.start()` before the context has ever been resumed, and `WorkletPortDevice` returns that constant for the whole session; nothing in the page-to-worker protocol can update it. The page-side sink re-reads the context on every block. Whether the start-up read is 0 and whether the browser revises `outputLatency` after a device change are browser facts to confirm by hand.

**Finder's original claim:** `AudioContext.outputLatency` is read while the context is still suspended (no gesture has happened at start) and before any route is chosen; browsers report it as the current device's figure and it changes when headphones or a Bluetooth sink are connected. The worker's sync deadline (WebAudioSink.deadlineFor adds outputLatencyNanos) therefore carries the start-up value for the whole session.

**Scenario:** Start the worker player on speakers (about 10 ms), then connect Bluetooth headphones (150 to 250 ms): the page's own KitePlayer would follow the new figure within one block; the worker player keeps 10 ms and lip sync drifts by the difference for the rest of the session.

**Impact:** Tens to hundreds of milliseconds of lip sync error after a route change on the worker path, labelled Estimated rather than Unreliable.

**Suggested fix:** Have the page post the current `outputLatency` to the worker periodically or on `devicechange`/`statechange` (it already has a channel for `Audio` messages), and let WorkletPortDevice return the latest value.

**How to check it yourself:** In the sample page, log `WebWorkletAudio.outputLatencySeconds` (or `ctx.outputLatency` in devtools) at three moments: right after `KitePlayerWorker.start()` returns, after the first play (context running), and after switching the system output to Bluetooth headphones. Compare with the worker's `stats.audioLatency` minus the worklet queue; the worker's figure stays at the first reading while the page's readings change.

**Verifier's note:** The mechanism is as described, with drifted line numbers in WebWorkerAudio.kt (the file is 222 lines). /home/user/KitePlayer/kiteplayer/src@wasmJs/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/KitePlayerWorker.kt:653 creates `WebWorkletAudio.createOrNull()` and line 704 puts `latencySeconds = audio?.outputLatencySeconds` into the one `PageMessage.Init` that `start()` sends; `WebWorkletAudio.outputLatencySeconds` (WebWorkerAudio.kt:35) reads `s.ctx.outputLatency` else `baseLatency` (lines 177-180) at that moment. The context has not been resumed then: `webWorkletResume` (line 183) runs only when the worker asks through `WorkerMessage.Audio(resume)` (WorkerRuntime.kt:67-69), after Init. Inside the worker, `workerOutputBackend` passes the figure into `WorkletPortDevice` (WebWorkerAudio.kt:83) whose `override fun outputLatencySeconds(): Double? = latencySeconds` (line 115) returns the constructor constant, and the KDoc at line 63 only says the three values 'are the page's figures'. No later message carries a new figure: `PageMessage` has Init, Call, Close and Send(Control) (WorkerProtocol.kt:51-60) and the `Control` kinds (lines 97-125) are playback settings only. `WebAudioSink.deadlineFor` (WebAudioSink.kt:179-183) and `latencyNanos` (lines 205-210) call `device.outputLatencySeconds()` per block, so the page-side `WebAudioWorkletDevice` (WebAudioWorkletDevice.kt:31, `webAudioLatencySeconds(state)` re-read each call) does follow a route change while the worker device cannot. Two parts I could not verify from code and the owner should treat as browser behaviour, not repository fact: that `AudioContext.outputLatency` reads 0 or a placeholder while the context is suspended (Chromium fills it from the device callback, so a pre-resume read is likely 0.0, which `takeIf { it >= 0.0 }` keeps and the sink turns into 0 ns), and that a browser updates `outputLatency` when the output device changes. The severity (low) is right: the deadline error equals the latency difference, and the worker's figure is already Estimated.

### F-190 Events from the worker are dropped silently when the page's collector falls more than 64 behind, with no counter

**Severity:** low · **Kind:** Defect · **Repo:** KitePlayer · **Area:** web/worker · **Lane:** web-worker-wasm-libass · **Verdict:** CONFIRMED · **Finder confidence:** medium

**Where:**

- `kiteplayer/src@wasmJs/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/KitePlayerWorker.kt:94`
- `kiteplayer/src@wasmJs/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/KitePlayerWorker.kt:105-109`
- `kiteplayer/src@wasmJs/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/KitePlayerWorker.kt:550-555`
- `kiteplayer-core/src/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/internal/PlaybackCore.kt:13480-13487`
- `kiteplayer-core/src/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/KitePlayer.kt:107-113`
- `kiteplayer/src@wasmJs/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/WorkerRuntime.kt:87`

**Evidence:** KitePlayerWorker.kt:94 `private val eventFlow = MutableSharedFlow<PlayerEvent>(extraBufferCapacity = 64)` and 550 `is WorkerMessage.Event -> eventFlow.tryEmit(...)`. `tryEmit` on a SharedFlow without replay returns false and drops the value when the buffer is full (default onBufferOverflow SUSPEND makes tryEmit fail rather than suspend); the return value is not read.

**Claim (as corrected by the verifier):** KitePlayerWorker forwards each WorkerMessage.Event with `eventFlow.tryEmit` on a 64-slot SharedFlow and discards the result, so when a page collector is suspended across event-loop turns while more than 64 events arrive from the worker, the overflow is lost with no counter; the engine's own events flow drops the same way but counts it in PlaybackStats.droppedEvents and offers losslessEvents, neither of which the facade mirrors. The worker-side forwarding collector (WorkerRuntime.kt:87) runs promptly in the worker, so the facade is the uncounted stage.

**Finder's original claim:** A page whose event collector is suspended on a long main-thread task (layout, a large render) while the worker emits more than 64 events (a burst of warnings on a bad stream, TracksAdded, ChapterChanged, MarkerReached, Ended) loses the overflow without any sign; PlaybackStats.droppedEvents counts only the worker player's own drops, not this facade's.

**Scenario:** A live stream that emits SegmentSkipped warnings for every segment while the page runs a heavy layout; the page's `events` collector never sees `PlayerEvent.Ended` or a `SeekCompleted` that arrived in the same burst.

**Impact:** Rare loss of state-carrying events on the page side with no diagnostic.

**Suggested fix:** Use `onBufferOverflow = BufferOverflow.DROP_OLDEST` with a larger buffer and count drops into a facade-side counter surfaced on `stats`, or deliver events through a Channel(UNLIMITED) feeding the shared flow.

**How to check it yourself:** In a wasmJs browser test subscribe a collector to `KitePlayerWorker.events` that suspends on a CompletableDeferred inside its body (so it is registered but parked), post 100 WorkerMessage.Event messages through the test entry point, then complete the deferred and count: 64 plus the one being processed arrive, the rest are gone, and nothing in `stats` or `events` reports it. A collector that was never subscribed proves nothing, because a no-replay SharedFlow keeps nothing for it.

**Verifier's note:** KitePlayerWorker.kt:94 `private val eventFlow = MutableSharedFlow<PlayerEvent>(extraBufferCapacity = 64)` and :550 `is WorkerMessage.Event -> eventFlow.tryEmit(...)` with the Boolean discarded. With the default BufferOverflow.SUSPEND, tryEmit returns false and drops the value when a subscriber has 64 undelivered events. The engine's own flow has the same shape but accounts for it: PlaybackCore.kt:266 `MutableSharedFlow<PlayerEvent>(extraBufferCapacity = 64)` and :13483 `if (!eventSink.tryEmit(event)) droppedEvents.incrementAndGet()`, published as PlaybackStats.droppedEvents and documented at KitePlayer.kt:108-112 (`when any one of them falls that far behind, the next event reaches none of them, and [PlaybackStats.droppedEvents] counts it. A collector that must see every event collects [losslessEvents] instead.`). The facade offers no losslessEvents (grep returns nothing) and no counter, while its KDoc (KitePlayerWorker.kt:44-47) says `[events] carry what the worker's player publishes`. So the mechanism and the missing counter are real. Two corrections. The scenario is wrong about how the collector falls behind: the worker's messages are delivered by `worker.onmessage` on the same main thread as the collector (KitePlayerWorker.kt:736), so a thread blocked in layout receives no messages either; the drop needs a collector that is suspended across event-loop turns (awaiting a fetch or a delay inside its collect body) while worker messages keep arriving. The check is also wrong: a SharedFlow with no replay and no subscriber discards every tryEmit, so `do not collect` then `collect and count` yields 0, not 64; the collector must be subscribed and parked.

### F-191 KitePlayerWorker makes item, subtitle and audio addresses whole for the worker but not thumbnails or linked files, so a relative one of those fails inside the worker

**Severity:** low · **Kind:** Defect · **Repo:** KitePlayer · **Area:** web/worker · **Lane:** web-worker-wasm-libass · **Verdict:** CONFIRMED · **Finder confidence:** high

**Where:**

- `kiteplayer/src@wasmJs/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/KitePlayerWorker.kt:491-499`
- `kiteplayer/src@wasmJs/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/KitePlayerWorker.kt:720-727`
- `kiteplayer/src@wasmJs/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/WorkerProtocol.kt:483-486`
- `kiteplayer-core/src@wasmJs/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/internal/ExternalText.wasmJs.kt:4`
- `kiteplayer-core/src/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/internal/PlaybackCore.kt:543-563`
- `kiteplayer-core/src/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/internal/LinkedFiles.kt:46-58`

**Evidence:** KitePlayerWorker.kt:494-498 `return media.copy(uri = pageAddress(media.uri), externalSubtitles = ... pageAddress(it.uri) ..., externalAudio = ... pageAddress(it.uri) ...)` with no mapping of `thumbnails` or `linkedFiles`. SyncHttpMediaIo.kt:26-27 `val scheme = uri.substringBefore(':', missingDelimiterValue = "").lowercase(); if (scheme != "http" && scheme != "https" && scheme != "blob") return null` (a relative address has no scheme and falls to the codec). PlaybackCore.kt:1931 `readSubtitleBytes(io.github.yuroyami.kiteplayer.SubtitleSource(wanted.uri, io = wanted.io), item)` reads the item's thumbnail file in the worker; LinkedFiles.kt:53 `val declared = item.linkedFiles.map { asItem(it.uri, it.io) }` opens linked files as items.

**Claim:** A page that gives `ThumbnailSource("thumbs.vtt")` or `LinkedFile("op.mkv")` relative to the page gets, in the worker, an address with no scheme that neither the synchronous resolver nor FFmpeg's wasm build can open; the thumbnail file warns ThumbnailsUnreadable and an ordered edition's linked segment warns EditionPartLeftOut, while the same item plays its relative `uri` and subtitles correctly.

**Scenario:** `player.open(MediaItem("movie.mkv", thumbnails = ThumbnailSource("movie-thumbs.vtt")))` on the worker: the film plays, the seek bar pictures never appear, the events carry ThumbnailsUnreadable naming "movie-thumbs.vtt".

**Impact:** Inconsistent address handling that only shows as a warning the page author may not look for.

**Suggested fix:** Map `thumbnails?.uri` and each `linkedFiles[].uri` through `pageAddress` in `crossing()`, and extend WorkerItemMapTest or a browser test with a relative thumbnail address.

**How to check it yourself:** Read KitePlayerWorker.kt:492-499 against WorkerProtocol.kt:483-486 and :1410-1412 (both fields cross, neither is made whole). Then in a browser test start a KitePlayerWorker from a page whose test media sits in a subfolder and open MediaItem("clip.mp4", thumbnails = ThumbnailSource("clip-thumbs.vtt")) with both relative to the page: the item plays and `events` carries PlaybackWarning.ThumbnailsUnreadable with reason `the file could not be read`, while the same item with ThumbnailSource("http://localhost:<port>/.../clip-thumbs.vtt") reads it.

**Verifier's note:** KitePlayerWorker.kt:492-499 is as quoted: `crossing` copies `uri`, `externalSubtitles` and `externalAudio` through `pageAddress` and leaves `thumbnails` and `linkedFiles` alone, while both do cross: WorkerProtocol.kt:483 `item.thumbnails?.let { put("thumbnails", it.uri) }` and :486 `put("linked", item.linkedFiles.encodeEach { file -> record { put("uri", file.uri) } })`, decoded at :1410 `thumbnails = o.str("thumbnails")?.let { ThumbnailSource(it) }`. `pageAddress` (KitePlayerWorker.kt:720-727) resolves only on the page (`typeof document === 'undefined'` returns the uri as is), so inside the worker a relative thumbnail stays schemeless. In the worker, PlaybackCore.readSubtitleBytes (lines 527-564) takes the http branch only for `startsWith("http://")`/`"https://"` and otherwise calls `readExternalFile`, whose wasmJs actual is `internal actual fun readExternalFile(path: String, limit: Int): ExternalFile = ExternalFile.Unreadable` (ExternalText.wasmJs.kt:4), so readItemThumbnails (PlaybackCore.kt:1920-1935) warns ThumbnailsUnreadable with `the file could not be read`. A linked file goes through linkedCandidates (LinkedFiles.kt:46-58) as a MediaItem whose schemeless uri SyncHttpResolver returns null for (SyncHttpMediaIo.kt:26-27), leaving it to the FFmpeg wasm backend, which has no file protocol on the web (MediaItem.kt KDoc: `A web page has no sockets, so there an address plays only through [io] or kiteplayer-network`). I found no other mapping in WorkerRuntime.kt (grep for thumbnails/linkedFiles/baseURI/location returns nothing). One nuance: the facade's own KDoc (KitePlayerWorker.kt:37-38) promises only `A relative address, of an item or of one of its subtitles, is read against the page's`, so the gap is between the `crossing` comment `with its addresses made whole` and the two fields it skips, plus the KDoc listing only two of the four address kinds. No test in kiteplayer/test@wasmJs covers a relative thumbnail or linked file (WorkerProtocolTest only checks crossingRefusal).

<!-- area: web/worker-io -->

### F-004 On the web worker the stall timeout is applied as a whole-request deadline over windows up to 16 MiB, so a slow link that is still delivering fails with SourceStalled.

**Severity:** high · **Kind:** Defect · **Repo:** KitePlayer · **Area:** web/worker-io · **Lane:** design-capabilities-crossmatch · **Verdict:** CONFIRMED · **Finder confidence:** high

**Where:**

- `kiteplayer/src@wasmJs/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/SyncHttpMediaIo.kt:216-219`
- `kiteplayer/src@wasmJs/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/SyncHttpMediaIo.kt:241-249`
- `kiteplayer/src@wasmJs/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/SyncHttpMediaIo.kt:332`
- `kiteplayer/src@wasmJs/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/WorkerRuntime.kt:75`
- `kiteplayer-core/src/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/PlayerConfig.kt:260-263`

**Evidence:** SyncHttpMediaIo.kt:216 `nextWindow = if (from == windowEnd && from > 0) (nextWindow * 2).coerceAtMost(MAX_WINDOW_BYTES) else FIRST_WINDOW_BYTES`; :247-248 `const val FIRST_WINDOW_BYTES = 1L shl 20` / `const val MAX_WINDOW_BYTES = 16L shl 20`; :241 `TIMED_OUT -> throw PlaybackException(PlaybackError.SourceStalled(url, timeout))`; :332 `xhr.timeout = s.timeout;`; WorkerRuntime.kt:75 `network = defaults.network.copy(ioResolver = SyncHttpResolver(defaults.buffer.stallTimeout))`. PlayerConfig.kt:262-263: "A packet from the source or bytes from the reader start it again, so a slow source that still delivers never stalls."

**Claim:** The worker's reader issues synchronous XHR range requests whose window doubles from 1 MiB to 16 MiB on sequential reads, and sets xhr.timeout to the stall timeout (30 s, and fixed, since the worker takes no PlayerConfig). A synchronous XHR timeout measures the whole request, not progress, so the knob documented as a no-progress deadline becomes a throughput floor: a 16 MiB window needs about 4.5 Mbit/s sustained to finish inside 30 s. Below that the request is aborted and the player fails with SourceStalled although bytes were arriving the whole time.

**Scenario:** A browser user on a 3 Mbit/s mobile connection plays a long MP4 or a DASH stream through KitePlayerWorker. After a few sequential reads the window reaches 16 MiB; that request takes about 45 s at 3 Mbit/s, the XHR times out at 30 s, and playback ends with PlaybackError.SourceStalled even though the server never paused. The same file plays on Android or the JVM, where the stall watch is reset by every byte.

**Impact:** Playback failure on exactly the networks where a player's buffering matters most; the error blames the server for a client-side policy; no configuration can change it because the worker builds its player on the default config.

**Suggested fix:** Bound the window by measured throughput so a window never asks for more than a fraction (say a third) of the timeout's worth of bytes at the current rate, or scale xhr.timeout with the window size (timeout per MiB plus a floor). Keep the doubling for fast links. Report SourceStalled only when the measured rate was zero for the timeout.

**How to check it yourself:** In scripts/web-tests/browser.mjs, throttle the response of a file over 32 MiB to about 3 Mbit/s and play it through KitePlayerWorker; the fifth sequential range request asks for 16 MiB (`Range: bytes=N-(N+16777215)`) and the player fails with SourceStalled at 30 s while the server is still sending. A fix can size the window from SyncDownloadMeter.bitsPerSecond() so one window needs well under the timeout, or make the timeout a no-progress deadline by reading in fixed small windows.

**Verifier's note:** All quoted lines exist. SyncHttpMediaIo.kt:216 `nextWindow = if (from == windowEnd && from > 0) (nextWindow * 2).coerceAtMost(MAX_WINDOW_BYTES) else FIRST_WINDOW_BYTES`, 247-248 `FIRST_WINDOW_BYTES = 1L shl 20` / `MAX_WINDOW_BYTES = 16L shl 20`, 241 `TIMED_OUT -> throw PlaybackException(PlaybackError.SourceStalled(url, timeout))`, 332 `xhr.timeout = s.timeout;` on a synchronous `xhr.open('GET', url, false)` (330), and 315 builds the state with `timeout.inWholeMilliseconds`. WorkerRuntime.kt:72-75 constructs `PlayerConfig()` and passes `SyncHttpResolver(defaults.buffer.stallTimeout)`, so the worker's value is the 30 s default and no page-side setting reaches it (WorkerProtocol.kt carries no PlayerConfig). XMLHttpRequest.timeout bounds the whole request, so with the window at 16 MiB after five forward reads the request is aborted at 30 s on any link slower than about 4.5 Mbit/s, and the class doc (89-91) confirms the window doubles while reads run forward. The reader has a throughput meter (SyncDownloadMeter, networkBitsPerSecond) but the window size never consults it. No guard, comment or test addresses a slow link: no test in kiteplayer/test@wasmJs or kiteplayer-web-worker mentions the window or a throttle. The PlayerConfig KDoc (262-263) promise that a slow source that still delivers never stalls is broken on this path.

### F-060 The worker's whole-request XHR timeout equals the 30 s stall budget, so a 16 MB window fails as SourceStalled on any healthy link slower than about 4.5 Mbit/s

**Severity:** medium · **Kind:** Defect · **Repo:** KitePlayer · **Area:** web/worker-io · **Lane:** web-worker-wasm-libass · **Verdict:** CONFIRMED · **Finder confidence:** high

**Where:**

- `kiteplayer/src@wasmJs/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/SyncHttpMediaIo.kt:99`
- `kiteplayer/src@wasmJs/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/SyncHttpMediaIo.kt:241`
- `kiteplayer/src@wasmJs/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/SyncHttpMediaIo.kt:332-338`
- `kiteplayer/src@wasmJs/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/WorkerRuntime.kt:75`
- `kiteplayer-core/src/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/PlayerConfig.kt:268`

**Evidence:** WorkerRuntime.kt:75 `ioResolver = SyncHttpResolver(defaults.buffer.stallTimeout)`; PlayerConfig.kt:268 `val stallTimeout: Duration = 30.seconds`; SyncHttpMediaIo.kt:99 `xhrState(headers.toJsObject(), timeout.inWholeMilliseconds.toDouble())`; 332 `xhr.timeout = s.timeout;` then 335-337 `catch (e) { ... return (e && e.name === 'TimeoutError') ? -1 : 0; }`; 241 `TIMED_OUT -> throw PlaybackException(PlaybackError.SourceStalled(url, timeout))`; the window reaches `MAX_WINDOW_BYTES = 16L shl 20` (249).

**Claim:** `XMLHttpRequest.timeout` limits the whole request, not inactivity. A 16 MiB window must therefore complete in 30 s, which needs 16 x 1048576 x 8 / 30 = 4.47 Mbit/s of sustained throughput. A slower but perfectly live connection fails the window with SourceStalled although bytes were arriving the whole time; the engine then treats the source as stalled rather than slow.

**Scenario:** A 3 Mbit/s audio-plus-video stream (which such a link can play) in the worker over a 4 Mbit/s connection. The first windows (1, 2, 4, 8 MB) succeed; the first 16 MB window takes about 34 s, the XHR throws TimeoutError and the player reports SourceStalled and reconnects or fails, repeatedly, around the 15 MB mark of forward play.

**Impact:** The worker cannot play a stream that the link could carry; the error names a stall that never happened.

**Suggested fix:** Size the window from the measured rate so that one request is a few hundred milliseconds of transfer, or compute the per-request timeout from the window size and a floor rate, keeping `stallTimeout` as a budget for inactivity (first byte) rather than for the whole body.

**How to check it yourself:** Throttle Chrome to 3.5 Mbit/s and play a 200 MB MP4 in the worker; observe SourceStalled (or a Reconnecting warning carrying it) once the window has grown to 16 MB, while the Network panel shows the request still receiving bytes when it is aborted.

**Verifier's note:** All cited lines exist as quoted. WorkerRuntime.kt:75 `network = defaults.network.copy(ioResolver = SyncHttpResolver(defaults.buffer.stallTimeout))`; PlayerConfig.kt:268 `val stallTimeout: Duration = 30.seconds`, whose KDoc at 258-266 promises "A packet from the source or bytes from the reader start it again, so a slow source that still delivers never stalls." SyncHttpMediaIo.kt:99 `xhrState(headers.toJsObject(), timeout.inWholeMilliseconds.toDouble())`, 332 `xhr.timeout = s.timeout;`, 335-337 return -1 on `TimeoutError`, and 241 `TIMED_OUT -> throw PlaybackException(PlaybackError.SourceStalled(url, timeout))`. `XMLHttpRequest.timeout` is a whole-request deadline (and is honoured on a synchronous request inside a worker), so a 16 MiB window must complete inside 30 s: 16 x 1048576 x 8 / 30 = 4.47 Mbit/s. Nothing adapts the window to the measured rate: SyncDownloadMeter only reports `networkBitsPerSecond()`, and fetch() doubles regardless. So a live but slow link gets SourceStalled while bytes were arriving, contradicting the config's own contract. The same timeout is also on the HEAD request (line 374) but that one is harmless. Severity medium is right.

<!-- area: webm/dash -->

### F-061 Webm.retrack recurses once per nested Cluster or BlockGroup with no depth limit, so a crafted DASH WebM segment overflows the stack, which on Kotlin/Native is a process crash

**Severity:** medium · **Kind:** Defect · **Repo:** KitePlayer · **Area:** webm/dash · **Lane:** kotlin-parsers-and-subtitles · **Verdict:** CONFIRMED · **Finder confidence:** high

**Where:**

- `kiteplayer-core/src/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/webm/Webm.kt:173-189`
- `kiteplayer-adaptive/src/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/network/dash/DashHlsMediaIo.kt:401-410`

**Evidence:** Webm.kt:173-177 `fun blocks(end: Long) { while (reader.position < end) { val child = reader.element() ?: return; when (child.id) { SEGMENT, CLUSTER, BLOCK_GROUP -> blocks(reader.end(child))` ... Webm.kt:189 `blocks(out.size.toLong())`. No depth counter anywhere in the function. Compare XmlMini.kt:57-63, where the owner documents exactly this failure ("parseElement recurses once per level, so a manifest of ten thousand opening tags raised StackOverflowError") and added MAX_DEPTH = 256. DashHlsMediaIo.kt:409 `Webm.retrack(moved, numbers)` runs on every WebM media segment whose header's track numbers differ from the base header's. The native nested-open trampoline (KiteFFmpeg MediaSource.native.kt:1143 `catch (failure: Throwable)`) cannot catch a Kotlin/Native stack overflow, which is a SIGSEGV, not a Throwable.

**Claim:** Each recursion level costs the attacker two bytes (a one-byte id 0xA0 and a one-byte size), so a 64 MB segment (MAX_SEGMENT_BYTES, DashMediaIo.kt:90) can nest millions deep. On the JVM and Android the resulting StackOverflowError is a Throwable and the bridge turns it into a failed segment open; on iOS, macOS and the other native targets a stack overflow kills the process.

**Scenario:** A DASH manifest with two WebM representations whose TrackEntry numbers differ (so numbersFor returns a non-identity map), and a media segment whose Cluster holds a BlockGroup inside a BlockGroup inside a BlockGroup, tens of thousands deep. An iPhone app playing that stream exits with a stack-overflow crash the moment the segment is served; the same stream on Android logs a failed segment and plays a gap.

**Impact:** Remote content can crash the host app on every Kotlin/Native target. Realistic nesting (one level) is unaffected.

**Suggested fix:** Rewrite `blocks` as a loop over a small explicit stack of (end) values, or add a depth counter and refuse past, say, 16 levels with WebmUnsupportedException (Matroska nests Segment > Cluster > BlockGroup > Block, three levels). Add a WebmTest that feeds a 100,000-level nested BlockGroup and asserts a typed refusal.

**How to check it yourself:** In WebmTest build the segment from the inside out: start with a SimpleBlock of track 1, then wrap it 200,000 times in `byteArrayOf(0xA0.toByte(), 0xFF.toByte()) + inner` (unknown-size BlockGroup, two bytes per level, no size arithmetic needed) and call `Webm.retrack(segment, mapOf(1L to 2L))` on the JVM: StackOverflowError. The same test on a native target (macosArm64 or linuxX64) aborts the test process rather than failing one test.

**Verifier's note:** Webm.kt:173-189 is exactly as quoted: `fun blocks(end: Long) { while (reader.position < end) { val child = reader.element() ?: return; when (child.id) { SEGMENT, CLUSTER, BLOCK_GROUP -> blocks(reader.end(child))` and the entry `blocks(out.size.toLong())`. There is no depth counter in Webm.kt (grep for depth/MAX_ finds only MAX_SHORT_NUMBER = 126). Reader.end at line 209 is `minOf(element.size?.let { position + it } ?: Long.MAX_VALUE, bytes.size.toLong())`, so an unknown-size vint (one byte 0xFF) makes each nested BlockGroup run to the end of the buffer, and `0xA0 0xFF` repeated is two bytes per level, as claimed. The only step before retrack, WebmRewrite.shiftClusters (TimelineRewrite.kt:13), is iterative and copies non-Cluster elements and Cluster children through unchanged, so it neither rejects nor flattens the nesting. DashHlsMediaIo.kt:401-409 calls `Webm.retrack(moved, numbers)` whenever `Webm.numbersFor(own, base)` is not identity, and the segment comes from `fetch(piece.url, piece.range, MAX_SEGMENT_BYTES)` with MAX_SEGMENT_BYTES = 64L shl 20 (DashMediaIo.kt:90). XmlMini.kt:57-63 shows the owner already met this failure shape in the XML parser and added MAX_DEPTH = 256; XspfReader has MAX_DEPTH = 64 (line 28, checked at 126). The Webm reader did not get the same guard. The native trampoline catches `Throwable` (MediaSource.native.kt:1143) and Kotlin/Native has no StackOverflowError; a stack overflow there is a signal, not an exception.

## 9. KitePlayer: design and performance

Shapes of the code that are not wrong on any one line but cost correctness, speed or maintainability as a whole.

<!-- area: api/java -->

### F-080 KitePlayerJava.close() leaves every listener's coroutines subscribed to the player

**Severity:** low · **Kind:** Design · **Repo:** KitePlayer · **Area:** api/java · **Lane:** public-api-and-docs · **Verdict:** CONFIRMED · **Finder confidence:** high

**Where:**

- `kiteplayer/src@jvmAndAndroid/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/KitePlayerJava.kt:54-56`
- `kiteplayer/src@jvmAndAndroid/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/KitePlayerJava.kt:73-97`
- `kiteplayer/src@jvmAndAndroid/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/KitePlayerJava.kt:351-357`

**Evidence:** 54-56: `private val root = SupervisorJob(); private val calls = CoroutineScope(root + Dispatchers.Default); private val registrations = ConcurrentHashMap<KitePlayerListener, Job>()`. 84-95: per listener a `Channel<PlayerEvent>(Channel.UNLIMITED)` plus four launched coroutines collecting losslessEvents, state, progress and the channel. 355-357: `override fun close() { player.close() }` with no cancel of root or registrations; KDoc 351-354: "Listeners stay until [removeListener], so they hear the closing state."

**Claim (as corrected by the verifier):** KitePlayerJava.close() closes the player but, by its own documented choice, keeps every listener's four collector coroutines, its unbounded channel and the listener object subscribed to the player's StateFlows until removeListener; nothing cancels `root`. The retention lasts as long as the KitePlayer object is reachable, which Java callers using try-with-resources will not expect, and the KDoc does not say so.

**Finder's original claim:** A Java AutoCloseable whose close() does not release what it created. After close() each registered listener keeps four coroutines parked on the player's StateFlows and lossless flow; the StateFlows never complete, so the coroutines, the unbounded channel and the listener object (typically an Activity or Fragment) stay reachable for as long as the player object is, which in a ViewModel-held player is the screen's lifetime or longer. Java code written as try-with-resources never calls removeListener.

**Scenario:** An Android app registers an Activity-implemented KitePlayerListener on a KitePlayerJava kept in a ViewModel, calls close() in onDestroy (or try-with-resources), rotates. The Activity is retained through the listener until the ViewModel is cleared and the player garbage collected.

**Impact:** Leak of UI objects and a few coroutines per listener; documented in passing but surprising for an AutoCloseable.

**Suggested fix:** In close(), after player.close(), launch a job that awaits player.awaitClose() and the terminal snapshot and then cancels `root`; or cancel root immediately and state in the KDoc that listeners receive nothing after close(). Add a test that a listener is unreachable after close() without removeListener.

**How to check it yourself:** In a JVM test: add a listener, call close(), then check `registrations` through reflection or a package-private accessor is non-empty and that `player.state` still has a subscriber (StateFlow.subscriptionCount); or run `closeAsync().get()` and then observe that `root.isActive` is still true.

**Verifier's note:** KitePlayerJava.kt 54-56: `private val root = SupervisorJob()`, `private val calls = CoroutineScope(root + Dispatchers.Default)`, `private val registrations = ConcurrentHashMap<KitePlayerListener, Job>()`. addListener (73-97) creates `val events = Channel<PlayerEvent>(Channel.UNLIMITED)` and launches four collectors: `player.losslessEvents.collect { events.trySend(it) }`, `deliver.launch { player.state.collect { listener.onState(it) } }`, `deliver.launch { player.progress.collect { listener.onProgress(it) } }` and the channel loop. close() at 355-357 is `override fun close() { player.close() }` and the only cancel paths are removeListener (103: `registrations.remove(listener)?.cancel()`) and the putIfAbsent duplicate branch. `state` and `progress` are `StateFlow` (KitePlayer.kt 74, 77), which never complete, so the collectors stay parked after close until removeListener, and the listener is reachable from the player's flow subscribers for as long as the player object is. The KDoc at 352-353 states this on purpose ("Listeners stay until [removeListener], so they hear the closing state"), so it is a documented design choice rather than an oversight, but the retention consequence is real and not documented, and `root` is never cancelled by close. KitePlayerJavaTest.java calls removeListener only in one test (line 121), never asserts the registrations are gone after close. Design finding with real evidence; severity low fits.

<!-- area: api/memento -->

### F-015 The memento's flat text form carries request headers and the full URI, and the Android resume card stores that text in plain SharedPreferences

**Severity:** medium · **Kind:** Design · **Repo:** KitePlayer · **Area:** api/memento · **Lane:** public-api-and-docs · **Verdict:** CONFIRMED · **Finder confidence:** high

**Where:**

- `kiteplayer-core/src/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/PlayerMemento.kt:97`
- `kiteplayer-core/src/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/PlayerMemento.kt:109`
- `kiteplayer/src@android/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/session/PlaybackResumption.kt:28-32`
- `kiteplayer/src@android/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/session/PlaybackResumption.kt:46-47`
- `kiteplayer-core/src/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/MediaItem.kt:224-232`

**Evidence:** PlayerMemento.kt 97: `put("queue.$n.uri", item.uri)`; 109: `item.headers.forEach { (name, value) -> put("queue.$n.header.$name", value) }`. PlaybackResumption.kt 28-32: `public fun save(context: Context, memento: PlayerMemento, title: String, subtitle: String? = null) { val editor = preferences(context).edit().clear(); resumptionEntries(memento, title, subtitle).forEach { (key, value) -> editor.putString(key, value) }; editor.apply() }`; 46-47: `context.applicationContext.getSharedPreferences(PREFERENCES, Context.MODE_PRIVATE)`. MediaItem.kt 224-232 KDoc of toString: "The item without its secrets: the URI cut to [label], and header and option names without their values. An `Authorization` header or a signed URL in a printed item is a leaked credential". PlayerMemento.kt 15-16 only says "Headers, raw open options ... are strings and travel."

**Claim (as corrected by the verifier):** PlayerMemento.asProperties() writes header values and full URIs, which restore() needs, but neither its KDoc, the resumption KDoc nor docs/module-contract.md says that the text carries credentials, and KitePlayerResumption persists it unredacted in default SharedPreferences, which Android backs up unless the app opts out; this contradicts the project's own rule that printed and cached items never hold an Authorization value or a signed URL.

**Finder's original claim:** The library is careful never to print a header value or a query string (MediaItem.toString, PlaybackError.toString, KiteLog.redactUris, every warning), yet the one serialisation it hands applications writes Authorization values and signed URLs verbatim, and its own Android resume feature persists that text in MODE_PRIVATE SharedPreferences, which Android's default `allowBackup=true` uploads to the user's cloud backup and which any rooted device or ADB backup can read. No KDoc, README or module-contract sentence warns that asProperties() carries credentials or that KitePlayerResumption stores them.

**Scenario:** An app plays a signed CDN URL or sends `Authorization: Bearer <token>` in MediaItem.headers and calls KitePlayerResumption.save at pause, as docs/module-contract.md suggests ("for example at a pause and when the player closes"). The token sits in shared_prefs XML until clear() is called, survives app updates, and travels with device backups.

**Impact:** Credential persistence the app did not knowingly opt into, in a library whose other surfaces promise redaction. Not exploitable remotely, but a hygiene gap a security review of a consumer app would flag against the library.

**Suggested fix:** Document plainly on PlayerMemento.asProperties and KitePlayerResumption.save that the text carries header values and query strings. Offer `asProperties(includeSecrets: Boolean = true)` that drops header values and the query string when false, and have the resumption service accept a memento whose items need headers re-supplied in onResume (or store with EncryptedSharedPreferences where available). Consider excluding the preferences file from auto backup via a documented `android:fullBackupContent` rule.

**How to check it yourself:** On a debug build call KitePlayerResumption.save with an item whose headers contain Authorization, then `adb shell run-as <pkg> cat shared_prefs/io.github.yuroyami.kiteplayer.resumption.xml`: the bearer token is in clear text.

**Verifier's note:** PlayerMemento.kt 97 `put("queue.$n.uri", item.uri)` and 109 `item.headers.forEach { (name, value) -> put("queue.$n.header.$name", value) }` write the full URI and header values. PlaybackResumption.kt 28-32 saves `resumptionEntries(memento, title, subtitle)` with `editor.putString(key, value)` into `getSharedPreferences(PREFERENCES, Context.MODE_PRIVATE)` (46-47), and `resumptionEntries` (line 171) is `memento.asProperties()` with a prefix. The contrast with the project's own redaction standard is real: MediaItem.kt 224-232 toString KDoc says 'An Authorization header or a signed URL in a printed item is a leaked credential', `label` drops the query 'because that is where a signed URL keeps its signature', and docs/segment-cache.md 108-118 keys cache entries by the Authorization and Cookie values precisely so a store never holds a credential readably and requires `privateToOneAccount = true` before storing such requests. Grepping PlayerMemento.kt, PlaybackResumption.kt, docs/module-contract.md 298-341 and README for credential, secret, token or backup finds no warning; the only mention is PlayerMemento.kt 15-16 'Headers, raw open options ... are strings and travel', and the only allowBackup=false in the tree is a verification app manifest. One narrowing: carrying headers is necessary for restore() to reopen an authenticated item, so the defect is not that they travel but that nothing says so and that the Android resumption store persists them unredacted in backup-eligible preferences. This is a design and documentation finding and the evidence holds.

<!-- area: audio/resampler -->

### F-082 The default rate converter rolls off the top octave and rejects near-Nyquist aliases by only 12 to 46 dB, while its documentation claims a properly deep stopband

**Severity:** low (finder said medium, verifier corrected) · **Kind:** Performance · **Repo:** KitePlayer · **Area:** audio/resampler · **Lane:** audio-clock-ring-sinks · **Verdict:** CONFIRMED · **Finder confidence:** high

**Where:**

- `kiteplayer-core/src/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/internal/SincResampler.kt:263-299`
- `kiteplayer-core/src/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/internal/SincResampler.kt:302-328`
- `kiteplayer-core/test/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/SincResamplerTest.kt:198-215`

**Evidence:** SincResampler.kt:310 `const val TAPS: Int = 32`; :328 `const val ROLLOFF: Double = 0.925`; :266 `val cutoff = min(1.0, targetRate.toDouble() / sourceRate) * ROLLOFF`; :294-299 Blackman window `0.42 - 0.5 * cos(angle) + 0.08 * cos(2.0 * angle)` over `ratio = distance / half`. KDoc :305-306 "the stopband is deep enough that the residual aliasing is far below anything a listener can hear"; :325-327 "At 44.1 kHz this puts the corner near 20.4 kHz, above anything most listeners can hear, and keeps the stopband properly deep." The only alias test, SincResamplerTest.kt:198-215, converts 48 kHz to 16 kHz with a 15 kHz tone, which is 1.875 times the target Nyquist. I computed the DTFT of the phase-0 kernel row exactly as buildKernel builds it (normalised to unity sum): 48k->44.1k: -0.3 dB at 18 kHz, -1.5 dB at 19 kHz, -4.3 dB at 20 kHz, -6.0 dB at 20.4 kHz, -18.6 dB at 22.05 kHz, -31.7 dB at 23 kHz (folds to 21.1 kHz), -49 dB at 24 kHz (folds to 20.1 kHz). 96k->48k: -1.3 dB at 19.2 kHz, -4.7 dB at 21.6 kHz, -11.6 dB at 24 kHz, -17 dB at 25.2 kHz (folds to 22.8 kHz), -24 dB at 26.4 kHz (folds to 21.6 kHz), -46 dB at 28.8 kHz (folds to 19.2 kHz), -78 dB at 31.2 kHz. 44.1k->48k upsample: -1.3 dB at 19 kHz, -4.2 dB at 20 kHz.

**Claim (as corrected by the verifier):** The default 32-tap Blackman sinc at ROLLOFF 0.925 has a transition band about a third of Nyquist wide: converting down, content between the target Nyquist and about 1.2 times it is attenuated only 12 to 32 dB before it folds into 19 to 22 kHz, and the passband is down 1.3 to 1.5 dB at 19 kHz and 4 dB at 20 kHz. The KDoc's "properly deep" stopband holds only from about 1.3 times Nyquist upward, and the one alias test measures at 1.875 times Nyquist. Audible impact is at the edge of hearing for most material; the documentation claim is what is wrong.

**Finder's original claim:** A 32-tap Blackman-windowed sinc has a transition band roughly 5.5/32 of the input rate wide, about a third of Nyquist. With the -6 dB corner at 0.925 Nyquist the passband already droops a decibel or more above 18 to 19 kHz, and when converting down the band from the target Nyquist to about 1.2 times it is attenuated only 12 to 46 dB before it folds back into 19 to 22 kHz. The KDoc's "properly deep" claim is true only from about 1.3 times Nyquist upward, which the existing test (1.875 times Nyquist) is the only thing that measures.

**Scenario:** Any playback where the file rate and the device rate differ with the built-in resampler (no AudioResamplerFactory configured): 44.1 kHz music on a 48 kHz Android or Mac device, 48 kHz video on a 44.1 kHz device, 96 kHz material on a 48 kHz device. Bright material (cymbals, synthetic test tones, high-resolution masters) produces measurable aliasing products at -17 to -32 dB in the 20 to 23 kHz region and a gentle treble roll-off in the last octave.

**Impact:** Measurable fidelity below libswresample's and mpv's defaults on the most common playback path; marginally audible on bright material for listeners with good high-frequency hearing, plainly visible on any spectrum analyser, and at odds with the project's own stated quality. The cost of fixing is small: the hot loop is TAPS multiply-adds per channel per output frame (about 3 M/s at 48 kHz stereo today).

**Suggested fix:** Raise TAPS to 64 (or use a Kaiser window with beta near 10 at 48 taps) and move ROLLOFF to about 0.95; keep PHASES at 512 with the existing linear phase interpolation. Add a test that converts 48k->44.1k with a 23 kHz tone and asserts the 21.1 kHz product is at least 60 dB down, and one that asserts a 19 kHz tone through 44.1k->48k keeps at least -0.5 dB. Rewrite the KDoc at lines 302-308 and 321-327 to state the measured numbers.

**How to check it yourself:** python3: build one row with cutoff = min(1, target/source) * 0.925, h[n] = cutoff * sinc(cutoff * d) * blackman(d / 16) for d = (n - 15), normalise to unit sum, evaluate 20*log10|sum h[n] e^(-j*2*pi*f*n/source)|. For source 48000, target 44100 expect about -18.6 dB at f = 22050 and -31.7 dB at f = 23000. Or run SincResampler(48000, 44100, 1) on a 23 kHz tone and measure 21.1 kHz with the test file's amplitudeAt helper.

**Verifier's note:** The cited code exists as quoted: SincResampler.kt:266 `val cutoff = min(1.0, targetRate.toDouble() / sourceRate) * ROLLOFF`, :274 `val value = cutoff * sinc(cutoff * distance) * window(distance)`, :294-299 Blackman over `ratio = distance / half` with `half = TAPS / 2` (:74), :310 `const val TAPS: Int = 32`, :328 `const val ROLLOFF: Double = 0.925`. KDoc :305-306 reads "the stopband is deep enough that the residual aliasing is far below anything a listener can hear" and :325-327 "At 44.1 kHz this puts the corner near 20.4 kHz ... and keeps the stopband properly deep." I rebuilt the phase-0 row in python exactly as buildKernel does (unit-sum normalised) and got the same numbers to 0.1 dB: 48k->44.1k -0.3 dB at 18 kHz, -1.5 at 19, -4.3 at 20, -6.0 at 20.4, -18.6 at 22.05, -31.7 at 23, -49.2 at 24; 96k->48k -1.3 at 19.2, -11.6 at 24, -17.0 at 25.2, -24.0 at 26.4, -46.4 at 28.8; 44.1k->48k -1.3 at 19, -4.2 at 20. The only alias test (SincResamplerTest.kt:198-215) uses a 15 kHz tone into 16 kHz, 1.875 times the target Nyquist; the passband test at :218 uses 1 kHz and :282 uses 10 kHz, so nothing measures the band between 0.8 and 1.3 times Nyquist. No AudioResamplerFactory is configured by default (PlayerConfig.kt:423 `val resampler: AudioResamplerFactory? = null`), so this filter is what ships. The numbers and the KDoc mismatch are real; the practical audibility is the only soft part, since real material above 20 kHz is weak and the droop sits above 18 kHz, which is why I would call it low rather than medium.
