### F-122 The quiesce handshake and the production dispatcher shape are never tested on real threads except on a developer Mac

**Severity:** low (finder said medium, verifier corrected) · **Kind:** Test gap · **Repo:** KitePlayer · **Area:** core/quiesce · **Lane:** engine-actor-open · **Verdict:** CONFIRMED · **Finder confidence:** high · **Related open issue:** #639

**Where:**

- `kiteplayer-core/test@macosArm64/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/RealThreadStressTest.kt:44-74`
- `kiteplayer-core/src/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/internal/PlatformDispatchers.kt:48-85`
- `kiteplayer-core/src/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/internal/PlaybackWorkers.kt:128-160`

**Evidence:** RealThreadStressTest lives in `test@macosArm64` only and builds `newSingleThreadContext("stress-session")` per lane (47-56). grep in kiteplayer-core/test for `Worker("`, `requestQuiesce`, `awaitQuiesced`: no matches, so Worker has no unit test. CoreHarness: `dispatchers = PlaybackDispatchers.sharing(engineDispatcher(scheduler))` (one StandardTestDispatcher for every lane). Production: `SharedLaneDispatchers(calm = Dispatchers.Default, blocking = Dispatchers.IO)` with `blocking.limitedParallelism(1)` per lane (PlatformDispatchers.jvm/android/native.kt 13-14; PlatformDispatchers.kt 53-77); grep of the test trees for `SharedLaneDispatchers`: no matches. CI runs macosArm64 tests (ci.yml 212-216) but no Linux/JVM real-thread equivalent.

**Claim (as corrected by the verifier):** The quiesce handshake has no targeted test on the shipped SharedLaneDispatchers shape: Worker has no unit test, and the only stress test (RealThreadStressTest) is macOS-only and uses one OS thread per lane. Real-thread coverage on JVM and Linux CI is incidental, through the whole-player real-media suites in kiteplayer-ffmpeg/test@jvm and kiteplayer/test@jvm, which use KitePlayer.create() and production dispatchers and do seek and close, so a Worker regression is not invisible there, but it is caught only if one of those runs happens to hit the interleaving.

**Finder's original claim:** The checkpoint ordering comment in Worker.checkpoint (134-141) describes a race fixed by reordering `parkedNow.value = false` before the deciding flag read; nothing in the common tests can reproduce that race because every lane shares one cooperative dispatcher. The only real-thread test runs on a Mac with one OS thread per lane, which is not the shape shipped: SharedLaneDispatchers lanes migrate between pool threads and ride the elastic IO pool, where thread parking and wake latency differ. JVM, Android and Linux CI jobs therefore never exercise the handshake under real concurrency.

**Scenario:** A regression in Worker (for example reverting the parkedNow ordering, or a stale wake token) passes every JVM test and every Android test, and is caught only if a maintainer runs the macOS job and the stress test happens to hit the interleaving.

**Impact:** The single most delicate piece of the engine has no CI coverage on the platforms most users run.

**Suggested fix:** Move RealThreadStressTest to the common test set for jvm and native (newSingleThreadContext exists on both; it uses runBlocking so exclude js/wasm), add a second variant that builds `SharedLaneDispatchers(Dispatchers.Default, Dispatchers.IO)`, and add a small Worker unit test on real threads that hammers requestQuiesce/awaitQuiesced/release against a checkpoint loop and asserts the worker never runs its body between a true awaitQuiesced and the release.

**How to check it yourself:** `ls kiteplayer-core/test@macosArm64`; `grep -rln 'KitePlayer.create\|KitePlayer(' kiteplayer-ffmpeg/test@jvm kiteplayer/test@jvm` and confirm none passes a dispatchers argument (grep 'dispatchers =' in those trees is empty), so they run on SharedLaneDispatchers; then note that no test in any tree references Worker, requestQuiesce or awaitQuiesced directly. The gap is a dedicated stress test of Worker on Dispatchers.IO lanes that runs on the jvm target, not an absence of real-thread execution.

**Verifier's note:** The factual parts hold: RealThreadStressTest lives only in kiteplayer-core/test@macosArm64 and builds `newSingleThreadContext("stress-...")` per lane (47-53); `grep -rln "SharedLaneDispatchers\|requestQuiesce\|awaitQuiesced" kiteplayer-core/test*` matches no test that exercises Worker's handshake (the hits are CloseDeadlineJvmTest, LatestSettingReplyJvmTest and SubtitleParseLaneJvmTest, which use Dispatchers.IO or one thread for other purposes); Worker (PlaybackWorkers.kt 107) has no unit test, and the checkpoint ordering comment at 136-141 describes a race no cooperative-dispatcher test can reproduce. But the headline claim that 'JVM, Android and Linux CI jobs therefore never exercise the handshake under real concurrency' is wrong. kiteplayer-ffmpeg/test@jvm and kiteplayer/test@jvm hold whole-player tests built through `KitePlayer.create(` (SeekRunUpSkipTest.kt 78, with `player.seek(TARGET_US.microseconds, SeekMode.Precise)` at 94; also ExternalAudioPlaybackTest, MatroskaEditionsTest, LateSoundStartTest, DashPlaybackTest, SegmentStorePlaybackTest), none of which passes `dispatchers =`, so they run on `SharedLaneDispatchers(calm = Dispatchers.Default, blocking = Dispatchers.IO)` (PlatformDispatchers.jvm.kt 13-14), and ci.yml runs them on macos-jvm (343-344) and on the Linux job (`for module in kiteplayer-ffmpeg kiteplayer; do ./kotlin test -m "$module" -p jvm` at 554-556). PlaybackCoreTest 1247 also closes a core built with platformPlaybackDispatchers(). So the shipped dispatcher shape, with seeks and closes, is exercised on real threads on Linux and macOS JVM; what is missing is a targeted, repeated stress of the quiesce handshake on that shape, as opposed to incidental coverage inside real-media suites that CLAUDE.md itself says are re-run when they fail under load.

### F-035 The one test of the pause-refused live resume cannot see the frame and sample loss it is meant to rule out

**Severity:** medium · **Kind:** Test gap · **Repo:** KitePlayer · **Area:** core/tests · **Lane:** engine-subtitles-output-tail · **Verdict:** CONFIRMED · **Finder confidence:** high

**Where:**

- `kiteplayer-core/test/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/LivePauseTest.kt:89-109`

**Evidence:** LivePauseTest 89-109 `aSenderThatCannotPauseIsReadAsBefore`: the only assertions are `assertEquals(1, source.pauseReadingCalls ...)`, `assertEquals(0, source.resumeReadingCalls)`, `assertEquals(PlaybackStatus.Playing, harness.status(), ...)` and `assertTrue(moved in 0.milliseconds..500.milliseconds, ...)`. No assertion reads the frames the renderer received, the decoded frame count, or the samples the sink took.

**Claim:** The test's name claims the stream 'is read as before', but it would pass with a frame and a packet thrown away and a buffer of sound abandoned on every resume, which is what the code does (finding 1). The #592 fix on the audio decode lane is also only indirectly covered here.

**Scenario:** Any regression in the non-flushing park path of any lane stays green.

**Impact:** The park-without-flush family of paths (resumeLiveSender, handleOutputChange, picture swaps) has no continuity oracle.

**Suggested fix:** Assert continuity: collect the pts of every frame the fake renderer presents and every buffer the fake sink pulls across the pause and resume, and assert there is no gap larger than one frame period and no missing pts between the last frame before the pause and the first after it. Reuse the same oracle for handleOutputChange and playPictureInPlace.

**How to check it yourself:** In aSenderThatCannotPauseIsReadAsBefore, record the renderer's received frame timestamps and the scripted sink's taken frame count before the pause and after the 200 ms of play, and assert the presentation timestamps across the resume step by one frame interval with no gap, and that the sink's taken frames equal what the decoder produced. Run it against the current tree: the video side should show a one-frame gap where handOver closed the frame in hand.

**Verifier's note:** LivePauseTest.kt 89-109 `aSenderThatCannotPauseIsReadAsBefore` asserts only `assertEquals(1, source.pauseReadingCalls, ...)`, `assertEquals(0, source.resumeReadingCalls)`, `assertEquals(PlaybackStatus.Playing, harness.status(), ...)` and `assertTrue(moved in 0.milliseconds..500.milliseconds, ...)`; nothing reads the renderer's received frames or the sink's samples. The premise that the path can lose work is real in the code: resumeLiveSender (7697-7716) parks every worker through unparkedWorkers (12308-12314, `for (worker in workers) worker.requestQuiesce()`), and for a refused hold takes `if (!hold.held) { releaseWorkers(session, requestedEpoch); return }` with no flush and no new epoch. On the video lane, handOver (14557-14625) returns false when quiescence is asked for and its finally does `if (ownsFrame) frame.close()`, after which the decode loop at 14379-14395 breaks out of `while (!videoDecoderSend(decoder, packet))` and its finally does `packet.close()` on a packet the decoder had not taken. The audio lane, by contrast, keeps both: 14728-14731 `What a park interrupted, kept for the release that follows it (#592). A park that does not flush, the output reopen and the resume of a live sender that could not hold its pause, used to close the buffer in hand and the packet the decoder had not taken yet, and the sound skipped them.` So the test's name claims continuity that no assertion checks, and the only test naming #592 is AudioSinkEventTest (the output reopen), not this path. The harness renderer records every presented frame in `received` (TestSupport.kt 282-292 use `received.size`), so a continuity assertion is available. Medium is fair given the video lane does lose a frame and a packet here today.

### F-037 The renderer SPI and VsyncAwarenessTest both claim the display interval improves pacing, and the test proves only that the number is stored.

**Severity:** medium · **Kind:** Test gap · **Repo:** KitePlayer · **Area:** core/video-schedule · **Lane:** video-render-colour · **Verdict:** CONFIRMED · **Finder confidence:** high · **Related open issue:** 696

**Where:**

- `kiteplayer-core/src/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/spi/VideoRenderer.kt:22-23`
- `kiteplayer-core/src/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/VideoPlayback.kt:124-129`
- `kiteplayer-core/test/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/VsyncAwarenessTest.kt:16-20`
- `kiteplayer-core/test/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/VsyncAwarenessTest.kt:46-58`

**Evidence:** VideoRenderer.kt:22-23: `4. [vsyncIntervalNanos] is advisory. Returning null costs smoothness on a high refresh display and nothing else.` VideoPlayback.kt:124-129: `Held here because the schedule is the one consumer pacing against a display.` VsyncAwarenessTest.kt:17-19: `Every renderer used to answer null and the engine discarded VsyncChanged outright, so a 120 Hz phone and a ProMotion Mac were paced no better than a display nobody asked.` The assertions at 46-58 compare `harness.core.videoScheduleVsyncNanos` to the fed value and nothing else.

**Claim (as corrected by the verifier):** SPI rule 4 and the VideoPlayback KDoc promise that a reported display interval buys smoothness, and VsyncAwarenessTest's class comment says the interval now paces 120 Hz displays, but no schedule code reads VideoPlayback.vsyncIntervalNanos, so a renderer answering null and one answering 8.33 ms produce identical presentation timing. The test proves only that the value is stored; the test method's own name says as much, the class comment and the SPI text do not.

**Finder's original claim:** The documentation promises a smoothness difference between answering null and answering a real interval, and the test is named as if it verified pacing, but the schedule never reads the value, so the two cases produce byte-identical presentation timing. The test cannot fail for the thing its name and comment describe.

**Scenario:** A renderer author reads rule 4, does the work to report the interval accurately (as UIKitVideoRenderer, AppKitVideoRenderer, AwtCanvasVideoRenderer and the Android view do), and gets nothing for it; a reviewer reading the test believes vsync pacing is covered.

**Impact:** Misleading contract for SPI implementers and a false sense of coverage over the pacing path, which is where #696 lives.

**Suggested fix:** Either make the schedule use the interval (see the pacing finding) and extend the test to assert on presentation targets landing on refresh edges with a scripted clock, or reword rule 4 and the VideoPlayback KDoc to say the value is recorded for diagnostics only and rename the test to what it checks.

**How to check it yourself:** Replace the interval the test renderer returns with null and run VsyncAwarenessTest together with VideoPlaybackTest: every timing assertion passes unchanged. Then search VideoPlayback.kt for any read of vsyncIntervalNanos.

**Verifier's note:** VideoRenderer.kt:22-23 reads exactly `4. [vsyncIntervalNanos] is advisory. Returning null costs smoothness on a high refresh display` / `and nothing else.` VideoPlayback.kt:124-128 KDoc says `Advisory, exactly as the SPI says: null costs smoothness on a high-refresh display and nothing else. Held here because the schedule is the one consumer pacing against a display.` VsyncAwarenessTest.kt:17-19 says `Every renderer used to answer null and the engine discarded [RendererEvent.VsyncChanged] outright, so a 120 Hz phone and a ProMotion Mac were paced no better than a display nobody asked.` Its two assertions (lines 46-50 and 54-58) compare `harness.core.videoScheduleVsyncNanos` to 16_666_666L and 8_333_333L and nothing else. As established for finding 0, nothing in VideoPlayback reads vsyncIntervalNanos, so the smoothness the SPI rule and the test comment promise is not produced by any code path, and the test only proves storage. The test's own name, `attach seeds the schedule's interval and VsyncChanged moves it`, is honest about what it checks; it is the class comment and the SPI rule that overreach. Test-gap and docs claim holds on the evidence.

### F-155 The browser run of the libass corpus test can pass while drawing no pixel, because the visibility assertion is skipped when no host font is readable

**Severity:** low · **Kind:** Test gap · **Repo:** KitePlayer · **Area:** libass/web-tests · **Lane:** web-worker-wasm-libass · **Verdict:** CONFIRMED · **Finder confidence:** high

**Where:**

- `kiteplayer-libass/test@wasmJs/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/libass/LibassWebTest.kt:20-26`
- `kiteplayer-libass/test@wasmJs/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/libass/LibassWebTest.kt:45-58`
- `kiteplayer-libass/test@wasmJs/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/libass/LibassWebTest.kt:94-128`
- `kiteplayer-libass/test@wasmJs/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/libass/LibassWebTest.kt:131-166`
- `kiteplayer-libass/test@wasmJs/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/libass/LibassColorTestFont.kt:3-12`

**Evidence:** LibassWebTest.kt:45-58 `hostFont()` reads `/System/Library/Fonts/Supplemental/Arial.ttf` or DejaVuSans through `webReadFileLatin1`, which has no filesystem in a browser; 97 `if (font == null) println("LibassWebTest: no host font readable here; comparing pictures without one")`; 127 `if (font != null) assertTrue(visibleSomewhere, ...)`.

**Claim (as corrected by the verifier):** In headless Chrome the corpus test `everyCorpusScriptStreamsToTheBytesItsWholeDocumentRenders` compares two empty region lists for every script and instant, because no host font is readable there, and the visible-pixel assertion is skipped by design (the class KDoc says so). The browser half is not entirely pixel-free: the colour test in the same class renders an opaque vector box through the authored LibassColorTestFont and checks its middle pixel. The streamed-versus-document equality itself is exercised with pixels only under Node on a host that has Arial or DejaVuSans.

**Finder's original claim:** In headless Chrome the font is null, every render of both paths is an empty region list, `assertSameImages` compares two empty lists for six instants of every corpus script, and the test passes having proved only that two empty renders agree. The streamed-versus-document equality that the test is named for is exercised with pixels only under Node on a host with that font.

**Scenario:** A regression in the wasm build of kite_ass.h's packing (for example a wrong stride) would pass the browser half of this test and be caught only by the Node half on a Mac or a Linux box with DejaVu.

**Impact:** Weaker browser evidence than the test's name suggests; the colour-matching test (theWebModuleMatchesAScriptsColoursToTheVideo) with its authored font fixture is the only browser test that proves the module draws.

**Suggested fix:** Use the authored LibassColorTestFont fixture (or a small bundled TTF in testResources@wasmJs) in the corpus test as well, so the browser run always has a font and always asserts `visibleSomewhere`.

**How to check it yourself:** Run `python3 scripts/web-tests/run.py --platform wasmJsBrowser --module kiteplayer-libass` and read build/web-tests/kiteplayer-libass-wasmJsBrowser.log for `no host font readable here`. To make the corpus comparison carry pixels in the browser without a text font, add one corpus script drawn with `\\p1` vector commands in the KiteColorBox style and feed `libassColorTestFont()` as a fallback when `hostFont()` is null; then a wrong stride in kite_ass's packing changes bytes that `assertSameImages` compares.

**Verifier's note:** The quoted code exists at the cited lines. LibassWebTest.kt:45-58 `hostFont()` reads Arial or DejaVuSans through `webReadFileLatin1`, which is `node:fs` only (line 228 comment: `Node only: the promise rejects in a browser, which the caller treats as "no font here"`). Line 97: `if (font == null) println("LibassWebTest: no host font readable here; comparing pictures without one")`, and line 127: `if (font != null) assertTrue(visibleSomewhere, ...)`. With no font every render is empty and `assertSameImages` compares two empty lists, so the streamed-versus-document comparison carries no pixels in the browser. Two things narrow the finding. First, this is documented, not accidental: the class KDoc (lines 20-25) says `in a browser there is no filesystem and no system font, so the comparison there proves the streaming path and the module plumbing, and the visible-pixel check is skipped with a note.` Second, the same class does draw opaque pixels in the browser: `theWebModuleMatchesAScriptsColoursToTheVideo` (lines 131-166) feeds `libassColorTestFont()`, an authored font whose only glyph is a rectangle, renders a `\\p1` vector box and asserts the middle pixel is opaque and the exact colour, in both Node and a browser. A stride error that moves pixels would likely show there (the box's middle is computed from width and height), though a solid box is a weak probe for a packing bug. The gap that stands: the corpus streamed-versus-whole comparison, which is the test's purpose, is pixel-free in the browser, and the authored font cannot fix that for text scripts because it has no letter glyphs (LibassColorTestFont.kt:4-5).

### F-159 The fMP4 and WebM readers have no truncation or mutation tests, while every text parser has a two-thousand-mutation fuzz

**Severity:** low · **Kind:** Test gap · **Repo:** KitePlayer · **Area:** mp4/webm tests · **Lane:** kotlin-parsers-and-subtitles · **Verdict:** CONFIRMED · **Finder confidence:** high

**Where:**

- `kiteplayer-subtitles/test/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/subtitle/ParserRobustnessTest.kt:21-44`
- `kiteplayer-adaptive/test/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/network/dash/Fmp4Test.kt:47-101`
- `kiteplayer-core/test/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/webm/WebmTest.kt:48-100`
- `kiteplayer-core/src/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/mp4/Fmp4.kt:245-249`
- `kiteplayer-core/src/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/webm/Webm.kt:173-189`
- `kiteplayer-adaptive/src/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/network/dash/DashHlsMediaIo.kt:182-188`

**Evidence:** ParserRobustnessTest.kt:21-37 fuzzes SubRip, WebVTT, ASS documents and ASS events with the invariant "parsing never throws, every cue ends at or after it starts, and one parse takes under a second". Fmp4Test's cases (lines 15-120) are hand-built positive cases plus five specific refusals; WebmTest has three positive cases; neither has a truncated-buffer sweep like SeiCaptionsTest's `aTruncatedPacketGivesNothingRatherThanFailing` (SeiCaptionsTest.kt:97-103), and no test nests EBML elements or shortens a sample entry.

**Claim (as corrected by the verifier):** Fmp4 and Webm, the two byte readers fed from the network, have no randomized or truncation test: Fmp4Test has five targeted refusal cases (#474) but no sweep, and WebmTest and WebmIndexTest have only positive cases plus one not-WebM refusal, while every text parser in kiteplayer-subtitles gets two thousand mutations per fixture. Fmp4's multi-byte reads are guarded by `require` in `u32`, so a hostile segment fails with an IllegalArgumentException that `dashFmp4` does not map and `serve` does not log; `u24` and the one-byte version reads are the only unguarded indexes, reachable by a mutation rather than a truncation. `Webm.retrack` recurses once per nested Segment, Cluster or BlockGroup with no depth limit, so a segment built of thousands of nested 5-byte headers overflows the stack, and that error also escapes the DASH and HLS call sites unlogged.

**Finder's original claim:** The byte readers are the ones fed by the network without the user's choice, yet they are the only parsers in this lane with no hostile-input test. The two defects reported above (unguarded indexes in Fmp4, unbounded recursion in Webm.retrack) would both have been found by a per-byte truncation sweep and a nesting case.

**Scenario:** A future change to Fmp4.fragments or Webm.header adds another direct index read; the suite stays green and the failure appears as an unlogged failed segment in the field.

**Impact:** Coverage gap where it matters most for the streaming ambition.

**Suggested fix:** Add a truncation sweep (`for (cut in 1 until segment.size) assert only Fmp4UnsupportedException or IllegalArgumentException from Fmp4.fragments(segment.copyOf(cut), track)`) and a byte-flip fuzz over Mp4Bytes and WebmTest's builders, with the same three invariants as ParserRobustnessTest and a wall-time bound, for Fmp4.tracks, Fmp4.fragments, Fmp4Rewrite.rewrite, Webm.header, Webm.numbersFor, Webm.retrack and WebmRewrite.shiftClusters.

**How to check it yourself:** Port the `fuzz` helper of ParserRobustnessTest to byte arrays: seed with `Mp4Bytes.segment(1, 90_000, listOf(Sample(2000, byteArrayOf(1, 2, 3))))` and `WebmBytes` fixtures, mutate two thousand times (flip, insert, delete, truncate), and assert each of `Fmp4.fragments`, `Fmp4.tracks`, `Webm.header` and `Webm.retrack` finishes under a second and throws nothing other than Fmp4UnsupportedException, WebmUnsupportedException or IllegalArgumentException. A plain truncation sweep of that segment will pass (empty result or IllegalArgumentException at the mdat cuts), so do not expect ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException from it. For retrack, build a segment of 50,000 nested `18 53 80 67 FF` (Segment, unknown size) headers and call `Webm.retrack(bytes, mapOf(1L to 2L))`; expect StackOverflowError.

**Verifier's note:** The gap is real but the finding misdescribes both what exists and what the proposed sweep would find. ParserRobustnessTest.kt:21-37 is as quoted (three invariants, two thousand mutations per seed). WebmTest.kt has exactly three positive tests (:49, :62, :80) and WebmIndexTest one refusal (`aFileThatIsNotWebmIsRefusedTyped`). Fmp4Test.kt, however, already has five hostile-input tests at :48, :56, :70, :81, :95 (`zeroSizeSamplesPastTheBudgetAreRefusedBeforeAnyIsMade`, `aRunWhoseSampleFieldsRunPastItsBoxIsRefused`, `defaultSizedSamplesThatOverrunTheSegmentAreRefused`, `aBaseOffsetPastTheSegmentIsRefusedRatherThanCutToItsLowBits`), so 'the only parsers in this lane with no hostile-input test' is wrong for Fmp4; what is missing is a sweep or mutation fuzz. The check recipe is wrong: Fmp4.kt:248-249 `fun u32(...) { require(at >= 0 && at + 4 <= bytes.size) { "a box ends inside its fields" }` guards every u32, s32 and u64 read, and `boxes()` at :232 `if (size < header || at + size > to) break` drops a box cut short. A truncation of `Mp4Bytes.segment(...)` (styp + moof + mdat, Mp4Bytes.kt:112) inside the moof therefore yields no fragment at all, and a cut inside the mdat trips `require(dataAt >= 0 && dataAt <= segment.size && size <= segment.size - dataAt)` at :197 (or :181), the IllegalArgumentException the KDoc at :136 documents. No cut raises ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException. The only unguarded reads are `u24` (:245-246) and the one-byte version reads (`segment[tfdt.dataStart]` :159, `segment[trun.dataStart]` :163, `init[tkhd.dataStart]` :83), which go out of range only for a box whose header is whole but whose payload is empty or shorter than the field, which is a mutation, not a truncation. The recursion in `Webm.retrack` is real: Webm.kt:173-189 `fun blocks(end: Long) { ... SEGMENT, CLUSTER, BLOCK_GROUP -> blocks(reader.end(child))`, bounded only by the segment's size over a 5-byte nested header, so a deliberately deep nest overflows the stack; a shallow nesting case would not find it. The 'unlogged' scenario holds for those non-typed failures: DashHlsMediaIo.kt:183-188 catches and logs only `DashUnsupportedException`, `dashFmp4` (DashSubtitles.kt:7-11) maps only `Fmp4UnsupportedException`, and HlsSwitching.kt:592-593 `plans != null -> Fmp4Rewrite.rewrite(plain, plans); renumbered != null -> Webm.retrack(plain, renumbered)` has no handler, so a plain IllegalArgumentException or a StackOverflowError passes the log line.

### F-181 No test checks that a real renderer's capability flags match what it draws, so a wrong flag defeats the warning system undetected.

**Severity:** low · **Kind:** Test gap · **Repo:** KitePlayer · **Area:** tests/renderer-capabilities · **Lane:** design-capabilities-crossmatch · **Verdict:** CONFIRMED · **Finder confidence:** medium

**Where:**

- `kiteplayer-core/test/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/PictureControlsWarningTest.kt:1`
- `kiteplayer-output/src@android/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/output/AndroidSurfaceVideoRenderer.kt:989-1006`

**Evidence:** grep -rln appliesAdjustments over test sources: kiteplayer-core/test/.../TestSupport.kt, PictureControlsWarningTest.kt, WarningAuditTest.kt only; none under kiteplayer-output, kiteplayer-compose-video or kiteplayer-view-bindings tests. The Android codec path answers true while applying nothing (previous finding).

**Claim (as corrected by the verifier):** No test asserts the appliesAdjustments value of any real renderer (the three false overrides at SampleBufferVideoRenderer.kt:217, AwtCanvasVideoRenderer.kt:279 and WebCanvasVideoRenderer.kt:359, and the default true everywhere else), so a renderer that keeps the default while drawing no picture controls would defeat the #610 warning undetected. The flags showsHdr and projects are asserted on real renderers, and the Metal, AppKit and Android suites do render non-identity adjustments and check the result, so the gap is the flag, not the drawing.

**Finder's original claim:** The warning mechanism of #610 is tested against a scripted renderer with a scripted flag. The flags of the fourteen real renderers are asserted nowhere, and the CLAUDE.md line "Render passes have a characteristic failure: a pass that compiles, costs every tap, and does nothing ... golden-image deltas can" already names the right tool. The same holds for showsHdr and projects.

**Scenario:** A renderer gains a new target or path (as the Android codec path did) and keeps a default flag; every host and device test stays green because none renders with non-identity adjustments and compares pixels against the flag.

**Impact:** The warning contract is only as honest as each renderer's hand-set flag, and nothing checks that.

**Suggested fix:** For each platform renderer test that already renders frames (the JVM AWT, the iOS simulator Metal and UIKit, the Android device test), draw a solid grey frame with brightness 0.3 and assert: pixels changed if and only if appliesAdjustments is true. Same shape for a two-coloured equirectangular frame against projects().

**How to check it yourself:** grep -rn appliesAdjustments --include=*.kt kiteplayer-output/test* kiteplayer-compose-video/test* kiteplayer-view-bindings/test*: no hits. Compare with grep -rn 'showsHdr\|\.projects(' over the same test folders, which do hit (AndroidSurfaceVideoRendererTest.kt:298-305, MetalShowsHdrTest.kt:30, AwtCanvasVideoRendererTest.kt:943-946). A fix is one assertion per real renderer: appliesAdjustments is false for the three renderers that do not override setAdjustments, and true for the rest.

**Verifier's note:** The narrow claim holds and the broad one does not. grep appliesAdjustments over the repository: in tests only kiteplayer-core/test TestSupport.kt, PictureControlsWarningTest.kt and WarningAuditTest.kt, all against the scripted renderer; the real overrides are SampleBufferVideoRenderer.kt:217, AwtCanvasVideoRenderer.kt:279 and WebCanvasVideoRenderer.kt:359, each `override val appliesAdjustments: Boolean get() = false`, and no test anywhere reads the property of a real renderer. VideoRenderer.kt:97 defaults it to true. But the sentence "none renders with non-identity adjustments and compares pixels against the flag" is contradicted by the platform suites: MetalFrameComposerTest.kt:436-449 renders grey with `VideoAdjustments(brightness = 0.25f)` and asserts each channel lifts by 56..72, and :451-463 asserts saturation 0 lands on grey; AppKitVideoRendererTest.kt:585-612 `the CPU fallback applies the picture controls` reads pixels back and asserts 54 to 54 for BT.709 luma; AndroidSurfaceVideoRendererTest.kt:702-729 asserts the colour matrix reaches every Surface target and that identity clears it (and :994-996 on a redraw). The last sentence "The same holds for showsHdr and projects" is wrong: AndroidSurfaceVideoRendererTest.kt:298-305 asserts showsHdr for the software path, an undescribed display, a described one and ToneMap; MetalShowsHdrTest.kt:30 asserts it on Metal; AwtCanvasVideoRendererTest.kt:943-946 asserts projects for Equirectangular, a tile, Cubemap and Other; and SphereViewDrawTest, WebSphereViewTest and SphereViewRemapTest compare drawn views against SphericalLens. The premise borrowed from a previous finding, that the Android codec path answers true while applying nothing, is not borne out here: AndroidSurfaceVideoRenderer.kt:1001-1002 says a MediaCodec picture "takes them with its next frame", :790 hands `dimColorMatrix(videoColorMatrix.value, flashFactor)` to the target on every draw, and I did not trace the codec target's GL blit further, so I do not rely on it. What remains is a real but small gap: nothing asserts a real renderer's appliesAdjustments value, so a renderer that gains a path and keeps the default true while drawing no colour would pass every suite.

**Severity:** medium · **Kind:** Test gap · **Repo:** KitePlayer · **Area:** web/tests · **Lane:** web-worker-wasm-libass · **Verdict:** CONFIRMED · **Finder confidence:** high

**Where:**

- `kiteplayer-web-worker/test/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/worker/KitePlayerWorkerBrowserTest.kt:85-119`
- `kiteplayer-web-worker/test/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/worker/KitePlayerWorkerBrowserTest.kt:1062-1070`
- `scripts/web-tests/browser.mjs:64-103`

**Evidence:** KitePlayerWorkerBrowserTest.kt:85 `val heartbeat = heartbeatStart()` (a requestAnimationFrame loop on the page) and 118-119 `assertTrue(frames > 60, ...)`, `assertTrue(worst < 50.0, "the page went ... ms without a frame while the worker played")`; 1062-1070 `assertHeard` waits until `loudestHeard(ear) >= 0.0125` once and asserts only that some sound was heard. browser.mjs:64-103 serves files from disk with no added latency or bandwidth limit. A grep of the test for `underrun`, `rebuffer` or `droppedFrames` finds no assertion.

**Claim:** The tests prove that the page stays responsive and that sound exists; they do not prove that the worker plays continuously. The property that finding 1 breaks (no audio underruns, no frozen picture during window fetches) is not asserted anywhere, and the test server returns a 16 MB range in milliseconds, so even a visible assertion would pass.

**Scenario:** A regression that makes every network read stall the worker for seconds passes the suite unchanged, as the present design does.

**Impact:** The one web path that plays network media has no gate on its playback quality.

**Suggested fix:** Give probe.mjs an optional per-response delay proportional to bytes (and a bandwidth cap), run one worker playback test under it, and assert `stats.audioUnderruns == 0`, `stats.droppedFramesLate` small, and that `progress.position` advances monotonically with no gap over, say, 200 ms wall time.

**How to check it yourself:** Add a 2 ms per 10 KB delay to serveFile in browser.mjs for /testmedia/ and rerun `python3 scripts/web-tests/run.py --platform wasmJsBrowser --module kiteplayer-web-worker`; print `player.stats.value.audioUnderruns` at the end of aNetworkClipPlaysInTheWorkerWhileThePageKeepsItsFrames.

**Verifier's note:** KitePlayerWorkerBrowserTest.kt:74 `fun aNetworkClipPlaysInTheWorkerWhileThePageKeepsItsFrames()`, 85 `val heartbeat = heartbeatStart()`, 118-119 `assertTrue(frames > 60, ...)` and `assertTrue(worst < 50.0, "the page went ${worst.toInt()} ms without a frame while the worker played")`: the heartbeat is a page-thread requestAnimationFrame loop, so it measures the page, not the worker. assertHeard at 1062-1070 `while (loudestHeard(ear) < 0.0125) delay(20)` then asserts only that some sound was heard once. `grep -n -i "underrun\|rebuffer\|droppedFrames\|audioUnderruns\|Buffering"` over the 1114-line test file returns nothing. browser.mjs serveFile at 64-103 pipes `fs.createReadStream(file, { start, end })` straight to the response with no delay, and grep for delay/throttle/slow/sleep in browser.mjs and probe.mjs finds nothing. The HLS, DASH and live tests at 133, 240, 307, 354 use the same server. So the property finding 0 breaks is unasserted and the server could not expose it anyway. A genuine test gap with the evidence as stated.

- `kiteplayer-libass/test@wasmJs/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/libass/LibassWebTest.kt:31-35`

**Evidence:** harness.mjs:3 "runs them one at a time with no time limit of its own" and 49-52 `await child.body(); counts.passed++;` with no race against a timer. browser.mjs:19 `timeoutMinutes: 45` and 254-258 the only timeout, which logs `The tests did not finish in ${args.timeoutMinutes} minutes`. CLAUDE.md:171-174: "A browser test that runs longer than two seconds is killed ... Every module that runs browser tests needs a timeout config file; copy the one that has it." `find . -name karma.config.d -not -path '*/build/*'` returns nothing; ci.yml:1196-1198 runs `python3 scripts/web-tests/run.py` instead of the toolchain's browser runner.

**Claim (as corrected by the verifier):** The scripts/web-tests harness has no per-test time limit and logs only failures, so a browser test that never settles stalls its module silently until browser.mjs's 45 minute whole-run timeout, and a Node test the same way until the CI job's 60 minute limit, with no test named either way. CLAUDE.md:130-133 (and the comment at LibassWebTest.kt:31-35) still describe a karma per-test 2000 ms default and a `karma.config.d` timeout config that no longer exist in the tree; CI's web job runs run.py, not the toolchain's browser runner.

**Finder's original claim:** Tests that use `runTest(timeout = ...)` end themselves, but a plain `@Test fun x() { ... }` that awaits a promise which never settles (a worker whose close never answers, a device promise under a missing gesture) hangs the module; the only report is a generic line after 45 minutes and the CI job's 60 minute limit, with no name of the test that hung. The documented remedy (a karma config file) no longer exists in the tree.

**Scenario:** A new browser test awaits `WebAudioWorkletDevice.resume()` on a page without the autoplay flag; the wasmJsBrowser run of that module prints nothing for 45 minutes and then fails without naming the test.

**Impact:** Slow, unlabelled CI failures and a stale instruction that sends a contributor looking for a file that is gone.

**Suggested fix:** In harness.runTests race each `child.body()` against a configurable per-test timer (for example 60 s, overridable per module through --config) and log `Failed <name>: timed out`; delete or rewrite the CLAUDE.md gotcha to describe the new runner.

**How to check it yourself:** Add a plain `@Test fun hangs() = Promise<JsAny?> { _, _ -> }` style test to any wasmJs module (no runTest) and run `python3 scripts/web-tests/run.py --platform wasmJsBrowser --module <module>`: nothing is printed until the 45 minute line, and the log names no test. Run the same under `--platform wasmJs` (Node) and confirm run.py has no timeout to stop it. Then `find . -name karma.config.d -not -path '*/build/*'` returns nothing, against CLAUDE.md:130-133.

**Verifier's note:** harness.mjs:1-3: `collects the tests, then runs them one at a time with no time limit of its own.` and :48-57 `try { await child.body(); counts.passed++; } catch (error) { counts.failed++; log(...) }` with no timer; the log callback prints only failures (runner.mjs:8, browser-runner.mjs:12), so a hung test is never named. browser.mjs:19 `timeoutMinutes: 45` and :253-258 is the only limit, printing `The tests did not finish in ${args.timeoutMinutes} minutes`. run.py has no timeout at all (grep timeout/minutes returns nothing), so the Node half of a module hangs until the CI job limit, which for the web job is `timeout-minutes: 60` (ci.yml:1169). CI runs `python3 scripts/web-tests/run.py --platform wasmJs --platform wasmJsBrowser` (ci.yml:1205) and its own comment says why: `./kotlin test -p wasmJs gives a module 30 seconds in the browser, so scripts/web-tests runs the browser half instead.` `find . -name karma.config.d -not -path '*/build/*'` returns nothing. The CLAUDE.md line is real but at 130-133, not 171-174: `A browser test that runs longer than two seconds is killed rather than failed, because the test runner's per-test default is 2000 ms and Kotlin does not raise it. Every module that runs browser tests needs a timeout config file; copy the one that has it.` That describes a karma runner the tree no longer uses; LibassWebTest.kt:31-35 also still speaks of `the proxies in karma.config.d`. Tests that use runTest do end themselves (kotlinx-coroutines-test's default timeout), and most wasmJs tests do; the 19 files without runTest are mostly synchronous. The gap is real for any plain @Test that awaits a promise that never settles.

## 13. KitePlayer: proposals and opportunities

Not defects. Capabilities the players this project measures itself against have and this one does not, or cheap wins the code already makes room for.

<!-- area: audio/loudness -->

### F-194 The loudness meter reports sample peak, not true peak, so a ReplayGain-style clamp built on it can still clip by up to about a decibel of intersample overshoot

**Severity:** info · **Kind:** Proposal · **Repo:** KitePlayer · **Area:** audio/loudness · **Lane:** audio-clock-ring-sinks · **Verdict:** CONFIRMED · **Finder confidence:** high

**Where:**

- `kiteplayer-core/src/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/audio/LoudnessMeter.kt:12-13`
- `kiteplayer-core/src/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/audio/LoudnessMeter.kt:96-98`
- `kiteplayer-core/src/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/internal/ReplayGain.kt:112-114`
- `kiteplayer-core/src/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/internal/PlaybackCore.kt:6460-6472`

**Evidence:** LoudnessMeter.kt:12-13 `/** The largest sample magnitude seen, where 1 is full scale. ... */ val samplePeak: Float` and :96-98 `val magnitude = if (raw < 0f) -raw else raw; if (magnitude > peak) peak = magnitude`. ReplayGain.kt:257-259 documents that the engine clamps a boost by `peak * gain` to full scale. The K-weighting itself I verified: the derived pre-filter and RLB coefficients at 48 kHz equal the BS.1770 table (1.53512485958697, -2.69169618940638, 1.19839281085285, -1.69065929318241, 0.73248077421585 and -1.99004745483398, 0.99007225036621) to within 1e-15.

**Claim (as corrected by the verifier):** `LoudnessMeter.samplePeak` is the largest raw sample magnitude, with no 4x oversampling, so it is a sample peak and not the true peak that BS.1770-4 Annex 2 and ReplayGain 2.0 define, and on a hot master it can read up to about 1 dB under the true peak. Nothing in either repository feeds it into a clamp: the engine's ReplayGain clamp (ReplayGain.kt:114, called from PlaybackCore.kt:6467) uses only the peak found in the file's tags. The gap matters only to an application that writes ReplayGain tags from this meter's result, and the ring's limiter would then catch the overshoot rather than let it clip. A true-peak reading, or a note in the KDoc that a tag writer should not use this value as REPLAYGAIN_*_PEAK, would close it.

**Finder's original claim:** BS.1770-4 Annex 2 and ReplayGain 2.0 define peak as true peak measured on a 4x oversampled signal; a sample peak understates intersample overshoot by up to about 1 dB on hot masters. The meter is honestly documented as sample peak, so this is a capability gap, not a defect: if `samplePeak` is ever used as the peak for a boost clamp, the clamp is loose by that amount and the ring's limiter then has to catch it.

**Scenario:** A scan that measures a track's loudness and peak with this meter and later applies a positive ReplayGain from them to a loud modern master.

**Impact:** Up to about 1 dB of limiter engagement that a true-peak measurement would have avoided; the integrated loudness figure itself is correct.

**Suggested fix:** Add an optional true-peak mode: a 4x polyphase interpolation (the Annex 2 FIR, 48 taps at 12 per phase) run on the raw samples before the magnitude check, reported as `truePeak` beside `samplePeak`.

**How to check it yourself:** In LoudnessMeterTest.kt the `sine(freq, seconds, rate, amp)` helper exists; add a phase argument or build the array by hand: at 44.1 kHz, `samples[i] = 0.98f * sin(2*PI*11025*i/44100 + PI/4)`. Every sample of that signal has magnitude 0.98*sqrt(2)/2 = 0.693, so `result().samplePeak` reads about 0.693 while the true peak of the waveform is 0.98 (about 3 dB low, the worst case; real masters lose about 1 dB). Compare with `ffmpeg -i file -af ebur128=peak=true -f null -`, whose "True peak" line reports -0.18 dBFS for the same clip, and with its sample-peak line, which matches the meter.

**Verifier's note:** The cited evidence is at the cited lines. LoudnessMeter.kt:12-13 reads `/** The largest sample magnitude seen, where 1 is full scale. May exceed 1 for material that clips. */ val samplePeak: Float` and :96-98 reads `val raw = samples[base + channel]; val magnitude = if (raw < 0f) -raw else raw; if (magnitude > peak) peak = magnitude`. There is no oversampling or interpolation anywhere in the file; the only other filters are the K-weighting biquads at lines 216-261, whose output never touches `peak`. The ReplayGain clamp is at ReplayGain.kt:94-115 (`return minOf(linear, 1f / knownPeak)` at line 114), and its one caller, PlaybackCore.kt:6460-6472 `replayGainFor`, builds the tags from `containerTags` and `stream?.metadata` only, so no code path in the repository ever feeds `samplePeak` into the clamp. The finding already says so ("if `samplePeak` is ever used"), and it labels itself info/proposal, which is the right weight. I searched both repositories for `truePeak`, `true peak`, `oversampl` and `intersample`: the only true-peak symbols are the loudnorm filter's `TP` parameter in KiteFFmpeg's FilterDsl.kt:203 and :338, which is unrelated, so nothing in the tree already offers a true-peak reading. CHANGELOG.md:1643-1646 advertises the meter as "the same number EBU R128 and ReplayGain 2.0 are defined against, plus the sample peak" and `AudioAnalysis.measureLoudness` as "for a normalise pass before playback starts", which is exactly the scenario where ReplayGain 2.0 asks for a true peak (BS.1770 Annex 2, 4x oversampled). The documentation is honest about sample peak, so this is a capability gap and not a defect, and the CLAUDE.md gotcha that both rings limit any sample past full scale (#504) means an overshoot that slips through such a clamp is caught by the limiter rather than clipped, which the finding also states. Nothing in CLAUDE.md's decided list fights a true-peak option. The claim as written holds; I only sharpen it to state that no in-tree consumer is affected today.

## 14. KiteFFmpeg: fix upstream

Everything here belongs to the media library and is fixed in its own repository and tracker. Findings marked repo "both" have a KiteFFmpeg half that must land first and a KitePlayer half that follows. KiteFFmpeg is an independent project and nothing here assumes it knows about KitePlayer.

<!-- area: api/compatibility -->

### F-063 Public data classes with many defaulted parameters make every new field a binary break for compiled consumers.

**Severity:** low (finder said medium, verifier corrected) · **Kind:** Public API · **Repo:** KiteFFmpeg · **Area:** api/compatibility · **Lane:** kiteffmpeg-kotlin-api · **Verdict:** CONFIRMED · **Finder confidence:** high

**Where:**

- `kiteffmpeg/src/io/github/yuroyami/kiteffmpeg/StreamInfo.kt:4`
- `kiteffmpeg/src/io/github/yuroyami/kiteffmpeg/StreamInfo.kt:115`
- `kiteffmpeg/src/io/github/yuroyami/kiteffmpeg/StreamInfo.kt:298`
- `kiteffmpeg/src/io/github/yuroyami/kiteffmpeg/MediaSink.kt:145`
- `kiteffmpeg/src/io/github/yuroyami/kiteffmpeg/dsl/DemuxOptions.kt:20`
- `kiteffmpeg/api/jvm/kiteffmpeg.api:1176-1177`

**Evidence:** `public data class StreamInfo(` (15 parameters, 9 defaulted), `public data class VideoStreamInfo(` (13 parameters), `public data class FrameInfo(` (18 parameters), `public data class VideoEncoderSpec(`, `public data class DemuxOptions(`; 79 `data class` declarations under kiteffmpeg/src. The JVM dump shows the generated shapes that change with every added parameter: `public synthetic fun <init> (ILio/github/yuroyami/kiteffmpeg/MediaType;JLio/github/yuroyami/kiteffmpeg/Rational;IILjava/lang/String;IIILjava/lang/String;Ljava/lang/Long;JZLio/github/yuroyami/kiteffmpeg/ColorInfo;Lio/github/yuroyami/kiteffmpeg/Rational;ZLio/github/yuroyami/kiteffmpeg/HdrMetadata;ILkotlin/jvm/internal/DefaultConstructorMarker;)V` plus `componentN` and `copy` with the full signature.

**Claim (as corrected by the verifier):** Every added field on a public data class such as StreamInfo, VideoStreamInfo, FrameInfo, VideoEncoderSpec or DemuxOptions is a binary break for compiled consumers, as the changelog's own 0.3.0 and 0.4.0 notes record. CONTRIBUTING.md accepts this before 1.0 and requires the release notes to name the classes, which they do; what KiteFFmpeg lacks is the counterpart of KitePlayer #676, a tracked plan for how these types stop breaking at 1.0.

**Finder's original claim:** Adding a field to `StreamInfo`, `VideoStreamInfo`, `FrameInfo`, `VideoEncoderSpec` or `DemuxOptions` changes the primary constructor, the `copy` signature and the defaults-mask synthetic constructor, so any consumer compiled against the previous release (KitePlayer pins KiteFFmpeg by version and is published separately) fails with NoSuchMethodError at run time when the two are mixed, even though source compatibility holds. The recent history of this repository is exactly that kind of growth: `hdr`, `dolbyVision`, `crop`, `spherical`, `stereo3d`, `mirrored`, `codecProfile` were each appended. KitePlayer already tracks the same problem on its own surface as #676; nothing tracks it here, and the ABI check guards the dump but cannot prevent the break.

**Scenario:** An app depends on KitePlayer X which was compiled against KiteFFmpeg 0.5.1, and also on a newer KiteFFmpeg 0.6 for a bug fix. Any `StreamInfo.copy(...)` or constructor call compiled into KitePlayer throws NoSuchMethodError on the JVM and Android; on native the klib link fails.

**Impact:** Every release that adds a descriptive field forces lockstep upgrades of every consumer, which is a tax on the 'go-to library' goal and a recurring source of runtime failures when versions drift.

**Suggested fix:** For the public descriptive types, replace `data class` with regular classes exposing read-only properties and an explicit builder or `copy` written by hand (keeping `equals`/`hashCode`), or at least freeze the constructor by taking new fields through a secondary, non-data holder. Decide this once in a design commit before 1.0, as the project's own rule for API shapes asks.

**How to check it yourself:** Read CONTRIBUTING.md:198-220 and CHANGELOG.md:646 and :786-790 to see the break is already acknowledged and announced per release; then confirm no KiteFFmpeg issue plans a non-breaking shape for 1.0 (issue search 'data class' returns only closed #91). The NoSuchMethodError reproduction in the original check remains valid.

**Verifier's note:** The mechanism is real and the cited lines exist: StreamInfo.kt:4 `public data class StreamInfo(` (6 required + 9 defaulted parameters), :115 `public data class VideoStreamInfo(`, :298 `public data class FrameInfo(`, MediaSink.kt:145 `public data class VideoEncoderSpec(`, DemuxOptions.kt:20 `public data class DemuxOptions(`; 75 `public data class` declarations under kiteffmpeg/src (79 `data class` in all). kiteffmpeg.api:1176-1177 holds the two synthetic FrameInfo constructors whose descriptor changes with every added parameter. Kotlin emits no bridge for the old constructor or `copy`, so a compiled consumer does fail with NoSuchMethodError, and the project's own CHANGELOG records exactly that: line 646 `Not binary compatible with 0.3.0: StreamInfo and DemuxOptions gained fields, which changes their constructors and copy. Rebuild a library compiled against 0.3.0.` and lines 786-790 for 0.3.0 versus 0.2.0 (`NoSuchMethodError on the JVM and Android, and at link time on native targets`). What the finding overstates is `nothing tracks it here`: CONTRIBUTING.md:198-220 (Binary compatibility) already states the policy, `A data class that gains a field cannot keep its old constructor that way, so the release notes say that the release is not binary compatible and name the classes`, README.md:72 says the API can change between minor versions before 1.0, and the changelog follows the policy. No KiteFFmpeg issue plans a post-1.0 shape the way KitePlayer #676 does (issue search for 'binary compatible' and 'data class' finds only closed #91 about release notes). So the design concern holds, the untracked half is the 1.0 plan, and under the stated pre-1.0 policy the present severity is lower than the finding's medium.

### F-005 Only the Apple profiles pass --disable-autodetect; Android, Linux and Windows let configure take whatever the sysroot carries, and the recipe check cannot see it.

**Severity:** medium · **Kind:** Design · **Repo:** KiteFFmpeg · **Area:** build/ffmpeg-recipe · **Lane:** kiteffmpeg-c-and-build · **Verdict:** CONFIRMED · **Finder confidence:** high · **Related open issue:** #186

**Where:**

- `build-plugins/native-build/src/BuildFFmpegTask.kt:458-459`
- `build-plugins/native-build/src/BuildFFmpegTask.kt:667-668`
- `build-plugins/native-build/src/BuildFFmpegTask.kt:762-795`
- `build-plugins/native-build/src/StaticLinkFlags.kt:72-76`

**Evidence:** desktopAppleArgs (line 458) and mobileAppleArgs (line 737) start with `"--disable-autodetect",`; portableDesktopArgs (line 667) is `listOf("--enable-zlib") + ...` and androidArgs (lines 762-795) has no such flag. StaticLinkFlags.kt:73-74 records the consequence: `iconv backs FFmpeg's subtitle charset conversion and msys2's sysroot has it, so the mingw configure autodetects it and the link must name it`. CheckFFmpegRecipesTask compares `recipeFingerprint(installedConfigureLine)` with the expected flags only; native-sbom.sh refuses only `--enable-gpl --enable-nonfree --enable-version3` (line 124).

**Claim:** With autodetect on, the set of components in a Linux, Windows or Android tree is decided by the konan sysroot or NDK contents at bake time (iconv on mingw today; bzlib, lzma, schannel, vulkan, libdrm are all autodetect candidates), not by the committed recipe. A Kotlin or NDK bump that changes a sysroot can add a dependency or a licence (GNU libiconv is LGPL and is now statically inside the Windows JNI DLL) or drop a decoder, and every gate stays green because the configure line did not change and the SBOM reads flags. The NOTICE and docs/platforms.md claim 'it links no third-party library except dav1d', which the Windows tree already contradicts.

**Scenario:** A release-binaries run after a Kotlin/Native upgrade whose msys2 or NDK package differs: the Windows tree gains or loses components, check-tree-patches and checkFFmpegRecipes pass, the SBOM lists FFmpeg and dav1d only, and the licensing page stays wrong.

**Impact:** The reproducibility and licensing claims the build is designed to make hold only for the Apple trees; the other eight depend on an input nothing records.

**Suggested fix:** Pass `--disable-autodetect` in portableDesktopArgs and androidArgs and name what each profile wants (`--enable-iconv` on mingw if it is wanted, `--enable-zlib` as already done, `--enable-mediacodec --enable-jni` as already done). Record `avutil_configuration()` or the configure banner's enabled-external-libraries line in BUILD-INFO.txt and have native-sbom.sh compare it with an expected list per target.

**How to check it yourself:** Compare `unzip -p ffmpeg-n9.0.2-lgpl-mingw-x64.zip BUILD-INFO.txt` with the macos one: the configure lines match the recipe, but `strings lib/libavcodec.a | grep -i iconv_open` is non-empty only on mingw. Then read the configure banner of a Linux bake for 'External libraries' and 'External libraries providing hardware acceleration'.

**Verifier's note:** Only two places pass the flag: desktopAppleArgs at BuildFFmpegTask.kt:458-459 `private fun desktopAppleArgs(): List<String> = listOf("--disable-autodetect",` and mobileAppleArgs at 737 `"--disable-autodetect",`. sharedCoreArgs (342-452) contains no autodetect flag (grep over that range is empty), portableDesktopArgs at 667-668 is `listOf("--enable-zlib") + if (target == TargetTriple.MingwX64) windowsHwaccelDecodeArgs() else emptyList()`, desktopTargetArgs adds only cross-compile and threading flags, and androidArgs (762-795) has none. FFmpeg's configure defaults autodetect on and its AUTODETECT_LIBS covers the external and hwaccel autodetect lists (configure:2301-2305, iconv among them at 2013). StaticLinkFlags.kt:72-74 records the consequence: 'iconv backs FFmpeg's subtitle charset conversion and msys2's sysroot has it, so the mingw configure autodetects it and the link must name it', and LinkKiteFFmpegJniTask.kt:382-384 links it statically (`"-Wl,-Bstatic" + ffmpeg + listOf("-liconv", ...`). The recipe guard compares flag fingerprints only: staleReason (BuildFFmpegTask.kt:1099-1105) computes `recipeFingerprint(installedConfigureLine.split(" "))` against the expected args, and native-sbom.sh:124-128 refuses only `--enable-gpl --enable-nonfree --enable-version3`. docs/platforms.md:54 claims 'it links no third-party library except dav1d'. So the component set of the Linux, Windows and Android trees is decided by the sysroot or NDK at bake time and no gate reads the configure banner or the archive's symbols. The notice and DLL-dependency consequences are already open as #185 and #186; the point this finding adds, that three profiles leave autodetect on and the recipe check cannot see what it picks up, is not covered by either.

<!-- area: build/hardening -->

### F-064 The desktop JNI libraries are linked without the hardening flags the Android ones get, and the helper archive is compiled without a stack protector anywhere.

**Severity:** low · **Kind:** Design · **Repo:** KiteFFmpeg · **Area:** build/hardening · **Lane:** kiteffmpeg-c-and-build · **Verdict:** CONFIRMED · **Finder confidence:** high

**Where:**

- `build-plugins/native-build/src/LinkKiteFFmpegJniTask.kt:378-390`
- `build-plugins/native-build/src/LinkKiteFFmpegJniTask.kt:309-320`
- `build-plugins/native-build/src/CompileKiteFFmpegCTask.kt:365-369`

**Evidence:** androidLinkFlags (line 314) passes `"-Wl,-z,defs", "-Wl,-z,noexecstack", "-Wl,-z,relro", "-Wl,-z,now"`; desktopLinkFlags for Linux (line 388) passes `toolchainFlags + ffmpeg + listOf("-lz", "-lm", "-ldl", "-lpthread", "-Wl,--no-undefined")` and nothing else. COMPILER_FLAGS (lines 365-369) are `"-O2", "-std=c11", "-fvisibility=hidden", "-fPIC", "-Wall", "-Wextra", "-Werror", "-Werror=vla"`, with no -fstack-protector or _FORTIFY_SOURCE, and `grep -rn stack-protector build-plugins` finds nothing.

**Claim (as corrected by the verifier):** The Linux and Windows JNI libraries are linked without BIND_NOW (full RELRO), so their GOT stays writable after load, unlike the Android libraries which pass -z relro -z now; partial RELRO and a non-executable stack come from lld's defaults, and the Windows DLL gets DEP and ASLR from lld's MinGW defaults. The kitecodec helper archive is compiled with no stack protector flag, which leaves it without canaries on the Linux and Windows targets (konan's clang adds none there), while Apple's and the NDK's clang add one by default. No _FORTIFY_SOURCE anywhere.

**Finder's original claim:** SECURITY.md says the library parses untrusted media and treats parsing bugs as security bugs, but the Linux and Windows JNI libraries ship without RELRO, BIND_NOW or a non-executable stack marking, and the project's own C (which handles subtitle rectangles, extradata copies and the AES reader) is built without stack canaries on every target but Android, where the NDK clang adds them by default. This does not create a bug; it removes mitigations for one when FFmpeg or the helpers have one.

**Scenario:** Desktop JVM on Linux or Windows: a memory-corruption bug in libavformat reached through user media is easier to turn into code execution than it would be in a distribution's FFmpeg, which is built with these flags.

**Impact:** Exploit mitigations that cost nothing at run time are absent from the published desktop libraries.

**Suggested fix:** Add `-Wl,-z,relro -Wl,-z,now -Wl,-z,noexecstack` to the Linux desktopLinkFlags, `-Wl,--nxcompat -Wl,--dynamicbase -Wl,--high-entropy-va` on Windows, and `-fstack-protector-strong -D_FORTIFY_SOURCE=2` to COMPILER_FLAGS (and `--extra-cflags=-fstack-protector-strong` in the FFmpeg recipe) for the non-Android targets.

**How to check it yourself:** On the published jar's linux-x64 library: `readelf -lW libkitecodec_jni.so | grep -E 'GNU_RELRO|GNU_STACK'` shows both (RELRO present, stack RW not RWE), and `readelf -dW libkitecodec_jni.so | grep -E 'BIND_NOW|FLAGS'` prints nothing, which is partial RELRO; `checksec --file=libkitecodec_jni.so` should read 'Partial RELRO, No canary found, NX enabled'. For the canary, `nm libkitecodec_jni.so | grep -c __stack_chk_fail` is 0 on Linux and non-zero on the Android .so. On Windows, `objdump -p kitecodec_jni.dll | grep -E 'DllCharacteristics|HIGH_ENTROPY|DYNAMIC_BASE|NX_COMPAT'` shows the lld defaults.

**Verifier's note:** The flags are as cited. LinkKiteFFmpegJniTask.kt:314 (Android) `"-Wl,-z,defs", "-Wl,-z,noexecstack", "-Wl,-z,relro", "-Wl,-z,now",` against desktopLinkFlags at 378-390, where Linux gets `toolchainFlags + ffmpeg + listOf("-lz", "-lm", "-ldl", "-lpthread", "-Wl,--no-undefined")` and Windows `"-Wl,-Bstatic" + ffmpeg + listOf("-liconv", "-lz", "-lm", "-lpthread", "-lole32", "-luser32", "-lws2_32", "-lbcrypt", "-static-libgcc")`. CompileKiteFFmpegCTask.kt:365-369 COMPILER_FLAGS are `"-O2", "-std=c11", "-fvisibility=hidden", "-fPIC", "-Wall", "-Wextra", "-Werror", "-Werror=vla"`; `grep -rn -i stack-protector|FORTIFY|relro` over build-plugins and native finds only the Android line. SECURITY.md:5 says the library 'parses untrusted media' and to 'treat media-parsing bugs as security bugs'. Two overreaches in the claim, from the linker in use: konanJniLinkTools passes `-fuse-ld=lld` (LinkKiteFFmpegJniTask.kt:125, KonanCrossTools.kt:53), and ld.lld defaults to `-z relro` and a non-executable GNU_STACK, so the Linux libraries do get partial RELRO and a non-executable stack by default; what they lack against Android is `-z now` (full RELRO). lld's MinGW driver likewise defaults to --dynamicbase, --nxcompat and --high-entropy-va, so the Windows DLL has DEP and ASLR; RELRO is not a PE concept. `-Wl,--no-undefined` is the ELF equivalent of `-z defs`, so that one is present. On the canary: konan's clang enables no stack protector for Linux or MinGW targets, but upstream clang defaults Darwin targets to -fstack-protector and the NDK clang to -fstack-protector-strong, so the helper archive lacks canaries on Linux and Windows, not 'on every target but Android'.

### F-192 A sibling checkout's ass chain is preferred over the pinned release with no pin check, and the sibling has already moved past the pin

**Severity:** low · **Kind:** Design · **Repo:** both · **Area:** build/libass · **Lane:** build-distribution-tests-ci · **Verdict:** CONFIRMED · **Finder confidence:** medium

**Where:**

- `build-plugins/build-support/src/AssChain.kt:18`

- `NOTICE:28`

**Evidence:** AssChain.kt:237-241: `localRoots(repoRoot).map { it.resolve("$dirName/ass-chain") }.firstOrNull { it.resolve("lib/libass.a").isFile }?.let { return Chain(dirName, it) }` before `val pin = pins[dirName] ?: return null`; the pin is checked only on the downloaded path (line 260). native-sbom.sh:28-31: `The document describes the pinned archives. A build that takes its chain from ../KiteFFmpeg/native-libs/deps ... links whatever that directory holds.` NOTICE:28: `HarfBuzz 14.5.0`. KiteFFmpeg CHANGELOG.md:93-94: `The recipe of the subtitle chain that KitePlayer links builds HarfBuzz 14.6.0 instead of 14.5.0. The published ass-chain-r2 assets keep 14.5.0 until the chain is built again.` KitePlayer pins `RELEASE_TAG = "ass-chain-r2"` (AssChain.kt:197); KiteFFmpeg's release-ass-chain.yml default tag is already `ass-chain-r3`. CLAUDE.md:97-99 documents publishing from the maintainer's machine as a normal path.

**Claim (as corrected by the verifier):** A local chain under ../KiteFFmpeg/native-libs/deps or KITEPLAYER_LIBASS_ROOT is taken before the pinned download with no digest or version check, so a maintainer-machine publish links whatever the sibling last built. The sibling's recipe already names HarfBuzz 14.6.0 while NOTICE, the pin file and the published r2 assets say 14.5.0; whether the maintainer's deps folder currently holds 14.6.0 could not be observed from this checkout. The scripts acknowledge the drift (native-sbom.sh:28-31, check-artifact-size.sh:41-44) but nothing fails the build or the SBOM when the linked chain differs from the pinned one.

**Finder's original claim:** A build on the maintainer's machine, where ../KiteFFmpeg/native-libs/deps exists, links whatever chain was last built there, which today is HarfBuzz 14.6.0, while NOTICE, the SBOM and the pin file all say 14.5.0. The SBOM script checks NOTICE against the pinned archives, not against the chain actually linked, so a maintainer-machine publish would ship artifacts whose bill of materials is wrong and whose bytes differ from a CI publish of the same commit. The artifact-size baseline caveat in check-artifact-size.sh:41-44 already acknowledges the drift.

**Scenario:** The maintainer runs `./kotlin publish mavenCentral` locally after rebuilding the sibling's chain. kiteplayer-libass ships HarfBuzz 14.6.0; the attached SBOM says 14.5.0; a security advisory for one of the two versions cannot be answered from the release metadata.

**Impact:** Release metadata that can be wrong about the library it describes, and two publish paths that produce different bytes.

**Suggested fix:** Make AssChain.find verify a local chain against the pin too (hash the four archives, or read CHAIN.txt and compare tags with a committed list), and refuse under publish unless KITEPLAYER_LIBASS_ROOT is explicitly set. Bump the pin to ass-chain-r3 and NOTICE to 14.6.0 together, in one commit, as the pin comment asks.

**How to check it yourself:** `sed -n 49,70p build-plugins/build-support/src/AssChain.kt` for the order and the pin-only-on-download. On the maintainer's Mac: `cat ../KiteFFmpeg/native-libs/deps/macos-arm64/ass-chain/CHAIN.txt` (if present) against NOTICE:28 and `unzip -p ass-chain-macos-arm64.zip CHAIN.txt` from the r2 release. `grep -rn CHAIN.txt build-plugins/` returns nothing, so no build check exists.

**Verifier's note:** The mechanism is real but the cited AssChain.kt lines are wrong: the file is 141 lines. AssChain.kt:18 `const val RELEASE_TAG: String = "ass-chain-r2"`; 49-52 `localRoots` lists `KITEPLAYER_LIBASS_ROOT` then `repoRoot.resolve("../KiteFFmpeg/native-libs/deps")`; 58-61 `localRoots(repoRoot).map { it.resolve("$dirName/ass-chain") }.firstOrNull { it.resolve("lib/libass.a").isFile }?.let { return Chain(dirName, it) }` runs before 62 `val pin = pins[dirName] ?: return null`, and the digest is checked only in `fetch` (70-80). No build code reads a CHAIN.txt or compares a local chain's versions to NOTICE (`grep CHAIN build-plugins/` finds only NATIVE_CHAIN_DIRS). native-sbom.sh:28-31 says so itself: `A build that takes its chain from ../KiteFFmpeg/native-libs/deps ... links whatever that directory holds. For that reason the document for a release comes from the publish workflow`. check-artifact-size.sh:41-44 repeats the caveat. NOTICE:28 says `HarfBuzz 14.5.0`; KiteFFmpeg CHANGELOG.md:93-94 says the recipe now builds `HarfBuzz 14.6.0 instead of 14.5.0` and `The published ass-chain-r2 assets keep 14.5.0`; BuildAssChainTask.kt:544 `DEFAULT_SOURCE_REFS = "... harfbuzz-14.6.0 ..."`. release-ass-chain.yml:21 defaults to `ass-chain-r3`, but `gh api .../releases/tags/ass-chain-r3` is 404 while r2 exists, so the sibling has moved past the pin in its recipe only, not in a published release. This checkout has no `../KiteFFmpeg/native-libs/deps`, so `which today is HarfBuzz 14.6.0` is an inference about the maintainer's machine, not something observed. CLAUDE.md does document the maintainer-machine publish (`./kotlin publish mavenCentral`, runs no tests) and publish.yml:39-40 notes such a publish carries no attestation, so the risk is acknowledged but not guarded.

### F-006 An AES-128 HLS segment addressed with EXT-X-BYTERANGE decrypts from the wrong place: the nested opener never learns the byte range and the crypto wrapper cannot seek.

**Severity:** medium · **Kind:** Defect · **Repo:** KiteFFmpeg · **Area:** c/io-bridge/hls · **Lane:** kiteffmpeg-c-and-build · **Verdict:** CONFIRMED · **Finder confidence:** medium

**Where:**

- `native/kitecodec-c/src/helpers_format.c:1223-1298`
- `native/kitecodec-c/src/helpers_format.c:1117-1150`
- `native/patches/ffmpeg/0002-hls-trust-io-open.patch:36-50`

**Evidence:** helpers_format.c:1249 `int rc = p->opener.open_fn(p->opener.opaque, inner, &source, &size, &seekable);` passes only the URL; the `options` dictionary is read only for "key" and "iv" (lines 1241-1243). Line 1267: `int can_seek = !encrypted && seekable && p->opener.seek_fn;` so an encrypted source gets no seek callback (line 1283 passes NULL). Lines 1140-1144 drop PKCS#7 padding only when `n->ended && n->cipher_len == 0`, which is the end of the whole file. The patch makes open_url `goto open;` before the block that sets `is_http = 1`, so FFmpeg's HLS reader treats every nested source as non-HTTP and seeks to the segment offset itself after the open.

**Claim (as corrected by the verifier):** With a nested opener, an AES-128 HLS segment addressed by EXT-X-BYTERANGE at a non-zero offset is decrypted from byte 0 of the resource: kc_io_open_nested ignores the offset/end_offset options hls.c passes and gives the encrypted context no seek, and because the trust_io_open patch leaves is_http at 0, hls.c's avio_seek to url_offset is served by reading and decrypting the whole prefix. The segment's first 16 bytes are chained from the previous ciphertext block instead of its IV, its PKCS#7 padding block is handed to the demuxer as data (padding is dropped only at end of resource), and each segment open is linear in its offset. Through KitePlayer this reaches only MPEG-TS AES-128 renditions (HlsSwitching decrypts EXT-X-MAP fMP4 streams in Kotlin and strips the key); a direct KiteFFmpeg consumer with a MediaByteOpener hits it for both shapes.

**Finder's original claim:** FFmpeg's hls.c open_input puts the segment's byte range into the options it hands io_open ("offset" and "end_offset") and, because the patched open_url never sets is_http, follows the open with avio_seek(*in, seg->url_offset, SEEK_SET). For a plain segment that seek reaches the opener's seek_fn and works (WebNestedRangeTest covers it). For an AES-128 segment the wrapper kc_io_crypt_read is installed with no seek function, so avio_seek reads forward from byte 0 of the file through the decryptor. CBC decryption is chained, so every segment but the first gets its first 16 bytes XORed with the previous ciphertext block instead of the segment's IV, each segment's own PKCS#7 padding block is handed to the demuxer as data (the padding is only stripped at end of file), and every segment open re-reads and decrypts the whole file prefix, which is quadratic over the rendition.

**Scenario:** Any platform. A single-file HLS rendition with #EXT-X-KEY:METHOD=AES-128 and #EXT-X-BYTERANGE lines (Apple's mediafilesegmenter and Shaka Packager both emit this shape), played through a MediaByteOpener. With MPEG-TS segments the first 188-byte packet of each segment is lost to resync and up to 16 junk bytes trail each one; with fMP4 segments the moof header is destroyed and nothing after the first segment decodes. Seeking late into a long file reads and decrypts the entire prefix on every segment.

**Impact:** Encrypted single-file HLS, a shape real packagers produce, plays with corrupted segment boundaries or not at all, and the network cost per segment is the whole file so far.

**Suggested fix:** Read "offset" and "end_offset" out of the options dictionary in kc_io_open_nested and hand the range to the opener (extend kc_io_opener.open_fn or seek the nested source to offset after open and cap its size), reset the CBC state and the IV when the wrapper starts at the range start, and give kc_io_crypt_read a seek that restarts decryption at a block boundary. Also treat a final pad byte outside 1..16 as AVERROR_INVALIDDATA rather than keeping the bytes.

**How to check it yourself:** In native/kitecodec-c/tests/test_nested_io.c add a case built from case_an_aes128_segment_decrypts: encrypt two WAV pieces separately with the same key and two IVs, concatenate the ciphertexts into one resource, write #EXT-X-BYTERANGE:<len2>@<len1> for the second piece, and compare read_all against the plaintext; the second piece's first 16 bytes and the 16 trailing padding bytes will differ. Run it with KC_FFMPEG_PREFIX=native-libs/lgpl/macos-arm64 ./scripts/build-host.sh plain && ./scripts/run-c-tests.sh plain test_nested_io (the Homebrew FFmpeg skips the HLS cases). Upstream confirmation: libavformat/hls.c n9.0.2 lines 1499-1500 (offset/end_offset), 1545 (`!is_http && seg->url_offset`), and 715 (the only `is_http = 1`, inside the block the patch skips).

**Verifier's note:** Both halves of the mechanism are real. KiteFFmpeg side (native/kitecodec-c/src/helpers_format.c): kc_io_open_nested reads the options dictionary only through `kc_hex_block(given, "key", key)` and `kc_hex_block(given, "iv", iv)` (lines 1241-1243), hands the opener only the URL at line 1249 `int rc = p->opener.open_fn(p->opener.opaque, inner, &source, &size, &seekable);`, and at line 1267 `int can_seek = !encrypted && seekable && p->opener.seek_fn;` so the encrypted AVIOContext is built at lines 1283-1285 with `kc_io_crypt_read` and a NULL seek, and `n->pb->seekable = 0`. kc_io_crypt_read strips padding only under `if (n->ended && n->cipher_len == 0)` (line 1140), i.e. at end of the whole resource, and its IV chain starts at byte 0 of the resource. Upstream side, read from libavformat/hls.c of tag n9.0.2 (fetched, not from memory): open_input sets `av_dict_set_int(&opts, "offset", seg->url_offset, 0); av_dict_set_int(&opts, "end_offset", end_offset, 0);` (lines 1499-1500), builds `crypto+%s` / `crypto:%s` for AES-128 (1519-1521), and then `if (ret == 0 && !is_http && seg->url_offset) { int64_t seekret = avio_seek(*in, seg->url_offset, SEEK_SET);` (1545-1546). `is_http = 1` is set only at hls.c:715 inside the protocol block that the patch's `goto open;` jumps over (0002-hls-trust-io-open.patch), so every nested open reports is_http = 0 and the seek runs. aviobuf.c:281-286 of the same tag shows a forward seek on a context without AVIO_SEEKABLE_NORMAL loops `fill_buffer(s)` until s->pos reaches the offset, i.e. it reads and decrypts the whole prefix. The input_reuse shortcut at hls.c:1460 is explicitly `seg->key_type == KEY_NONE`, so it does not rescue the encrypted case. read_from_url (hls.c:1211-1212) bounds the read to seg->size, so the segment ends where it should but includes its own padding block as data, and the first block is XORed with the previous segment's last ciphertext block instead of the IV. No test covers it: `grep -rn -i byterange` over native/kitecodec-c/tests and docs finds nothing, and the only AES case (test_nested_io.c:412-460) uses one whole-file segment. One narrowing: KitePlayer's HlsSwitching.kt (lines 38-40, 101-106) says 'the switch decrypts the AES-128 segments of an MP4 stream itself ... and shows FFmpeg a playlist with no key. FFmpeg still decrypts MPEG-TS segments', so through KitePlayer only the MPEG-TS shape reaches this path; the fMP4 shape in the scenario applies to a direct KiteFFmpeg consumer.

### F-007 A byte-source open without a nested opener has no protocol whitelist, so a playlist handed over as bytes can make FFmpeg open http addresses and local media files of its choosing.

**Severity:** medium · **Kind:** Design · **Repo:** KiteFFmpeg · **Area:** c/io-bridge/security · **Lane:** kiteffmpeg-c-and-build · **Verdict:** CONFIRMED · **Finder confidence:** high

**Where:**

- `native/kitecodec-c/src/helpers_format.c:1343-1451`
- `native/kitecodec-c/src/helpers_format.c:140-156`
- `kiteffmpeg/src/io/github/yuroyami/kiteffmpeg/dsl/DemuxOptions.kt:31-35`
- `native/kitecodec-c/fuzz/kc_fuzz.h:110-112`

**Evidence:** ffkmp_fmt_open_input_io2 builds its options only from the caller's pairs (`kc_open_options(keys, values, n, &options, &forced)`, line 1416) and adds only `KC_TRUST_IO_OPEN_KEY` when an opener is given (line 1417); nothing sets protocol_whitelist. DemuxOptions.kt:35 `val protocolWhitelist: Set<String> = emptySet(),` with the doc `empty allows all` (line 33). The fuzz harness protects itself: kc_fuzz.h:110 `The open passes one option, protocol_whitelist=none. A playlist or a reference inside the input then cannot make FFmpeg open a file or a network address during a fuzz run.` docs/decoding.md:56-57 states `Without a nested opener, FFmpeg's HLS reader opens only file, http and data addresses`. BuildFFmpegTask.kt:387 enables `--enable-protocol=file,fd,pipe,data,http,tcp,udp,rtp,rtmp`.

**Claim:** FFmpeg derives an input's protocol whitelist from the protocol that opened it (file inputs get file,crypto,data; http inputs get the network set), but a custom AVIOContext from avio_alloc_context carries none, so avformat_open_input leaves s->protocol_whitelist NULL and every nested io_open is unrestricted. The HLS demuxer in the build then opens http:// segment and key addresses, and file:// addresses with a media extension, that the playlist names. The only thing standing between untrusted playlist bytes and outbound connections from the user's device is a DemuxOptions field that defaults to open. The project's own fuzz harness treats this as a hazard and closes it; the product does not.

**Scenario:** JVM, Android, Kotlin/Native. An app that lets a user open a downloaded .m3u8 (or any file, since probing recognises an M3U8 from its bytes) through MediaSource.open(io = bytes) with no nestedOpener. The file names http://10.0.0.1/... or http://attacker/beacon?...; FFmpeg connects from inside the app to the internal network or leaks the device's address, and can read local .ts/.mp4 files by path. KitePlayer always passes an opener, so it is not exposed; a direct KiteFFmpeg consumer following the README's MediaSource.open(io=...) example is.

**Impact:** Server-side-request-forgery and local file read from media content on every platform that has FFmpeg's http and file protocols, which is every published target except the web.

**Suggested fix:** In ffkmp_fmt_open_input_io2, when no opener is given and the caller passed no protocol_whitelist, set protocol_whitelist to "data,crypto" (or "none"), so a byte-source input reaches nothing by itself and the opener is the one door; let DemuxOptions.protocolWhitelist widen it explicitly. Document the change in DemuxOptions and docs/decoding.md.

**How to check it yourself:** Write a one-line M3U8 naming http://127.0.0.1:<port>/seg.ts into a byte array, open it with MediaSource.open(io = ..., nestedOpener = null) on the JVM, and watch a local listener on that port receive the GET. Then set DemuxOptions(protocolWhitelist = setOf("none")) and see the open fail instead.

**Verifier's note:** The evidence is as cited. helpers_format.c:1416-1417 `int built = kc_open_options(keys, values, n, &options, &forced); if (built >= 0 && opener) built = av_dict_set(&options, KC_TRUST_IO_OPEN_KEY, "1", 0);` is the only option assembly, and kc_open_options (lines 140-156) only copies the caller's pairs and refuses trust_io_open and the forced-format key; nothing sets protocol_whitelist. Without an opener, c->io_open stays FFmpeg's default (the `if (opener)` block at 1403-1409 is the only override). DemuxOptions.kt:31-35 documents `protocolWhitelist ... empty allows all`, and `grep -rn protocol_whitelist kiteffmpeg/src*` finds no other writer, so the Kotlin open path adds none. kc_fuzz.h:110-112 states the harness passes `protocol_whitelist=none` so 'A playlist or a reference inside the input then cannot make FFmpeg open a file or a network address'. The build has http enabled (BuildFFmpegTask.kt:387 `--enable-protocol=file,fd,pipe,data,http,tcp,udp,rtp,rtmp`). Upstream hls.c n9.0.2 open_url (lines 705-720) allows file (with the allowed_extensions check), http (`is_http = 1`) and data, which matches docs/decoding.md:56-57. An AVIOContext from avio_alloc_context has no protocol_whitelist, and avformat_open_input copies the whitelist only from an existing pb whitelist, so the nested io_open_default runs unrestricted. No guard found in the tree. This mirrors stock FFmpeg's behaviour for custom IO and the docs state what the HLS reader may reach, so it is a design gap (the default is open) rather than a defect, which is how the finding is filed. KitePlayer is unaffected because it always passes an opener, which the finding already says.
