### Lane: kiteffmpeg-c-and-build

The C layer is in better shape than most FFmpeg bindings I have read. The opaque boundary (three headers, no libav type crosses), the generation-tagged handle table shared by JNI and the web, the identity gate, the bounded string builders, the per-thread swscale cache with a destructor, the premultiplied palette conversion, the Dolby Vision composer and the keyframe-landing seek are each careful about ownership and error paths, and the comments say what a reader needs. I found no memory-safety defect in the helper units, the handle table or the JNI adapter on a full read: buffer lengths from FFmpeg are checked, failure paths free what they allocated, JNI local references are released inside loops, exceptions are checked before the next JNI call, and the critical-region rule is honoured everywhere except the caption path already filed as #207. The patches are small, well explained, and stay inside the bounds FFmpeg's own parsers keep; the two that touch parsing (HLS variables, Matroska payload export) are length-checked.

The structural weakness is at the edges of the custom I/O bridge, which is the path every KitePlayer https stream takes. Three things sit there. First, the trust_io_open patch changes one upstream invariant (the HLS reader now believes no nested source is HTTP), and the bridge does not read the byte-range options FFmpeg hands it, so an AES-128 playlist with EXT-X-BYTERANGE segments decrypts from the wrong point with an unseekable crypto wrapper: wrong first block, padding kept, and a full-file re-read per segment. Second, a byte-source open without a nested opener has no protocol whitelist at all, so a playlist handed over as bytes can make FFmpeg open http addresses and local media files of the file's choosing; the fuzz harness guards itself with protocol_whitelist=none, the product does not. Third, the web FFmpeg carries no data protocol, yet the bridge routes data: URLs around the opener to FFmpeg, so an HLS key in a data: URI works on every target except the browser.

The second structural worry is evidence, not code. The C suite that exercises the nested opener and the hand-written AES-CBC/PKCS#7 reader runs in CI only against Homebrew's FFmpeg, which lacks the patch, so those cases print a note and skip; the replay corpus and the fuzzers link Ubuntu's FFmpeg 6.1. Nothing in CI executes the project's own decryption code or the HLS-through-bytes path at the C level against the FFmpeg that ships. The Kotlin contract tests cover plain HLS against the vendored tree, which is why this has not shown up.

On the build, the recipe is reproducible in the ways the owner designed (pinned commits, pristine checkouts, patch evidence inside each tree, a configure fingerprint check, an SPDX document) and the LGPL story is honest about static linking. The gap is that only the Apple profiles pass --disable-autodetect; Android, Linux and Windows let configure take whatever the sysroot offers, which is how GNU libiconv became a Windows link dependency without a decision, and the recipe check compares flags, so a sysroot bump that adds or drops an autodetected component would pass every gate. Smaller items: the desktop JNI libraries are linked without the hardening flags the Android ones get, the helper archive has no stack protector anywhere, and the JNI log forwarder attaches and detaches a JVM thread for every line FFmpeg's worker threads log.

If I were to rewrite one thing it would be the nested-open contract: hand the opener the byte range FFmpeg asked for (offset and end_offset), make the AES wrapper seek-capable by re-keying at the segment start, and give byte-source opens a closed default whitelist that the opener widens. The single biggest risk to the ambition is that the custom I/O path, which is the whole network story on every platform, is validated against the shipped FFmpeg only through Kotlin tests of the happy path.

### Lane: kiteffmpeg-kotlin-api

The Kotlin binding is, in the main, carefully built. The ownership story is consistent and unusually explicit: frames and packets are closeable handles with per-object locks on the JVM and native, the JNI side never hands out raw pointers (generation-tagged tokens, kind-checked), the flow operators (`bufferFrames`, `FilterGraph.process`, `audioForEncoder`) are hand-written so a frame is either delivered or closed on every cancellation path, byte sources are owned by the source that opened them and closed exactly once with the caller's exception carried as the cause, and the C helper layer polls the interrupt cell between byte-source reads so FFmpeg's own blind spots are covered. The send/receive loops handle EAGAIN and EOF correctly on all three backends, the keyframe seek in C (`kc_seek_keyframe`) fixes a real FFmpeg landing problem and is pinned by a contract test on MP4, Matroska and MPEG-TS, and the async runtime's lane has a defensible cancellation model with tests that prove a cancelled read never writes into a buffer FFmpeg reads. The decode contract suite running the same bytes through JNI, cinterop and the wasm module is the right shape for a three-backend library.

What is structurally weak is the uneven application of the invariants across the three backends. The JVM backend holds its state lock across the native seek and across decoder opens because a concurrent close would otherwise free the context mid-call, and says so in a comment; the native backend checks the flag and then releases the lock before calling into FFmpeg, so the same race it was written to prevent is open on macOS, iOS, Linux and Windows, and `interrupt()` after `close()` reads a freed context there while the JVM throws a typed error and the web returns quietly. Error mapping is similarly uneven: the web decoder path maps every failure to `Internal` with code 0 while the other two use the typed table, and that table itself leaves the errors a player most wants to match (a network timeout, a connection refusal, the ENOSYS a missing hardware accelerator returns, whose number differs per platform) as `AvError` with a raw platform-dependent integer. Each of these is small, but together they mean a consumer cannot write one piece of error handling or one lifecycle sequence for all platforms, which is the whole promise of a multiplatform binding.

The second structural concern is the async runtime's lane. Every operation of a runtime, including copying or closing a frame that has nothing to do with the demuxer, waits behind whatever demux call is parked on a byte source. On the web that is close to unavoidable with one module; on the JVM, Android and native it is a choice, because `Frame` has its own lock and no dependency on the `AVFormatContext`. For a player on a stalling live stream this means the picture cannot be read while the read waits, which is the shape of KitePlayer's open issue #568 and will reappear on every platform that uses the runtime.

Smaller things worth fixing because they cost real time or mislead: `extractFrame` and a trimmed `Transcoder` still seek five seconds early and decode forward, a back-off whose justification (MPEG-TS overshoot) the C keyframe seek has since removed, so every thumbnail decodes up to five seconds of video it throws away; `DemuxOptions.ioTimeoutMicros` promises a timeout for every network read but only sets `rw_timeout`, which RTSP, RTP and UDP ignore; the JNI log forwarder attaches and detaches a JVM thread for every line FFmpeg logs from a worker thread; and `Frame` has no leak diagnostic at all beyond an internal test counter, so a leaked 4K frame (25 MB) is invisible until the process dies. The public surface is almost entirely `data class`es with many defaulted parameters, so each new field is a binary break for compiled consumers, the same problem KitePlayer already tracks for itself.

If I were to rewrite one thing it would be the native `MediaSource` so that it mirrors the JVM's locking discipline exactly (one `withContext(lock) { checkOpen(); nativeCall }` shape shared by both), and I would make the three backends' error mapping one common function fed by the raw code. The single biggest risk to the ambition is not any one bug but the drift between backends: the contract suite proves bytes and timestamps agree, but nothing proves that locking, lifetime and error typing agree, and those are what a player built on top will trip over on the platform the owner tests least.

### Lane: design-capabilities-crossmatch

The shape of the engine is right and unusually disciplined for a player this young: one Kotlin actor owns every decision, the SPI in kiteplayer-core is genuinely backend-free (the FFmpeg backend is one implementation and the scripted one in commonTest proves the contract), the module graph does what docs/module-contract.md says it does (kiteplayer-adaptive has no Ktor import, kiteplayer-compose-ui builds no player, the view bindings sit below construction), and the config surface is validated once at construction instead of being silently ignored later. ABR, trick-play thumbnails, A-B loop, frame stepping, chapters, markers, recording, typed DRM refusal, time-of-day seeking and a media session on four of five platforms are all wired end to end. That is a wider feature set than Media3 or AVPlayer expose, and closer to mpv's.

The structural weakness is that the player grew by adding defaulted members to its interfaces. VideoRenderer has 20 members and 13 of them default to a no-op or false; PlayerMediaSource has about 25 defaulted members. That keeps third-party backends compiling, but it means every capability degrades silently: setRenderQuality does nothing on the default Android view and the desktop AWT view, HDR shows only through two of fourteen renderers, the Android MediaCodec path drops picture adjustments while answering appliesAdjustments = true, and a backend that leaves interrupt() defaulted turns stallTimeout into a dead knob with no warning. The docs still say "the player refuses anything it cannot do with a typed error", and for the whole renderer side that is not true. The fix is one pattern applied everywhere #610 applied it to adjustments: a capability flag per silent member, and a warning when the player holds a value the renderer will not draw.

The config knobs mostly do not collide with each other, but they collide with hidden constants in other modules. "The server went quiet" is answered by four different timers with three different error types depending on which transport happened to open the item: BufferPolicy.stallTimeout in the engine, HttpReaderPolicy.readTimeout times maxReconnects in the automatic Ktor provider (hard-coded defaults, no path from PlayerConfig), a fixed 10 s in the FFmpeg URL fallback, and on the web worker the same stallTimeout misapplied as a whole-request XHR deadline over windows of up to 16 MiB, which fails slow links that are still delivering. DemuxPolicy.lowLatency and BufferPolicy.readyDuration are two knobs for one goal that do not know about each other, and readyDuration doubles as the live-edge delay target. These are the things I would fix first, because each one produces a wrong error on a real user's screen.

The largest single risk to the ambition is the web target: network media on the web only plays in the worker, and the worker accepts no PlayerConfig, no memento, no thumbnails, no renderer attach, and carries 120 KB of Ktor it never calls because the worker runtime lives inside the umbrella module. A go-to library cannot have its most constrained platform also be the one where every configuration surface is unreachable. Second is the PlaybackCore file itself: at 17,351 lines its rules are already written more than once (the gapless eligibility predicate exists in three variants with three different exclusion lists; the speed bounds exist as two pairs of constants), and the next contributor will add a fourth variant. A single predicate per rule, named and tested, is cheap now and expensive later.

Against mpv, VLC, Media3 and AVPlayer: KitePlayer has ABR, DRM refusal (not playback), picture in picture everywhere, media session everywhere but desktop JVM, hardware decode on Android, Apple and Windows (unproven on real hardware) but not Linux, HDR only through the native Metal and Android codec paths, subtitle rendering in two tiers plus libass, trick play, chapters, playlists, speed with pitch, A-B loop, frame step, and analytics through stats, events and KiteTrace. Missing outright: casting, audio passthrough (#180), spatial audio (#699), offline download (#680), low-latency HLS (#458), 3D (#697), live seek-back (#677). That is a credible position for a sub-1.0 library; what separates it from mpv today is less the feature list than the number of places where a feature exists on one renderer and silently does not on another.

## Appendix B. Claims examined and refuted

A finder raised each of these and a verifier who re-read the code rejected it. They are kept so the same claim is not raised again without new evidence, and because the verifier's reasoning is itself a small piece of documentation.

- **The audio sink event feed is collected only after the device is open, so an event published between open and startWorkers is lost on a no-replay flow** (engine-subtitles-output-tail). Verifier: The cited code exists as quoted: startAudioEventCollector (PlaybackCore.kt 13736-13740) launches the collector from startWorkers (13733), and the sink is created and opened earlier in the build (4384-4400). But every shipped sink already guards the window, and the only emitter of FormatChangeRequested keeps it. CoreAudioSink.kt 295-299: `What the route changed to, when a sink opened now would get another channel count than this one has, until a collector takes it (#563). Kept like [pendingNoisy], because the engine opens a new output on it and a dropped one would leave surround playing into two speakers.` and 309-315: `override val events: Flow<AudioSinkEvent> = eventFlow.onSubscription { failedWith.value?.let { emit(AudioSinkEvent.Failed(it)) }; emit(RouteTick) }.transform { event -> pendingNoisy...; pendingFormat.getAndSet(null)?.let { emit(AudioSinkEvent.FormatChangeRequested(it)) } ...`. No other sink emits FormatChangeRequested at all (rg over kiteplayer-output: AudioTrackSink, DesktopAudioSink, WebAudioSink have no such emit), so the macOS scenario is the only one and it is kept. Failed is kept too: DesktopAudioSink.kt 112-118 `Why this sink cannot play again, or null. Kept as well as sent, so a late collector cannot miss it.` with `onSubscription { failedWith.get()?.let { emit(AudioSinkEvent.Failed(it)) } }`. DeviceLost on Android and desktop is emitted only from the writer thread inside write (AudioTrackSink.kt 473-474, DesktopAudioSink.kt 435-436), which runs only after the feed worker started, i.e. after startWorkers; AudioTrackSink.kt 411-413 names this exact trap as already handled: `Said from here, once for the sink, and not from open: the engine listens to the events only once the session that opened the device exists, and a flow with no listener drops what it is given (#445).` The proposed check (publish FormatChangeRequested from inside the fake's open) would test a fake that violates what the real sinks do, not the engine. What remains is a documentation gap only: AudioSink.kt documents the keep-until-taken rule for BecameNoisy (273-274) but the FormatChangeRequested (281-293) and Failed (300-304) KDoc do not say a sink must keep them for a late collector, so a third-party sink could drop one.
- **CHANGELOG [Unreleased] lists fixes for issues the tracker still shows open** (public-api-and-docs). Verifier: The cited lines exist as quoted: CHANGELOG.md:264 "A `MediaItem.videoFilter` and the deinterlacer apply on the Android views too (#609).", :278 "The Android video Surface's frame rate request follows a new item and a new speed (#598).", :367-368 "A live fMP4 HLS stream with two or more variants no longer stops at its first advertisement (#621)." The GitHub REST API (gh api repos/yuroyami/KitePlayer/issues/N) answers for all three: "state":"open","state_reason":"reopened". The issue events show each was closed on 2026-11-02T05:03 by the commit that carries `Fixes #n` in its body (b119644 "Keep a stream that needs a filter off the renderer's own decoder" for #609, 68259cc "Ask the display again for a new stream or speed on the same Surface" for #598, d8c6d1a for #621), and reopened by the owner about twenty seconds later with a comment of the form "Reopened: the merge of yuroyami/KitePlayer#694 closed this through <sha>'s message. <what the fix did>. Still open: <residue>." The residues are: #609 "the backend's decoder options still do not reach a renderer's decoder"; #598 "an item that simply ends keeps its frame-rate request until the next picture or a stop"; #621 "one initialization for each map is not served". So neither horn of the claim holds. The issues were not "fixed and not closed": the closing commits said Fixes #n exactly as the project rule asks, and the owner reopened them on purpose to hold the named leftover. The entries do not "overstate partial fixes": each describes only what the commit did, the headline symptom in each issue title is what the entry says was fixed, and the #621 entry itself says "The advertisement itself is not played; a switch that serves one map per discontinuity is the fuller fix." The scenario that "the owner closes a release with issues marked fixed that are not" is wrong on the facts: the owner is the one who reopened them and wrote down what remains. The only thing left is a wording nit, that the #609 and #598 entries do not say the issue stays open for a residue the way the #621 entry does, which is a matter of taste and not an inconsistency a reader trips on, since the issue page carries the explanation.
- **Every HLS and DASH segment reader is leaked until the item closes, because hls.c keeps the previous input open on the persistent path and the nested opener drops the stale pointer without closing it.** (network-adaptive-io). Verifier: The claim rests on hls.c taking the http_persistent path (input_read_done kept, open_url reusing *pb). In FFmpeg n9.0.2 (fetched libavformat/hls.c at tag n9.0.2, the pin named in KiteFFmpeg/.github/workflows/ci.yml:48), hls_read_header turns that path off for exactly this configuration, lines 2279-2286: `if (!ffio_geturlcontext(s->pb)) { if (c->http_persistent) { av_log(s, AV_LOG_WARNING, "Disabling http_persistent due to custom io_open.\n"); c->http_persistent = 0; }`. avio.c 107-116: `if (s->opaque && s->read_packet == ffurl_read2) return s->opaque; else return NULL;`. The nested opener is installed only in ffkmp_fmt_open_input_io2 (helpers_format.c 1406-1412, `if (opener) { ... c->io_open = kc_io_open_nested; c->io_close2 = kc_io_close_nested; }`), whose s->pb is `avio_alloc_context(buffer, KC_IO_BUFFER_SIZE, 0, bridge, kc_io_read_packet, NULL, seek_fn ? kc_io_seek : NULL)` (1389-1391), so read_packet is never ffurl_read2 and http_persistent is 0 for every HLS or DASH item opened through the Kotlin transport. With http_persistent 0, read_data_continuous ends every segment through `} else { ff_format_io_close(v->parent, &v->input); }` (hls.c 1861-1863), which calls kc_io_close_nested (helpers_format.c 1301-1311: `kc_io_nested_unlink(p, n); kc_io_nested_free(n);`), and parse_playlist closes each playlist read (`close_in = 1`, 867). The one path that keeps an input open, `segment_reusable` (1193-1203, consecutive byte ranges of one seekable file), is consumed by the next open_input with `avio_seek(*in, seg->url_offset, SEEK_SET)` on the same input (1461-1476) and closes it when that seek fails. `*pb = NULL` in kc_io_open_nested (1228) therefore never overwrites a live input, and kc_io_bridge_free's sweep is a safety net, not the release path. The patch's `is_http` staying 0 is real but changes nothing here, because the branches it guards are all also conditioned on http_persistent. The Kotlin and store evidence (BlockingMediaIo per address, BytesMediaIo, MemoryMediaIo, the holders filter) describes normal per-segment allocation that the close path frees.
- **readableFrame() races on downloadedTwin: two threads reading one hardware frame can download it twice and leak the first copy** (ffmpeg-backend). Verifier: The code is as quoted: KiteFFmpegSource.kt:1819 `private var downloadedTwin: KiteFrame? = null`, :1832 `return downloadedTwin ?: frame.downloadFromHardware().also { downloadedTwin = it }`, lazies at :1840 and :1843-1845, close at :1867-1871; and the class makes no thread-safety claim. But the scenario the finding needs, the renderer converting a frame while captureFrame reads the same frame on another thread, does not exist in the engine. The capture copy is taken on the video lane before the frame reaches the renderer: VideoPlayback.kt:480-486 `// The capture copies BEFORE ownership moves: from the renderer's first instruction the frame may be recycled into a decoder pool, and a headless present closes it outright.` / `captureRequest.getAndSet(null)?.let { request -> runCatching { CapturedFrame.of(frame)... } }`, and PlaybackCore.kt:11548-11550 says the same ('the copy is always taken at the presentation boundary, before ownership moves to the renderer'). CapturedFrame.of (CapturedFrame.kt:108-145) copies every plane into plain arrays right there and holds no reference to the frame afterwards. Snapshots.kt:124 (`tightlyPackedPlanes`) runs on its own decode of a thumbnail, not on a presented frame. CLAUDE.md's invariant is single ownership: 'Frames and packets are closeable, closed exactly once, on the worker that owns them.' So within the engine a frame is read by exactly one thread at a time, and the double download cannot happen. A third-party renderer that itself fans one frame out to two threads could trigger it, but that is not what the finding or the SPI (SoftwareReadableFrame, VideoFrame.kt:142-173, which promises nothing about concurrent readers) describes. At most an info note that the twin cache is not thread-safe and relies on single ownership.
- **MediaItem.openOptions reach FFmpeg with no allowlist, which KiteFFmpeg's own notes say breaks MP3 seeking when fast seek or the table of contents is set** (ffmpeg-backend). Verifier: The quoted code at KiteFFmpegMediaBackend.kt:176 and ItemSources.kt:147 exists, but the claim that fastseek and usetoc reach FFmpeg "with no warning" is wrong on two layers, and the owner's own grep recipe finds the first one. kiteplayer-core/src/io/github/yuroyami/kiteplayer/MediaItem.kt:197-214, in MediaItem's `init`: `refuseSeekBreakingOptions()` with `openOptions["fflags"]?.let { flags -> require(flags.split(',', '+').none { it.trim() == "fastseek" }) { "openOptions fflags=$flags: fastseek breaks exact seeking and is never applied" } }` and `require("usetoc" !in openOptions) { "openOptions usetoc: the engine owns MP3 seek strategy and this key is never applied" }`. So `MediaItem(uri, openOptions = mapOf("fflags" to "+fastseek"))` throws IllegalArgumentException before any open. Below that, KiteFFmpeg refuses the same two keys on every open route: /home/user/KiteFFmpeg/kiteffmpeg/src/io/github/yuroyami/kiteffmpeg/AsyncLane.kt:424 `refuseSeekBreakingOptions(options)` inside the byte-source open, and DemuxOptions.kt:96-110 throws `FFmpegError.InvalidArgument(... "Refused open option ... MP3 seeking is only correct with the table of contents unused and fast seek unset")`, whose KDoc at :16-17 says "Two keys are refused on every route, typed or raw". That is exactly the rule the KiteFFmpeg CLAUDE.md line states, and both repositories enforce it as a denylist of the two keys that matter. The finding's check "grep -n fastseek -r kiteplayer-ffmpeg/src kiteplayer-core/src: no guard" is false; that grep hits MediaItem.kt:208-213. The scenario "seeks land off by seconds" cannot happen because the item cannot be constructed.
- **On the web, KiteVideo rebuilds its GL programs whenever the render target changes size** (views-compose-ui-samples). Verifier: The finding is conditional on `rememberWebGLRenderTarget(size)` returning a new object when its size changes, and it does not. The project uses Compose Multiplatform 1.13.0-alpha02 (compose.module-template.yaml line 5). In that version's `compose/ui/ui/src/webMain/kotlin/androidx/compose/ui/platform/webgl/WebGLRenderTarget.web.kt` (identical on tag v1.13.0-alpha02 and jb-main), lines 383-400 read: `val renderTarget = remember(window) { ... WebGLRenderTarget(..., initialSize = size) } ?: return null` then `SideEffect(size) { renderTarget.requestNewSize(size) }` and `DisposableEffect(renderTarget) { onDispose { renderTarget.dispose() } }`. The target is remembered on the window only; a new size is applied through `requestNewSize` (line 121 `requestedSize = size.coerceAtLeastOnePixel()`) on the same object, and its KDoc (line 373) says `a changed [size] reallocates its GPU resources on the next [WebGLRenderTarget.render]`, the framebuffer `is created once and remains stable for the target's lifetime`. So in KiteVideo.wasmJs.kt line 47 `remember(target) { ... WebGlVideoPass(it.webGLContext) }` keeps the same pass across resizes, `glvCreate` runs once, no programs are relinked and `uploadedPicture` is not reset. The file's own KDoc (line 34) `a resize redraws it from the texture the node keeps` matches. Only the target's own colour attachment is reallocated on resize, which is the cost the finding's suggested counter would not see rise.
- **Web subtitle images are premultiplied in the rasterizer, un-premultiplied in the canvas renderer and premultiplied again by putImageData, losing precision on soft edges** (web-worker-wasm-libass). Verifier: The quoted code exists: WebSubtitleRasterizer.kt:507-513 premultiplies with `Math.round(data[i] * a / 255)`, and WebCanvasVideoRenderer.kt:579-597 `straightAlphaLatin1` divides back with `minOf(255, (value * 255 + alpha / 2) / alpha)` before `putImageData`. But the claim that this round trip loses precision or shifts hue on screen is a misreading of what the canvas stores. A 2D canvas backing store is 8-bit premultiplied, so `putImageData` re-premultiplies the straight bytes, and that step restores the rasterizer's premultiplied byte exactly: for premultiplied value p and alpha a (1..254), s = floor((p*255 + floor(a/2)) / a) satisfies |s*a - p*255| <= floor(a/2) < 128, so round(s*a/255) = p for every p and a. The finding's own example shows it: colour 200 at alpha 3 premultiplies to 2, divides back to 170, and the canvas stores round(170*3/255) = 2, the same byte a GL upload of the premultiplied bitmap gives. The '170 versus 200' difference exists only in the straight-alpha intermediate, which no compositor ever displays; what reaches the screen is value times alpha, and 170*3/255 and 200*3/255 differ by 0.35 of one 8-bit step. The only rounding is the first one, to 8-bit premultiplied, and that is the project's stated contract ('The cue alpha contract is premultiplied end to end'), shared by every renderer; the canvas path is not worse than the GL path. Keeping straight alpha for the canvas would change nothing either, because the browser's backing store would quantise to the same premultiplied byte. `WebOverlayAlphaTest` (kiteplayer-output/test@wasmJs/.../WebOverlayAlphaTest.kt) pins the division's round-to-nearest, and #607 is the reason the division exists (without it a half-alpha white edge drew at a quarter of its light). The owner's proposed check (compare straight-alpha bytes with the canvas's original `getImageData`) would show a difference in the straight domain and prove nothing about the picture; a fair check composites both paths and compares the final pixels, which match.
- **The gapless eligibility rule is written three times with three different exclusion lists.** (design-capabilities-crossmatch). Verifier: The three functions exist as quoted (joinTarget 9874-9877, passMayFollow 10102-10109, crossfadeOutUs 10914-10918), but they are not three statements of one decision; they decide three different things and are layered, and the differences are documented. passMayFollow decides whether a preload may open; crossfadeOutUs decides how long a fade may be and is only ever reached after passMayFollow passed: maybeStartPreload calls `if (!passMayFollow(active, index)) return` at 10534 and then `crossfadeOutUs(active, repeat)` at 10540, and the other caller crossfadeIntoUs (10926) takes a `PendingNext` that only exists once a preload was allowed. Its repeated `gapless && preloadNext > 0` clause is redundant, not divergent. joinTarget decides a join on the current item's reads for parts of one file, a third mechanism; its A-B loop and LoopMode.One exclusions are not missing from passMayFollow because maybeStartPreload handles those cases itself via `repeat` (10530-10533) and passes `queueIndex`. Each guard set is written down with its reason in docs/gapless-queue.md: the preload rules at 54-64 (sleep timer, seekable, duration known, not a still image), the crossfade rules at 222-232 (runsIntoNext, next queue item only, no picture, stated length not an estimate "because the fade starts that long before it"), and the join rules at 318-320 (LoopMode.One, an armed A-B loop, SleepTimer.EndOfItem, next item preloading). crossfadeOutUs's own KDoc (10911-10912) says "Only the current item's side of the rules in docs/gapless-queue.md". The scenario is also wrong: a new exclusion added to crossfadeOutUs alone makes it return null, which per docs:223 means "the join is the gapless one, with nothing warned, because a missing fade is not a failure"; it cannot produce a GaplessFallback. The only true residue is that the two-clause core (`gapless && preloadNext > 0`) is spelled three times and could be one named predicate, which is cosmetic.
- **Refusals of a command arrive as three plain exception types and a warning, while open failures are typed, contrary to the documented one-error-model.** (design-capabilities-crossmatch). Verifier: The quoted code exists as cited (PlaybackCore.kt:2768-2800, :2901; PlaybackError.kt:679; KitePlayer.kt:1650-1656), but the claim that this is contrary to a documented one-error model is wrong: the two channels are the documented model. KitePlayer.kt:53-60, the class KDoc's "### Errors" section: "A suspending call that fails throws [PlaybackException], which carries the typed [PlaybackError]. ... A call made in the wrong order, or with a value outside its documented range, throws [IllegalStateException], [IllegalArgumentException] or [UnsupportedOperationException] instead: those are mistakes in the calling code, not failures of the media or the device, and telling them apart is what lets an application decide whether to show the user anything." Every cited refusal is declared on its member: seek's KDoc at KitePlayer.kt:203-206 lists all three, selectVariant's at :1650-1655 lists all four, and docs/spi-cookbook.md:152-153 says startRecording without RecordingCapable "throws UnsupportedOperationException". The worker facade restates the same four types (KitePlayerWorker.kt:42-46). Issue #654 (closed), which the finding cites as precedent, enforced this exact rule: its body reads "a suspending call that fails throws PlaybackException ... and mistakes in the calling code throw the standard IllegalStateException, IllegalArgumentException or UnsupportedOperationException. readPlaylist and openPlaylist break the rule" because they threw a plain PlaylistException outside both channels. docs/player-api.md:39 says "a typed error, instead of accepting the call and ignoring it", which an UnsupportedOperationException satisfies; nothing in player-api.md suggests `catch (PlaybackException)` alone. The scenario also overstates: a CompletableFuture from KitePlayerJava that completes exceptionally does not crash an app that fails to match it. Preferring one sealed hierarchy over the standard exceptions is a taste the owner already decided against in the class KDoc, and the finding brings no new evidence.

## Appendix C. Claims that duplicate an open issue

- **Every Duration-typed member is unusable from Swift because kotlin.time.Duration crosses as its raw Int64 encoding** (public-api-and-docs): 393. Verifier: The cited code is as quoted: `public suspend fun seek(to: Duration, mode: SeekMode = SeekMode.Precise)` (KitePlayer.kt 209), `requestSeek(to: Duration, ...)` (228), `SleepTimer.After(val duration: Duration)` / `At(val position: Duration)` (PlayerState.kt 243-246), and MediaItemBuilder.kt 10-12 says Java cannot call the MediaItem constructor because of Duration. No millisecond helper exists outside the JVM/Android: `grep -rln Millis` over kiteplayer/src@apple, src@ios, src@macos and kiteplayer-core/src@native finds nothing, and kiteplayer-core has no src@apple folder. But KitePlayer #393 ('The player needs a Swift package with an API that feels native in Swift') already states this exact gap: 'Durations. Every position and length is a kotlin.time.Duration, which reaches Swift as an opaque number instead of a TimeInterval or a Swift Duration', and its plan says 'TimeInterval or Swift Duration wherever the Kotlin API takes or returns a kotlin.time.Duration'. The same issue also records that no library module declares a framework and nothing builds an XCFramework, so a Swift consumer today builds its own framework, which lowers the exposure the finding describes. The finding adds only the detail that the Int64 is Duration's raw bit encoding and that millisecond helpers could bridge the gap before the Swift layer exists; it does not change what #393 already tracks.
